Your lozenges have done wonders in relieving my terrible cough. Since I had the operation of • Tracheotomy (the same as the late Emperor of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still alive) per- formed at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, no ono eould possibly 'have had a more violent cough ; it was so bad at times that it quite exhausted me. The mucus, which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I have been able to get rid of it without difficulty.--I am, sir, your truly. J. HILL.

MEDICAL NOTE. The above speaks for itself. From strict inquiry it appears the benefit from using Keating's Cough Lozenges is under- stated. The operation was a specially severe one, and was performed by the specialist, Dr. H. T. Butlin, of St. Bartho- lomew's Hospital. Since the operation the only means of relief is the use of these Lozenges. So successful are they that one affords immediate benefit, althoegh from the nature of the case the throat irritation is intense. UNRIVALLED TESTIMONY. Under date Sept. 8, 1891, Mr. Hill writes : " I should long since have been dead, but for your Lozenges—They are wcrtl, their weight in gold. I will gladly see and tell anyone what a splendid cough remedy they are." Keating's Lozenges are sold in tins, is. lad. each. The un- rivalled semedy for COUGHS,HOARSENESS, and THROAT TROUBLES.

LORD ELDON, in allusion to Lord Stowell's love •of good things, which induced him to dine in the Temple Hall at five, by way of a whet for an eight o'clock dinner at the west end of the town, would say, "My brother takes regular exercise twice a-day —in eating." HUSBAND—" Well, ,my dear, did you see some beautiful things on your mountain excursion?" Wife-----" No. The guide told me to look where I walked; so all I was. able to see was my boots." Six GEORGE BOSE, being introduced one day to two charming young ladies, whose names were Mary and Louisa, instantly added, with a bow, " Ah, yes, Marie-Louise—sweetest pear I know"—a compli- ment almost worthy of being coupled with that most beautiful one of .4ydney Smith, suggested by the sweet pea. Ix Turkestan every 'wedding engagement begins with the paymentof a substantial consideration to the girl's parents. If the girl jilts her lover the engagement gift has to be returned, unless the parents have another daughter to give as a sub- stitute. The 'plan is said to work well, and results in few divorces.

John—" lam only trying to console myself for my loss." Count—" And how long is this goingto last r John—" Oh, sir, 'I aan inconsolable!".

JUDGE (to negro woman, who had been sum- moned as a witness)—" Is this-man your husband?" Woman—" He's my step-husban'." Judge—" What?" Woman—"l says that gennerman is my step- husban'." Judge--,-" How do you make that out 7" Woman—" Wall, sah, yer see, dat jes' 'bout de time my Lust husban' wuz buried, dis gennerman • come steppin' er long, an' I.married him."

LADY of the thouse--" Will you have the • steak now, or wait till you've chopped the wood?" Coloured tramp (who'd called at same place twelve months before)--" Is de steak de same kind as you geb away Las' year?" Lady—" Yes." Tramp— " Well, den, I'll -chop de wood first so as to git me appetite enuff to-tackle it Whar's de are 7" SOME years age a grammarian gave a conjugation of the verb "kiss" as follows :—" 'Buss,' to kiss; 'rebus,' to kiss again— pluribus,' to kiss without regard-to number; silly7bus, to kiss the hand instead of the lips; 'blunderbuss",' to kiss the wrong per- son.; 'omnibus,' to kiss everybody in the room; • erebus,' to kiss in,the, dark." WHEN Sir George Rose was dining one day-with some friends, the out-door servants had been enlisted into the service of the dining-room; and It chanced that-one of them, in carrying out a tray a glass, as he left the room stumbled and fell with a heavy crash, "What is -that?" exclaimed Sir George's next door neighbour, in great alarm. "Oh, nothing," he replied; "only the coachman gone -out with his break."

ON one occasion, when a new -serjeant had been -created, and it became his duty, according to cus- tom, to present rings to the judges, insoribed with the usual brief" posy" in Latin, Sir George Rose -indicated k•is appreciation of the then-existing corn. pany of sergeants by suggesting for-the 'motto in .question, "Scilicet " (Silly set). RICHARD COODEN once asked, speakine, in his noble, upright fashion, and thinking of abfamous, -successful and unscrupulous statesman—" How will it be with him when all is retrospect 7" This is the great touchstone of life—how it looks when regarded, through all its loner porspective, at a time when its chief actor has little or no power to add to .or improve the pictxre. ELIJAH—" Say, Zeke, I hear yo' brudder married rich heiress; am dat so ?" Zeke—" Yes, she 's wuth 'bout fi' million." Elijah (surprised)—" So much as dat 7" Zeke---" It 's fi' million or fi' hun- dred, I duuno which. but I know it 's 'normous 'mount."

What sort of lute.k did you have ?" M. Bt. John—" Well, I scared up seven partridges." Miss S.—" How many did you shoot ?" Mr. St. -John—" I did not hag any, of course. for I had my sniping suit on, don' you know!" SOME Oxford students ring a much-beloved professor's bell at midnight. He puts his head out of the window, and waits to know what's up. of your windows is wide open." "Which 7' exclaimed the startled professor. "The one you are looking out of," was the tantalising reply. "Do you think a simpleton, sir?" thundered a fiery Scotch laird to his new footman. "Ye see, sir," replied the canny cot 7, "I'm no' lang her and I dinna ken vet."

Aw've no idea wod thingell come to iz.;a. bit, but mi own private opinion is as th' clerk o'th' weather 'ill ged a month's nooatice afoore so varra long iv things doesn'd awter. Fancy that <facial givin' orders for a tooathri weeks' sun belle supplied to this planet, an' no rain—nod one clrop—ov o' th' time, so heaw mony theawsand paysons prayed for a swap; an' then fancy us poor mortals (as hes olez heal to put up wais arrangements) bein' able to bring rain deawn by machinery. Id Wks Prometheus bringin' deawn tire fro' heaven. There'll be no swore grumblin' fro' th' fermers abeawt th' crops wantin' wayter, an' there'll be one excuse less for some on us suppirf so much " booze " th' summer time on ackeawnt o' th scarcity o' wayter. An' still some o' t 42 Tappers isn'd 6happy. Wod they want neaw is another machine as 'ill werk back'ards rooad an' stop th' rain comin' deawn when id isn'd wanted, an' aw darsay a machine o' thad soort wad tek i' every pert o' th' world, an' mek th' patentee a fortune; becose, yo' know, sich places as Blackpool, an' Ireland, an' Scotland, an' the Lakes wod be able to put on viler trip bills " _Fine weather vuaranteed." _ _ _ _ _ . .
Thad wod fotch fooak, th' machine wod be bowt, even iv they were ifty theawsand peawnd apiece ; Wwod come in rayther expensive for th' Lakes, as tiowt less nor a ,dozen machines wod act, theere.

• But why nod manage wi' th' present machine? There couldn'd be owt better ayther for th' seeaside or th' lake side, for th' machines could be sent up every neet after twelve o'clock to lot deawn o' th' water as were hingin' abeawt, soon as there'd be nooan left to fo' th' next day; look heaw grand Lodore an' sich places wod be, then, to say nowt• o' th' comfort i' hein' able to goon to see id or ony other place beawt hevin' to tek mackintoshes goloshes, umbrells, leggin's, yigh, an' a life belt or two, r case yo' were wesht eawt th' the cooach. Aw mek th' country a present o' this idea, sooa happen American an' other pappers 'll kindly copy.
Aw mixt th' followin' dose o' brimstooam VW- her fleet, an' aw hooap idle do some fooak good.

NE'ER MIND WHAT THEY THINK. Yo' may nod do as others do, Becose yo're nod inclined; An' they may say as yO're a foo', Or owt else they'n a mind. Id may be yo've no wish to bet, Or wear.yo'r wage i' drink; But then—yore keepin' mot o' debt, Sooa ne'er mind wod they think. Yo' may nod veer to sell a mate For little bits o' gowd ; Yo' may nod harbour thowts o hate, Nor theft an' lies uphowd. Yo' may hie shown disgust for vice At which they nobbut wink; Iv sooa they're thowts'll nod be nice, But ne'er mind wod they think. Yo' may forgive a chap—an' oft— As ceawrdly blows hes struck, An' other fooak may co' yo' soft; An' say yo' hey no pluck. But, spite o' thad, iv yo're on land, An' see 'he's beawn to sink. Reych eawt a gradely helpin' hand, An',ne:er mind wod they think.

Yigh' iv a chap's on th' road to hell. Nod knowin' which is reight, Goo eawt o' th' way a bit yo'rsel' To show him th' rooad 'at's streight. Ne'er trouble at a harmless sneer, Nor fro' yo'r duty shrink; Keep up yo'r heart—there's nowt to fear Fro' wod o' th' world may think. * *

Aw see fro' th' noospappers as a mon an' his wife were committed for trial last Alonda' at Wolver- hampton, for th' manslaughter o' their little lad, four year owd.; th' evidence pointed to awful treat- ment o' th' child, an' as the coffin were bein' carried to th' grave th' Coroner interfered an' stopt th' fun- eral. Aw hooap th' parent's 'll be med a example on as a wernin' to others as callous an' inhuman as, they are. It's cases o' this soort as meks me put up wi' th idea o' sich societies as these for th' prevention o cruelty to childer, for aw ne'er wor so midi i' favour on 'em up th' last month or twv ; aw olez lookt on th' chaps as were connected wi"em as a lot o' meddlin busybodies as would be better employed mindin' their own bizness. Aw've just bin readin' th' repoort o'th' fost ten months' werk Blegburn bi th' society, an' id med mi blood run cowd, yigh, an' aw wondered iv id were possible for sich things to be:in a civilized country sich as England is. Eawt ov 112 cases (affectin' 365 childer) no less nor 84 were cases o' neglect, 13 ill-treatment, 2 abandon- ment, 2 exposure, etftttera. 1'24 o'th' cases there wur convictions, an' i'.79 th' parents werned ; eawt o' th' 365 childer mentioned 335 lived at hooam ? an' 165 on 'em were insured for o'er six hundred peawnd among 'em. Th' average wage o' these offenders torned thirty shillin', sooa id worn'd poverty as were th' cause o' th' neglect; but as th' Society's Inspector said, through th' parents Win' at th' factory o'th' day. an' at th' jerry-shop o'th' neet. One chap as dashed a little girl wean th' foot o'th' bed, an' P mashed id skull, simply becose id cried for milk' geet off wi' three month ! Yigh, an' th' child deed till he were i'. prison. Another brute nobbut geet two month for punchin' his step childer abeawt th' street like footbo's, an' tornin' his wife an' child i' street wnen th' child were deawn wi' th' maysles; an' this child deed till th' fayther were i' prison! A couple—fayther an' step-mother—nobbut had three month for welly stervin four o' their childer to deeath ' • th' heairse were varra cleyn, an' were fornished, but childer hed to eyt brokken bread an refuse as had bin thrown to th'nebbur's hens! FOOTBALL.

* * Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that rep.oe' ta of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-stmt, Warrington, liot later than ten o'clock on WednesdayMbrning.

the early portion of this half, failed to take advantage of a fine opening. Lawless got clear on one occasion, but Peters followed and brought him down in fine style. Nevins gained an apparently fair try, but a minor was the only point scored by Warrington this half, and a fine exhibition terminated as Warrington 1-2-1 to 0-1-0, or nine points to two.

Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back ; P. Lawless J. W. Evans, and H. Webster, three-quarter backs ; J.T. Bate and J. Bate, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Jolley, J. W. Nevins, J. Holmes, J. Berry, T. Dohohue, W. Handles, and A. Buckley, forwards. Widnes: J. Hartles, back ; H. Peters, D. Brennan, and H. Barber, three-quarter backs; W. Mullinger and J. Drummond, half backs; J. Hardman, C. Emery, J. Holmes, J. John- son, H. Farmer, A. Lyons, E. Gordon, J. Whelan, and G. Hewitt, forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Seddon, Brough- ton Rangers.

WARRIXOTON "A " v. WIDNES "A"—At Widnes. It was very little after the advertised time when Warring- ton, having lost the toss, started against the wind. There was nothing very brilliant for a start, although the home team forced the visitors back, and a long kick by Morris was allowed to roll dead. Dropping out, Warrington, chiefly through the instrumentality of Thornley, Davies, and Barber, made matters more even, and Potts further improved the state of affairs for his side. Taylor, by a long kick, gained a lot of ground, which was as quickly re-taken by Hampson, Barnes, and James, only to see the Vi'idnesians, with a vigorous rush, get to their opponents' line, and almost score. Although a temporary relief was effected by Knowles and Thornley, the ball was soon on the Warrington line, but ultimately, Heesom intercepting a pass, kicked finely to touch in neutral territory. For sotne time the game partook of a scrambling character, the Warrington forwards playing in anything but good style. Passing between Lally, Antrobus, and Potts carried the ball to midfield, where after Flampson, Teare, and Rowlands had been promin- ent, a splendid run by Daniels forced Widnes back on their goal line, and from a long kick a minor was con- ceded. Forster cleverly frustrated the visitors' backs, but was overtaken by Potts, and a splendid kick by Sampson neutralized the advantage gained. Antrobus and Lally then caused the leather to be taken to the Widnes half, but offside play by Warrington lost a lot of ground. Thornley by a run and kick found the game hovering around the home quarters, where from a free kick Samson made a fine attempt at goal, a minor ensu- ing. The first decent bit of combination by Warrington was shown at this stage, by a grand display of passing, but luckily for Widnes, the oval was held near the line. Antrobus, by some good passes, gave his side several opportunities, and after a dashing bit of loose play by llampson, a rush by Davies gained the coveted point. The rival backs then showed their kicking powers, but a mull by Briggs was fortunately saved. Antrobus and Daniels became conspicuous by a certain smartness, but Morris was to the fore by a fine punt, bringing relief to his side. While the game was careering about the half-way, Lally seized the ball and made a splendid run, and it was only owing to exhaustion that he was unable to cross the line, and half-time arrived with the score Waringtcn one try to nil. Widnes restarted, and very quickly assailed their antagonists' line, but the offside displayed by the homesters lost the position at- tained. Wright's dribble was the means of returning the ball, and after some indiscriminate mixing up of the combatants, a minor was given to avert disaster. Directly after this Wright got clear away, but a grand tackle by Sampson stopped his impetuous career at the quarter line. The game proceeded in an unpleasant and scramb- ling nature, owing to the 4ncompetence of the referee, but eventually Morris put in a long kick, and by a glaring piece of offside play, Davenport was allowed a try. Suc- cess still seemed to follow the Widnes team, until from a very tine shot at goal by Morris, Sampson splendidly sent the leather to midfield, where Lally received the ball, and made a most brillant run clear under the posts, from which Fleesmn placed a goal. Warrington livened up 1 after this, and a dribble by Thornley, Barber, Barnes, and Teare, drove the homesters back, and from a pass by Thornley, Lally ran well into the home 25. Potts and Teare were next prominent a bad pass losing the ground. Davies, Knowles, James, and Rowlands renewed the pressure, and Fleesom was within an ace of scoring. Noth- inglfurther was scored,and Warrington won a poor game by 1-1-2 to 0-1-2. STOCKTON HEATH v. WARRINGTON STAR.—The first match of the season between these two local teams took place on Saturday, when the Stockton Heath team paid the Stars a visit. The lint half of the game was chiefly confined to the forwards, and neither side were able to make much progress. At half-time, the Stars led by two minors to nil. The visitors had slightly the best of the second portion of the game, Broady, after a grand run, crossing the line, Glover failing at the goal. On the call of time nothing further had been scored, and the try proved to be the winning point for the visitors.
FUNERAL OF GENE RAL BOULANGER.

An immense crowd collected early on Saturday after- noon in the immediate vicinity of the late General Boulanger's residence to witness the starting of the funeral corVve for the Ixelles cemetery. The police, be- ing insufficient to keep the mob in order, had to apply for help to the gendarmerie, arid a number of persons who gave trouble were arrested. M. Rochefort, D6roulede, Laur-Millevoye, and other Boulangist leaders arrived at the house to attend the funeral. More than ' a hundred wreaths, with tri-coloured ribbons, had been sent from France to be placed on the coffin. On reach- ing the grave the coffin was immediately taken from the hearse and lowered to its final resting-place. No re- ligious service took place, neither were any speeches delivered, but M. Deroulede, taking up a French tri- colour, put it to his lips and then threw it down over the lid of the coffin, exclaiming "Farewell my friend." This was the only incident which occurred. M. Roche- fort was hooted by the crowd on leaving the cemetery. The chief followers of the late General held a private meeting on Saturday, in Brussels, at which they drew up a manifesto declaring that they would continue the work of the party, which had been undertaken in the interests of France.
MR 'GLADSTONE AND fHE FREEDOM
OF NEWCASTLE.

Mr. Gladstone was on Saturday forenoon presented with the freedom of Newcastle-on-Tyne. in presence of a vast and deeply interested assemblage of ladies and gentlemen, who had crowded the Town Hall more than half an hour before the time fixed for the ceremony. In acknowledging the honour conferred on him, Mr. Glad- stone spoke of the progress of Newcastle since his last visit to the city in 1862, as illustrative of the power of the principle of self-government, and of the value of local communities as training grounds for legislators and statesmen ; pointed out that England had become among the great nations of the world almost the selitary witness to the principle of freedom as applied to trade, as she had long been in Europe the solitary witness to freedom applied to social and political associations ; expressed belief that, as the countries in time began to follow her example in regard to freedom in general, so, if she proved faithful to fee,edom of commerce, Europe and America would alike in the long run, and atter no very great delay, be influenced by her firm- ness and consistency • and that ifi the future the im- partial historian would record that for the purpose of establishing the rights of industry, of giving every man fair play, of enablini him to turn to the best account his gifts, mental or corporeal,England was also the standard bearer of the nations, and taught them the safe, just and. honourable way to durable public prosperity. After the ceremony in the Town Hall, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone lunched with the Mayor and Mayoress at the Mansion House. They then drove to the railway station, the streets en rouse and the windows of houses and shops. being fully occupied by enthusiastic citizens., whose greetings Mr. Gladstone continuously acknowledged. At a quarter to one, amid the cheers of those who crowded the station plWorm, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and party left Newcastle for Hawarclen, which Was reached about a quarter past six o'clock. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone seemed somewhat fatigued by the long journey ; but on Monday it was stated • that Mr. Gladstone had not suffered either in voice or health by the exertions of the two previous days.

Score, Halton View, 2 goals, 4 tries; Earlestown, nil. • RUNCORS RECREATION DITTON RECREATION.—PIayed at Runcoartt on Saturday afternoon' a grand game re- sulting. The home team scored a try in the first half. In the second half the home team had the best of the game. Final result :—Runcorn Recs., 1 goal, 3 tries, minors; Ditton Recs., f 2 minor. WIVNIS Sr. Marres-V.SILTEIRWELL.—PIayed at Widnes, on Saturday,before a small attendance. Silverwell kicked off, and play was of a very even character until the visitors after a combined rush compelled'Oook to touch dawn to save his lines. Both teams pressed remarkably well, and were evenly matched, the result being that each end was visited in turn. Towards the close of the first half St. Mary's had hard lines in not scoring. Final result :—Widnes St. Mary's 2 goals, 1 try (11 points) ; Silverwell. nil. RUNCORN T. SALFORD "A " TEAMS.—Played at Salford before a large attendance, Tongue kicked off, the ball being charged down by the Runcorn forwards. After a brief scrimmage, George Robinson picked up, and ran very strongly into the Salford 25, where Blomley tackled him, but having transferred to May, the latter ran in a beautiful try, but the place kick failed. An extra spurt was now made by Salford, who registered two minors in quick succession. Lee and Derbyshire dribbled the ball out of danger, when Edge gave Barratt a pass, which he took in good style' and was only. stopped by T. Robinson a slight injury to the latter player causing Coleshill to be brought out of the " scrum " to full back. Score at half time :—Runcorn, 1 try (2 points) • Salford, nil. In the second half the game was stubbornly contested and the score remained unaltered.

div.head: SALFORD v. RUNCORN.
div.p: SALFORD v. RUNCORN.

At Runcorn before 3,000 spectators. Both teams were well represented, T. Craven being the oaly absentee from the Salford ranks. Owing to the train service, it was fully half-past four when Barrett kicked off for the visi4ors. Crompton returned well, but Sudlow neutra- lized by a fine kick into touch. Salford then pressed, Miles showing conspicuously with a fine run and kick into touch. Following this Houghton made his mark, but this did not benefit the home team, as Manwaring more than neutralized by a splendid return. Some fine passing by Barrett and Sudlow resulted in the RuncOrn territory being invaded. The leather did not stay here long, as Houghton caused play to be transferred to the "Reds' "end. Here France got possession, and passing to Sudlow, the latter player kicked to midfield, where] Crompton picked up, and,with his left foot, dropped a splendid goal from the centre of the field. Kent lost no time in kicking off, but the leather went into touch,and from the line out the Cheshire team worked the leather I down the field. Davies then got hold and looked a,cer- tain scorer, but Roberts sprinted and dragged him into touch. Salford then pressed, and had very hard lines, the efforts of Houghton. Crompton, and Pendlebury be- ing taxed to the utmost to keep their line intact. Miles made two splendid efforts to get in, but he was tackled ; , from behind each time, just on the goal line: Roberts also had hard lines. Eventually Miles got possession, and after a magnificent run scored a try half way between the uprights and the touch line. ' Manwaring made a good attempt to kick a goal. and half time arrived with the score—Runcorn 1 dropped goal (4 points), Salford 1 try (2 points). After the interval Miles worked splendidly, his running and kick- ing being superb. After some even play he got posses- sion at midfield and essayed a drop at goal, but the leather struck the upright and bounded into play. Even play followed, and then Crompton. who was playing , very well, received severe injury to his collar bone, and had to seek medical aid. Salford worked hard to score, hut they could not break through the home defence. Eventually Barrett got possession at midfield and spoiled a splendid chance of scoring by wildly passing forward. Sudlow was conspicuous after this by some good kick- ing, and then the home forwards came away with a strong rush, but Faulkner kicked too strongly, the ball I going into touch-in-goal. Just on time the visitors were awarded a penalty kick, but Manwaring's attempt, though well placed, fell short, time being called immedi- ately after with the score: Runcorn 1 dropped gcal (4 points), Salford 1 try (2 points). The game did not add to the reputation of either side, and evidently Salford. who have suffered by numerous defeats this season,came fully prepared to stem the tide of disasters at any cost. Their play was of the close order,and their efforts mainly directed to upsetting any attempt on the part of Cheshire's Champions to bring their fine open expositions into force. Crompton's injury was not so serious as at first anticipated. and in all probability he will be seen in his old position in the course of a few weeks. Faulkner was the best forward on the field, whilst Houghton was ' brilliant at.back. WARRINGTON V. WIDNBS.

The fine form displayed by both the above named or- ganizations this season was certainly responsible for the large crowd assembling at the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday. The Widnes fixture is about the oldest on the Warrington card, and though a suspension of the matches occurred some few years ago, when the teams were engaged in the West Lancashire Cup, the hostile spirit has been abandoned, and the fixture at both Wid- nes and Warrington is now looked upon as a sort of happy reunion. There would be a gate of over 7,000, and a better humoured assemblage has never been seen at the Warrington enclosure. Special trains were run from Widnes, nearly two thousand accompanying their team, so that it will be seen Widnes did not lack any- thing in the shouting line. The teams were as selected with one exception, Hardman did not take his place in the Widnes forwards.

1 Ashton loosing the choice of ends, started towards the pavilion goal, and although Warrington had the dis- advantage of a slight breeze, they early assumed Ow aggressive. The exchanges between Brennan and J. T. Bate were followed by a.ccuple of smart pieces of play by Webster. Holmes (Widnes) charged James Bate's kick, and Widnes were now within easy reach of the railway goal, but this advantage was only temporary, for Jolley, Fair Turner, and Ashton with separate efforts forced the game beyond the half way flag. A strong partiality for the home half backs on three occasions penalized the Widnesians, and Turner's kicks were negatived by the rushing tactics of the visitors' for- wards. Webster passed across to Lawless, but the lat- ter missed, but redeemed his failing by executing a smart save a moment later. From a pass from J. T. Bate Webster punted finely, and it was from this point that Warrington began to assert their superiority. From a scrimmage near the centre the home half-backs passed finely across the scrimmage, with the result that James Bate slipped his opponents one by one, and making but short work of Hartles, he wound up the effort by gain- ing the smartest try seen at the enclosure this season. With the place kick failing, Warrington again attacked, and although Peters kicked well and Whelan was pro- minent in the forward division' the safe returns by the two Bates, Evans and Nevins led up to Warrington at- tacking more vigorously. A dribble by Fair Turner was supplemented by, another smart run by James Bate, but Hartles defended well, and Peters earned a hearty round orapplause for a smart tackle of Webster.- That Warrington were masters of the situation, especially when the passing out was brought into force, was shown the next minute, for a scrimmage being formed the two Bates again passed finely, and Evans eventually taking up the movement handed; over the charge to Webster, who with a few strides and a few Opponents.to push aside, landed a scorer in a favourite positson for-Evans to kick a fine goal amidst a I,earty round of applause. Boscow had been comparatively idle, but now found work to do imstoppin„g if rush of the Widnes front rank, and though the visitors passed neatly, their final essay was generally bungled. Jolley got clear. from a line out, and a capital run was nipped in the bud by Peters and Brennan tacklingjihn finely. J.T.Bate saved in daring style,and Holmes and Emery by a couple of smart passes took the oval in the mouth of the home goal. Re- lief was forthcoming at the hands of Nevins making his mark, and a penalty kick falling to each side, with no distinct advantage, Peters wound up the bout of kicking by placing the leather safely in touch at half way. The 'visitors were now playing up manfully, and after Whe- lan had dribbled finely, a spell of passing between Bren- nan, Peters, and Barber, saw the Warrington goal being hotly assailed. The• attack was but brief, for Ashton. Nevins, Evans, and Randles pressed the visitors back. A penalty kick to either side was next witnessed, and although Turner kicked well, the excitement reached its fullest extent when Jolley dribbledsingle-handed through the Widnes backs, eventually crossing to Donohue, the latter finishing the try. Ashton failed at the place. Wid- nes pressed from the drap out, and although Brennan passed well to his three-quartters, they failed to utilise the chances offered. Ashton, Fair Turner, and Handles were applauded for a dribble near the call of half time,but nothing tangible resulted, and when the interval arrived the score read as Warrington, 1-2-0 ; Widnes, nil. With the substantial lead of nine points the home en- thusiasts were quite jubilant, and the result was looked upon as a foregone conclusion. A fine dribble by Jolley was the first interesting item, which Hartles stopped in his best style. The visitors were now playing well, and taking advantage of a slight ease which •Warrington were apparentlftaking, the game was carried on in the home quarters. Repeatedly the Widnes backs passed finely, and Boscovr only kicked indifferently. J. T. Bate got clear on one occasion, and Donohue failed to take a fine chance. Not to be denied, the Widnes men played in surprising style, and a just reward was forthcoming when Whelan scored from some exchange kicking, Bar- ber failing at the place. . Widnes had had their last chance now, for Warrington settling down to their work again harassed the Widnes defence. After a grand dis- play between the Batelg, Weber, who had been hurt in

div.head: DARING IMPOSTOR,
div.p: A DARING IMPOSTOR,
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER XV. AN IMPOSTOR.
Although only the middle of the afternoon, it was so dark in the tenement house that the men and women working the restless machines lit their lamps earlier than usual.

The pale-faced children, driven from the narrow dirty street by the rain, crouched on the stairs, or drowned out the rattle of the sewing machines by their shrill yells in the halls. Hitherto Allen, who loved children, had always met the little ones with a smiling face, and once a week he appeared before them with his pockets full of peanuts and candies, and he gave the boy or girl, voted " best " by the others, the largest share. To-day he ascended the bare steps with heavy feet and a sad face, and the children at sight of him, drew back and let him pass on without a word.

The account of "A Daring Impostor" had ap- peared in the papers a few days before, and had been read by Allen and his sister, but, eager to save their mother, they took care that she should not see it.
Mrs. Gilbert, who had not been feeling very well, was asleep in her own room when Allen entered.
On tiptoe Florence met him, and kissing him, she led him to a seat by the window that commanded a view of the street below.

Do not tell me what I already know, Allen," she said, with her hands clasped about his arm. "Let it comfort you to know you have lost only after having made a brave fight in a good cause." "I am so accustomed to defeat," he said, gloomily, "that I should not have expected anything else. Every one of my customers has taken his collections away from me. They protested that they were eager to help me, but they were shocked to find their names in the papers, as the employers of an ex-convict; so they sent me adrift after wishing me well."
"And the doctor ?" she said, with her eyes on the floor.

"Far be it from me to speak or think unkindly of a man who has been so good a friend to me. But he persists in thinking I deceived him in not con- fessing all. My position is gone, to my new acquain- tances I am an impostor, and to my old ones a crim- inal. The name Gilbert is as thoroughly disgraced in the eyes of the world as the name Lee. I feel like giving up the struggle, for it seems as if Heaven and earth were against me ;" and Allen buried his face in his hands and a tremor ran through his frame.

"My brother, God knows how I love you and why I love you," said Florence, taking one of the hands from his face, and pressing it between her own warm palms. "But, though I realise the trials that beset us, I cannot despair, for that would mean death. All day I have been thinking that this is a great, broad land, and if it absorbs the world's sur- plus people—good, bad, and indifferent—there surely should be room enough in it for us. I have saved up nearly two hundred dollars, and our furni- ture ought to sell for fifty. This will be enough to take us to the great new West, and support us until we can get work. There we can begin life anew, and taking the dear name of our father again, struggle so as to deserve success, and then leave the rest to God"

"That seems to be the only thing left= "That, and youth and hope," she mid, encourag- ingly. "Do not speak of the hope, sister.' "But I shall; leave that out and what is fife "Life without hope is the earth without the sun." These words were spoken by some one who had entered the room unobserved, and looking quickly up, the brother and sister saw Irene Lefferts in the act of throwing back her veil. "I knocked," she said, "but as I got no reply I took the liberty of coming in, as of old." Allen and Florence rose to their feet. They had not seen Irene since the night when Reybold ap- peared at the meeting, and by his accusations made those assembled forget the object for which they were called.
Allen bowed, but his heart was in his throat, and he could not utter a word.

With a woman's quick perception, Florence read her visitor's face, and coming to her she threw her arms about her neck, and kissing her said, with a sob of joy: "God bless you for this!" "Did you -think I believed neybold 7 Did you Imagine I would forsake you In the - hour of your great tribulation?" asked Irene, as she approached the window and reached out both hands to Allen. "I have been so shocked and confused," he said, "that I did not know what to think. Other good friends have cast me off, why should you cling to me 7"

She looked at him steadily for some seconds, then repeated, in a low, questioning tone: "Why should I cling to you 7 " "I am sorry if I've pained you," he said. As if she had not heard him, she continued: "I cling to you because I believe in you." "Then you run the risk of having your name associated with that of a criminal and an imposter," said Allen, half delighted, half desperate. "Should Ibe swerved from doing what I think is right simply by fear of what the world would say? Why should I degrade myself to keep the approval of the world? No, no; I have no war with the world, but I can defy its prejudices to save my own sense of honour.' Irene Lefferts did not raise her voice, yet so clear and penetrating were her words that they struck on the heart of the brother and sister with a more thrilling effect than the trumpet tones of an orator.
----- With tears in her eyes, Florence thanked the friend who, like a good angel, had brought light and warmth into the darkness of their lives.

—Allen then told her of his sister's plan, to go to the far West and begin life anew, but this Irene promptly opposed. "No, ' she said. "To 'fly from the scene of our suffering—of your social degradation—would be to assure the world that you deserved it. Your foes might follow you to the ,new land, or in some unex- pected way the story of the past might come out and crush you again. Here are to be found the facts and the people to clear you, and here you must remain and fight it out to the end like a knightly man."
"Irene—you know you told me to call you Irene—"
"And Irene I am still to you, my dear," said Irene, kissing Florence again. _ _ _

"Let me s-ay this for illy brother': He and I be- lieve as you do, and if he could live here and main- tain himself while he fought, I am sure he would do so. But the. knight with an empty purse fights at a disadvantage. My brother will not beg, and he will not steal. He is ready to work, and he has shown his ability to work well and honestly, but his employers have cast him off. Other employers will do the smile should Reybold appear to tell of the past. " I have thought all that over, Florence. Indeed, I have talked to my, father about it. He is some- what conservative, but at heart he is a nobleman. He . believes with me that Allen Lee has been wronged; and, for the good he actually knows of he is willing to give him a place in his main shipping office on Broad-street." "And for that I thank him," said Allen. "But so long as Reybold has access to your father, so long my position would be in danger." "I think not," she replied, quickly. "Through you his eyes have been opened to the doings of Mott Reybold, and the man who could cast off his own son because he persisted in a life of disgrace, will hardly cling to the son of another when convinced of his perfidy. What say you 2 In this matter will you be guided by me 7" Irene reached out her hand to him, and as Allen bent over it and pressed it to his lips he said, reverently: "I will."

Shortly after this Irene went home alone, for it was not yet dark, and Allen and -Florence sat for some time by the window in silence, for they felt as if an angel had been in the room and that any noise would be a profanity. The very next morning Allen, at the hands of a messenger, received a note from Mr. Lefferts, ask- ing him to come at once to his office.

_ lie complied, and the old gentleman met him with the kindness of manner he had *always shown, and never by even the slightest hint did he refer to the charges made by Reybold. After some talk as to his qualifications, Mr. Lefferts called his superintendent, introduced Allen„ and asked to have him assigned to what was known as "The Custom-House Department" of the business.
Allen entered at once on his duties, which took him to his "old stamping ground" in Wall-street, Again the resolution to win stirred him, and he uraverfully resolved to do his whole duty—as he

bad ever done it—uncaring for the opinio-n of the world. Often, as he went to and from the office to the Custom House, he saw Mott Reybold, and more than once he was brought face to face with Frank Lefferts, the latter always more or less under the influence of liquor. Allen would have been more than human if he had been able to overcome a spirit of resentment against these men. With all the strength of his honest nature he loathed and hated the heartless ruffian, and if he had had only himself to think of, a collision would have taken place between the two long since. One night Allen was returning home, after having been to see Mr. Lefferts on some business, when a man, evidently under the influence of drink, stag- gered against him, and nearly knocked him down. Though the act was rude, Allen would have brushed his hat and hurried on without further notice of the man, had not the electric lights in the square near by revealed the face of Mott Rey- bold. The sight fired his blood, and, with a cry of rage, he leaped forward and caught the ruffian by the throat.
CHAPTER XVI. MORE PLOTTING.

Mott Reybold was naturally an active, athletic man, and, if his powers had not been sapped by dissipation, and his courage weakened by a life of clime, Allen Gilbert might have paid dearly for his rashness.
Reybold was certainly surprised at the assault, though he had deliberately planned the meeting and altercation.
He was armed, and his purpose was to have it appear—from his own statement—that Allen had committed a murderous assault on him, and then to shoot him down.

The instant Reybold felt the young man's clutch on his throat, he threw back his hand and managed to draw a pistol from his hip pocket. He was being strangled, yet he succeeded in raising the weapon and pressing it against Allen's heart.

Though furious beyond expression, Allen's anger but intensified his mental activity. With his free hand he threw up the pistol, seized it, and wrench- ing it from Reybold's grip, hurled it away. This done, he struck one blow, that sounded like the report of a rifle, and Reybold, with a blood- covered face, fell in a heap at the foot oi the lamp post. A hundred yards away, Allen could see an officer leisurely pacing his beat, and his first impulse was to go to him and report what had happened. This certainly would have been the wiser course; but he hurriedly reasoned that, if he had Reybold arrested, he must appear against him in court, and so be forced again to acknowledge the withering features of his own past, and have them published, with all the embellishment of a degraded imagination, to the world.
It did not take him many seconds to decide what he should do. With another glance that assurea him Iteybolcl was not seriously injured, he turned and, without increasing his former speed. went home.
Though stunned by Allen's well-planted blow, Reybold did not lose consciousness, but he had too much sense to rise and renew the contest while his assailant was within reach.
Waiting till Allen was out of sight, Reybold rose, and after wiping the blood from his face, he picked up his pistol and hurried away, without attracting any attention.
He and his partner had not yet secured money to enable them to re-open their gambling place, which they ever assured their friends was "run for plea- sure, not profit." _
"Hello, deah boy! what the mischief is up with you ?" asked Jack Hyde, when Reybold appeared before him with blood-covered clothes and a swollen face. •

"Do I look bad?" was Reybold's response, as he glanced at his face in a glass. "Well, I should say you do look bad. Dash it I have a horror of blood. How did it happen, old chappie 7" "I was attacked by an assassin." "Oh, horrible! Did he get away? "Yes." "And no clue to him?"

"Clue to him! I can lay my hand on him in an Instant. He is my old foe, Allen Lee," said Rey- bold, with a ghastly laugh. "And he attacked you? He must be desperate." "He is all that, Jack. However, I meant to kill him, and failed; so let that go. Now, I shall go on with the plans you urged me against." "But the danger, the awful danger, deah boy If it wasn't for the fear of the law, I 'd be quite as yourself to go into this thing, you know— ' " I tell you what I do know, Jack," interrupted Reybold, as he stopped in the act of pouring out a glass of liquor for himself. "What is that, old boy 7" _

"That there will be a thousand times more danger if I remain quiet. Ah 1" he added, smacking his lips after he had tossed off the liquor, "if I'd known what lay ahead before I began, I should not have done it; but I'm into it now, and, though it results in the destruction of the world, I shall fight It through to the end. Ruin must come to this fellow or to me. Neither of us can avoid it. Why didn't I shoot him when I had the chance 2"

I "The other man was quicker, I suppose. But, I beg you, deah boy, not to get excited. Hello I Was that a rap at the door? Yes, it was." And, answering his own question, Jack Hyde unlocked the sitting-room door, which opened into a com- mon hall, and Mingo entered with his hat slouched and his coat collar turned up, though it was a balmy spring night. Mingo still retained his place as night watchman for a jewellery firm near by, and so well had he per- formed his duties as to retain thb regard of all who had been instrumental in securing him the place.
' "It's a bit foggy out to-night," said Mingo, as he eyed the glass and bottle near by. "An' this kind o' weather do make me feel awful hoarse."
Taking the hint, Reybold told him to help him- self, and when Mingo had taken a drink that would insure the drunkenness of an ordinary man, he asked :
"How's things with you, Mr. Farley?" "All right. Fell and hurt my face a little. But how's the trap?" asked Reybold. ._
- "Most ready to be sprung," said Mingo. "Be sure it doesn't spring and catch the wrong person."

"Trust me for that, Mr. Farley. Bnt, I say, if you had fifty dollars to spare, I could put it to good use. You see, I've got to pay my pals, an' some of 'em awful high-priced fellers. No one can't expect good' work onless they pays for it," said Mingo, just as if he were discussing the most ordinary business transaction.

"I am short to-night, Mingo; but if you call to-morrow evening. I'll have the Rioney for you. By the way, I wish you could manage to see that fellow in the meantime, and End out if he suspectr anything." "What feller 7" • "Lee."

' Oh, 367. Well, he don't 'spec awthin. W'y, I kep' a valise at his plaoa an 'Lim an' his sister an' the t'other young lady_-you :r7-ow who I mean —they all think I'm a right do wr. angel. Oh, I've got the whole thing arranged; out you can't expect me to go on till you pay me the rest of the money. Business is business, an' men that take big risks want big pay. . But I won't crowd you. I know how 'tis mysd. An' I'll call round 'bout this time to-morrow night. Guess I'm free to help mysel' to another 'before I go 7" said Mingo, as he pulled on his hat and stood looking down at the bottle.

Reybold said, "To be sure," and after taking another drink, that nearly exhausted the contents of the bottle, Mingo went out. He had been gone but a few minutes when Frank Lefferts came in, his face wearing its look of chronic dissipation, and his manner showing that he was in no good. humour.

After a gruff salutation, he finished the liquor left by Mingo, and then declared that if something didn't turn up to put money in his pocket that there would be only two courses open to him; one to go to the poorhouse on Blackwell's Island, and the other to fill his pockets with bricks and jump into the North River.

"Well," said Reybold, after he had heard Frank through, "I've got no pity for you. . A man that loses all his pluck deserves to suffer. I showed you how you could replenish, as you have often done before, but you back out, and poverty is on you, and destruction threatens you and your friends.' "See here, Reybold 1" exclaimed Frank, einpha- sizing his words with an oath and a ringing blow on the table, "I don't want to write my father's name any more. I've done itl and he sent me adrift but kept my secret. Strike me dead, if I want to do it again ! '

, You'd better join the Young Men's Christian Association," sneered Reybold.- "You are getting altogether too good for men. like me end. Jack Hyde. But let me put the care to "Blaze awa' I am de,ne.ra..e." ialLI frank
Lefferts struck the table again, and ran his hands through his bair, as if he were going to pull it out.

Reybold knew what these protestations meant. He had seen Frank before when he was suffering from what he called "spasms of conscience," and he knew that he would not long adhere to this, or to any other resolution whether good or bad. Frank Lefferts was weak rather than naturally vicious. His time was spent in doing wrong and regretting it. He was a moral chameleon and took on the character of his surroundings. Had he been put to work, after it was demon- strated that he could never make a scholar, he• might have developed into a good citizen. Perhaps. his father was not blameless in this, though all his motives were above approach. With an intellect so weak that it might be called stupid in every other respect, Frank Lefferts was a wonderful mimic; and on the stage he might have made a fortune by this talent. In addition he could imitate, in a way that had deceived the fore- most experts, any writing placed before him. It was he who forged the note on which Allen Gilbert was convicted; and, as has been hinted, he signed his own father's name to the paper, and was turned out of door for a crime that should have sent him, as it has sent many another, to prison. Reybold understood his man. Signalling for his partner to leave, he gave Frank more liquor, and the effect was soon evident in his manner, which, from being despondent, became hilarious. After having worked him up to the proper pitch, as a violinist tunes his instrument, Reybold began to - state the case in his own forcible way. He skilfully concealed the fact that he needed. money as much as did Frank, and dwelt from first to last on the danger to them both, so long as Allen Lee was free.

"The fellow is now in your father's confidence, in your place; do you understand me, Frank 7" "Yes, I do; fire away," growled Frank. "More than that, old fellow, he has succeeded in poisoning Irene's mind against me. She is con- vinced he is a great fellow, and it will take a great. deal of strong evidence to change her mind. Why,. man, we are not fighting for money; we are fight- ing for our lives. We must connect him with anothei forgery, or you at least will find yourself in. gaol before the summer is over. If forced to it, I can clear myself, but it is not in my nature to forsake an old friend." "But what can Ido?" asked Frank. again help- ing nil trom the bottle that was lett convenient to his reach.
"Prepare the papers, write as I say, and I will attend to the rest. Here, let me show you what I want."
Reybold placed a desk on the table and took out

a lot of blank cheques, drafts, and notes. "We've got some of Lee's writing. Mingo at- tended to that for me. Here, write his name In his own hand, as if he were vractising on this sheet; you sse it has Dr, Ptitnarakiiiie on it then nail over these names. The exercise will get you into shape and the paper will be of value to me. AN, that's it 1 You are a genius, Frank, and have not lost your wonderful skill 1" exclaimed Reybolci, as Frank placed himself before the desk and begannt4:l write.

He but half comprehended what be was doing-,, yet his hand was steady and his imitation marvel- lously perfect. Before he rose from his. seat, to drink again, he had done all that Reybold wanted. (To be continued.)

div.head: ONLY FLATTEN THE END.
div.p: ONLY FLATTEN THE END.

That cld story about Columbus and the egg. How- many thousands of times it has been told, and the moral of it is not stale yet. How easy it is to see through a. millstone after somebody else has drilled a hole. "Make an egg stand on end? Of course we can. Just flatten the shell a bit." But to be the first man to think of that I Ah, yes, to be sure.

There is an idea nowidays—which is best illustrated by a short story. "ALL my life," says a lady, "I have been subjsct to bad headache and bilious sickness. Al- most every week I had an attack, when I would have dreadful pain at the temples and a weight over the eyes, so I could scarcely see. I went quite dizzy, and had to be constantly lying down on the couch, and but for the necessity of caring for my family would have been con- fined to bed. I had a bad taste in the mouth in the morning, and a thick phlegm in my mouth obliged me to rinse it out frequently. My appetite was very poor; in fact, I ate next to nothing, and even after taking the simplest food I would go deadly sick and vomit it up. "At times I also threw up a quantity of green fluid, and had a heavy, dull, sinking pain in the right side. After every attack I felt very weak, languid, and tired, and bad great diffculty in getting about—new better and now worse ; this was my condition for several years, during which time I took all kinds of medicines that I could hear of, and was under a doctor for two years, but grew worse in spite of all that was done.

"One day, in April, 1890, a book was left at my house. telling of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Sy- rup, and in it I read of a case which described my com- plaint. I procured a bottle of the Syrup from Mr. John Beckett, the chemist, Monkgate, and, after taking it for but a short time, to my surprise and joy all my headache and sickness left me, and I never felt so well. Had I known about this medicine and used it years ago, how much suffering it would have saved the."
(Signed)
ELIZA WAIIE,
April 23rd, 1891.
65, Newbro' Street, York.

But we cannot know until we learn. From her letter- it is plain that Mrs. Ware was a sufferer from chronic indigestion and dyspepsia, with liver complaint. The latter accounts for the presence of the" green fluid " she speaks of, which was bile. Now the business of the bile- is to tans from the liver to the intestines or bowels and to lubricate them, and so assist in the expuifion of the waste matters. Yet in this, as in all cases of dyspepsia, the bile was out of its place. Remaining in the blood, where it is a poison, it caused the headache, the dizzi- ness, and other painful and dangerous symptoms. All this happened because the liver was overworked, until it finally struck work altogether, as abused labourers often do. The liver was thrown into this condition by the stomach, which, on account of indigestion and dyspepsia, tried to make the liver do the work of both. Thus we see that the latter tronble was the real one, and all the rest only consequences and symptoms; and in curing the gastric disorder Mother Seigel's Syrup necessarily delivered the patient from all the results which arose therefrom.

Mr. John McDonald, Green Park, Canterbuly, New Zealand, writes : "It is with great pleasure that I bear testimony to the efficacy of Mother Seigel's Syrup. About seven years ago my health broke down completely. I tried four different doctors, each for six weeks, without any benefit at all. Somebody told me to try the Syrup.

I did so, and in three weeks I was cured. •Ever since that time, about seven years ago now, I have enjoyed perfect health and gained two stones in weight. lam over _fifty years of aye, and look better to-day than when I was twenty-five. lam very thankful to Almighty God end to Mother Siegel." So we learn how to make an egg stand on end, and also that to cure indigestion and dyspepsia is the straight road to health.
