div.head: WARRINGTON . LIBERAL BAZAAR.
div.p: WARRINGTON . LIBERAL BAZAAR.
ENTHUSIASTIC PROCEEDINGS.
INTRODUCTION.

The objects of the Liberal bazaar, which was opened by the Countess of Carlisle in the Public Hall, on Tuesday,and continued on Wednesday,Thursday, and 'Friday, were" to provide funds tc continue the work of political education by means of public meetings, lectures, and literature ; and to ensure the registration of every person entitled to the par- liamentary and municipal franchise." The War- rington Liberal Association through its long career of close upon sixty years—for it may be said to have originated from the passing of the Reform Act of 1832' which gave the town a direct repre- sentation in Parliament—has never been without supporters who were willing to give freely of their time, energy, and money foi the advancement of the cause of progress in politics. During the last few years, however, there has been a singular and lamentable depletion by death of the number of those who are able and willing to give substantial pecuniary aid towards the carrying on of the work of the Association. In proof of this we need only recall the names of Mr. George Crosfield. Mr. J. G. McMinnies,Mr. S. Rigby,and Mr. C. Broadbeat,whose deaths were a loss not only to the Liberal party,but to the town as a whole. From this and other causes -Game the necessity of raising funds in a special way to defray the expenses of the political work of the Association. Some months ago a meeting of members of the Association was held, and at this meeting it was decided to bold a bazaar. Mrs. Z. Amitage, at the request of the Association, called together a meeting of ladies who are interested in the cause of Liberalism, and this meeting was very well attended. The following officials were after- wards appointed for making all the preliminary • arrangements :—President, Mrs. Ziba Armitage; treasurer, Mrs. Julian Winser ; joint secretaries, Miss Bessie Dutton and Miss Beatrice Burgess; general secretary, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes ; chairman of tbe General Committee. Mr. F. A. Roberts; chair- man,amusements, Mr. D. Tinnion ; secretary, amuse- ments, Mr. J. S. Haynes; secretary,Programme Cora- mittee,Mr.T.Pemberton ; secretary,refreshment stall, Mr. W. Roberts. A large ladies working committee was formed and it threw itself into the work of preparing for the bazaar with an ardour that en- .aured success. Working meetings were held at the Liberal Club on Friday afternoons and in addition to this, many ladies did work at home. Indeed, it is no more than the truth to say that nearly all concerned with the bazaar displayed a real and 'practical enthusiasm for the success of the work they had undertaken. As was to be expected the heaviest share of the burden fell upon the shoulders of the general secretary, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes,and it will be generally conceded that it was in a high degree due to the energy, tact, and the courtesy of Mr: Holmes that the bazaar was opened on Tuesday with sT much eclat and so large a promise of com- plete success. ~

div.head: SCENE IN THE PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: THE SCENE IN THE PUBLIC HALL.

The style of the bazaar was that of a "Grand Ice Oarnival " which was designed and carried out by a well- known decorator,Mr. G. M. Bridges,of King's Lynn. The whole of the Hall was illuminated with numerous electric lights, and the scenic effect was exceeditgly attractive, although the Hall was too small for the most effective dis- play. The views, lit up as they were with the bright soft light of the electric arcs gave striking exemplification of the winter views of many nations. On the one hand we had contrasted the picturesque architecture of the Krem- lin, the ancient palace of the Czars, with a rude hut of the Siberian steppes, an abode of the victims of Russian justice or tyranny. Next to the Siberian cabin is a pretty chalet typical of the rural architecture of Switzer- land. It has a balcony giving access to the front, and a heavily-timbered projecting roof, shielding it from the storms of winter. Passing from this there is a representa- tion of one of the famous ice palaces of Montreal which are constructed of blocks of translucent ice. Passing on, the spectator might, in imagination, pass from the busy and populous city to the wild and lonely Canadian backwoods, for we have here also depicted a semblance of the uncouth but substantial cabin of pinewood blocks which the pioneer setter throws up in the forest. From the wilds of Manitoba the passage is quick to Norway, the land of the "midnight sun," which is represented by a picturesque dwelling with a curiously carved front, suqw resting upon every projection. England is repre- sented by a flint-gabled house of the sixteenth century, a view which harmonises admirably with the rest of the scene. One of the most admired parts of the display was the view of the "eternal " Alps at the back of the platform. In this scene were depicted with realistic force, the snow-capped mountains, the peaceful valley, and the wild rushing cataract, the water foaming round the huge rocks and breaking into vapoury masses. As a whole, the scenic part of the bazaar was much admired, and was in every way satisfactory, notwithstanding that the smallness of the Hall and the projecting galleries were not favourable to the decorator's designs. The electric lights, it should be mentioned, were supplied by Mr. W. Morton, of Sankey-at., who is to be congratu- lated on the successful and brilliant result of his labours. Outside the Hall there was a large flag hung across Rylands-st., bearing an announcement of the bazaar.

div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: THE OPENING CEREMONY.

_ When the bazaar was opened at two o'clock, on Tues- day afternoon, the scene was one of great brilliancy. The body of the hall was densely crowded, and among those present, in addition to the Countess of Carlisle were Mr. F. A. Roberts, who presided, Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield, the Misses Crosfield, Mr. J. E. Barlow (Liberal candidate for one of the Salford Divisions, and a former candidate for the Knut,sford Division), Mr, Henry Lee, of Manchester, Dr. Gornall, Alderman Holmes, the Revs. John Yonge and F. K. Freeston, Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Mrs. Mills, Bowdon; Mrs. Jesse Howarth, Mrs. Faulkner Armitage, Mr. E. J. Guest, Coun. William Pierpoint, Garner, H. Roberts, Blackhu rat, Shaw Green, Beaman, Fleming, Browne, F. W. Monks, and G. Plumpton. and Messrs. Thomas Morris, Robert Gareett, Richard Roberts, Claude Morris, William Roberts, J. S. Garland, W. Robinson. C. E. Parker, D. Tinnion, S. Jones. F. Loughlin. Julian Winser, James Dodds, Charles Plinston, John Walker, Thomas Birchall, John Bonnell, Miss Dutton (Moore), Captain Rodger, Mrs. Martin (vice-president of the St. Helens Liberal Association), and Miss McKinley (secretary). The CHAIRMAN said they were all aware that, owing to the death of many good friends of the Liberal Asso- ciation, their funds had not been in the best condition. They would have found that out by the aggressive war- fare of the association having diminished of late. Then they had to mourn the loss of their ex-member, Mr. McMinnies, whose death hastened on the appeal which was now being made to them for assistance. They had also to mourn the death ef Mr. George Crosfield and Mr. Samuel Rigby, and as they had no Liberal candidate for the constituency, the party was to a great extent lan- guishing for want of some common work. The bazaar was mooted at a meeting of the Central Committee, and a feeling was expressed that it might knit them more closely together, and that funds would be obtained to enable them to carry on-their work in the future success- fully. These, shortly, were the objects they had in view. Principally owing to the ready sympathy of Mrs. Ziba Armitage—(applause)—the ladies were called together to help them; and their debt of gratitude must be primarily paid to them. The Ladies' Committee had done yeoman, or rather, he would say. yeowomen service. They had also formed in their midst a Women's Liberal Associa- tion—(applause)—who had assisted materially in that work, and through them they were honoured that day by the presence of the Countess of Carlisle, who had kindly consented to open the bazaar. Their thanks were, therefore, due to Mrs. Armitage, to the Women's Liberal Association, and to all the lady workers who had as- sisted them to produce such effects as they saw before them that afternoon. He hoped that the Liberals of Warrington would generously respond to the efforts which were now being made on their behalf. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts also referred in complimentary terms to the energy and tact displayed by Mr. C. Jackson Holmes,the general secretary. (Applause.) He then asked the Coun- tess of Carlisle to open the bazaar. • LADY CARLISLE'S SPEECH. The Countess 'of CARLISLE, who was received with loud applause' said: My Liberal friends,—l am right down glad to be amongst you to-day and to open this bazaar. It is a very interesting ceremony to see the Liberals of Warrington, both men and women, buckling on their armour for a valiant electoral fight. I fancy that you have had some little rest from electioneering work, but I trust that you arenever, never going to rest again, and that from this day forward until the general election you are going to work with all your might and main to carry the Liberal candidate to the top of the poll—(cheers)—and I do believe that you will win the fight. (Renewed cheers.) The spirit shown in getting up this bazaar, the unstinted labour which has been be- stowed by all ranks and classes in this town to promote the success of this sale of work, and the magnificent quantity of work piled on your counters show what workers there are in Warrington, and how we may de- pend upon thent as champions of the Liberal cause and of our great leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Loud cheers.) I am told that a great many of the richer people have left the ranks of the Liberal party and are giving their alle- giance now to the Tory brewer. ("Shame.") This ex- odus of the rich has taken place elsewhere too, and per- haps some of you might think it a great disaster, but I for one do not think it is wholly a loss, for when a poli- tical division is managed by a few wealthy and socially influential persons, the constituency is apt to become enervated and apathetic—the few have a ten- dency to think and decide and pay for' the many, and we do not get a sound robust democratic basis for our organisation, and the absence of that basis is not compensated ;foryv all the purses in:the world.

(Hear, hear.) Political life is never vigorous in such a district. But I would have you look at the bright side of the defections in our Liberal party, and convince yourselves that the people when once called upon to make independent and self-reliant efforts will not fail, but will become worthy of their opportunities, and will put forth their best efforts in the fight. The very cream of a constituency is to be found amongst the thoughtful well-educated, public-spirited tradespeople of a town, and amongst those workmen who, having foresworn public-house company—(hear, hear)—live elevated lives, using each leisure hour for reading, discussing, and shaping the political thought of the couatry. In every town and county we find such men and women, who, loving Liberalism with a fervent ani disinterested devo- tion, foster around them such a high One, such a robust political faith, such an unswerving loyalty to the for- ward party, that Tories assail their fortress in vain. Such may Warrington be! You who live here know whe' her Warrington is already awake and ready for action. If it is not, you who are now present must speedily arouse each individual member of the party in the town by a strenuous canvass, undertaken now, and not postponed until the actual time of battle. You must kindle such a faith in what can be accom- plished by political work, such a hope for the good things coining, in every Liberal man, woman; and child, as shall make you missionaries for the Gospel of humanity and our great Radical brotherhood and sister- hood. Without enthusiasm we shall do nothing; without its glowing light the task will seem too difficult and the sacrifices too hard. They tell me that there is a temperance party in Warrington—(hear, hear) —and where there is a real, strong temperance party there is never any lack of enthusiasts, for the work thatl the temperance party has to do is so uphill that it has turned temperance workers into enthusiasts. (Cheers.) Where much endeavour is made, joy is felt in the work, and en- deavour brings its own satisfaction, even when no imme- diate result is achieved. The distant achievements seem so far, and the sweet of enthusiasm is to be able to work dauntlessly when a thing is not sure of victory. And here, in Warrington, I have heard that you are to have the promise of men and women working together as they were meant to work. were we are not to hear of that wretched divorce in public life between man and woman. From the outset I trust that both associations will work on the truest democratic baais. What a magnificent programme lies before us now ! Alter the utterances at Newcastle the other day, the work of Radicals need not now lie mainly in agitation outside the doors of Parliament, though it has too often had to do so in the past. (Hear, hear.) At last a great statesman of experience, sagacity, and years, Mr. Gladstone— (cheers)—has given his seal and sanction to many ef the reforms which the democratic party had so long desired, but which had never yet reached the safe position of being Front Bench measures,yet which in our hearts we have long desired. At last we hear that public opinion is ripe for an onward move, and that the time has come for our leaders to adopt a thoroughgoing people's programme. (Applause.) The actual measures foreshadowed by Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Morley, and Sir W. Harcourt, are an enormous advance on anything yet promised to us, and the principles on which those mea- sures are admittedly based are capable of indefinite ex- pansion and of much further application in a popular sense. That is to say, that the cowing Parliament is to be based upon trust in the people. (Hear, hear.) We might have thoughtit enough that the grand old states- man should carry the Irish Home Rule cause to victory. (Applause.) To our feeble hands this might have seemed task enough for him, but, to our surprise, the veteran said, "I will still march forward with my Liberal party; I will never be hehind." (Loud cheers.) Which of us , could have hoped that Mr. Gladstone in his old age would champion our temperance cause and put the control, which may, I pray, prove to be the stamping out of the liquor traffic, in the hands of the pe,sple ? Who c3uld have foreseen that he would anticipate the demands of the working class for a fuller direct labour representation and that he would make this easy by advocating the payment of all members—a most far- reaching and urgent reform, and one which will greatly curtail the much-abused power of the possessors of wealth, who, at present, so often misuse their powers in electoral matters ? (Hear, hear.) The one advantage I see in the 1 ory dodge of stealing our reforms, such as Local County Government and Free Education, and passing them in some sort of inferior fashion in order to take the wind out of our sails, is that it obliges our party to go forward more quickly with new and more drastic measures of reform, such as we of- the advanced wing hail with delight. This is not the place to speak of political details. To-day is a gala day, and full of social pleasure. I saw the other day at Black- pool, that the candidate for the division, Mr. Walker, told the people that bazaars were very good things, be- eause he had actually found his wife at one of them 17 years ago. (Laughter.) Now, Mr. Booth's matrimonial , agency does not smile very much on us at a Liberal bazaar, where we are safe from any matches except in the case of the soundest Liberal women. (Laughter.) ' This, therefore' appears to me to be a very safe affair. , This is a very beautiful bazaar, and I would like to add my testimony to that of Mr. Roberts to the indefatigable zeal of Miss Burgess, Miss Dutton, as well as to that-of Mr. Holmes. We want the sinews of war; and when we have got them we will use them. When you have got the money, you must get a candidate. lam told on all sides that the difficulty of getting candidates is very great, for this reason—and it is a very encouraging reason—namely, that so much work now-a-days is ex- pected from them that the busy ones cannot find time, and the lazy ones don't feel inclined to do so. (Laughter.) But when we get our paid members, we shall be able to have men who, instead of giving the fringe of their time, will givei the whole of their energy to the legisla- tive work n this country. May I say a word about electioneering in this town ? It is a matter of great grief to me to hear from all parts of the country how terribly is intimidation practised. It passes all belief. Whether from capitalists or landowners, or from customers at shops, every person who intimidates or boycotts anyone of a different political persuasion to themselves is a con- temptible person. (Cheers.) I am not sure that we Liberals are particularly immaculate in this matter. The old leaven is strong. We say that those who are with us are, perhaps, more entitled to our comrade- ship than those who are against us, but strain a point, and make an effort to deal with those of the opposite political persuasion, and thus set an example, for rith what measure ye mete it shall be meted to you again. (Applause.) If Liberals didn't set the example of a more high-minded tolerance, and of a more perfect justice, 'how shall the party of privi- lege ever learn that democratic lesson? There will be reprisals, and by-and-by, with the fierce contest which will rage in our midst. England will be an intolerable place to live in, where everyone is a foe. After the elec- tions are over, let strife be forgotten, and let us all join hands in our different ways to work for the good of our district. It will be a gritit lesson for you women in Warrington to take a part in public life, for you will learn self-control in great matters which is much needed. You will learn how to respect your neighbour's opinions, and how, as well as fighting hard for the cause, not to let temper or vindictiveness enter into your minds. May I say a word about the Manchester election, which is I filling our hearts? We have there a candidate who is tra- ly enlightened, absolutely straightforward, and who wiil never have any trickery with principles,any skating over thin ice. He has illumined many hundreds of readers by his splendid newspaper, which has been the fearless and staunch advocate of all that is best and worth caring for in Liberalism. As to his competitor, it is difficult to be- lieve that any working-man can be found to support him. One anecdote of him is enough to make me feel that working-men if they have any reasoning powers in them, will not vote for him. I read that in sending his subscription to the Orphan Fund of a railway company he wrote thus :—" I have serious objections to subscribe to a society which includes strikes in its programme." Now, how long are the working-classes of this country going to accept any eleemosynary help from the richer classes when they deny to them that right of combina- tion which alone will make them independent, and put them into a dignified and self-respecting position, where I no almsgiving is needed, where there are sufficient , wages and reasonable hours of work, and a condition of life exists in which the liquor traffic shall be rooted out of the land, when working-men shall pay their way without the patronage of the rich ? (Hear, hear and applause). This is the programme Mr. Scott has, before him. This is the goal he strives after, and if the working-men of Manchester prefer Sir James Fergusson, you Liberals in Warrington must go over and teach them a lesson, and show them what true Liberalism is, and what the true self-interest of the working-classes is. Now, find your candidate, and let him be as good as Mr. Scott is, and from these two places send men you can rely upon in days of difficulty- in the House—men who will lead rather than follow, and who will be the champions of what we believe in, and who will not be at the mere nod of expe- diency or opportunity. I have now much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Cheers.)

div.head: VOTE OF THANKS.
div.p: VOTE OF THANKS.

Miss DUTTON, in proposing a vote of thanks to Lady Carlisle for her presence and services, said she hoped the audience would pardon her addressing a few words to them after the noble and spirited address which had been given by her ladyship. She wished to express to her the thanks of the ladies of the bazaar, and the members of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, and that fact had induced her to break the silence which, as they knew, went without saying was a perpetual characteris- tic of the weaker sex. (Laughter and applause.) War- rington Liberal women would be cold indeed if they for- got the fact that Lady Carlisle was the first to rouse them to realise their privileges as daughters of Britain, to go a step further for the good of their country, and to do something to better the condition of their countrymen and countrywomen. (Applause.) Very gratefully they desired to thank her,and assured her that her words had been an inspiration to them, and had helped them to realize what a delight it was to work together for freedom, light, progress, sobriety, and truth. But most of all they thanked her for that, while urging them to the very highest sphere in politics, she had not ignored the fact that a woman's best and highest and most prized privileges were those of her home and her family; and she trusted that every member of that As- sociation would always feel of the opinion that those simple homely duties—they were not always simple, but they were the sweetest—must and ever would be their inestimable privilege and their highest heritate. (Hear,

div.head: Tin EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1891.
div.p: Tin EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1891.

hear,and applause.) They should, however, never fulfil them less well if they widened the sphere of their in- fluence by working and speaking in those great political causes, which were, slosey perhaps.but surely, bettering the condition of every class of the community in their be- loved country. (Loud applause.) Miss Dutton concluded by expressing an ardent wish that Lady Carlisle would long have health and strength to prosecute her great po- litical and moral mission,and her noble temperance work which all must so appreciate, and she also asked, her ac- ceptance, in the name of the Women's Liberal Associa- tion, of a beautiful bouquet. (Loud applause.) Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD seconded the motion. He said Lady Carlisle was a very uncommon lady. She pos- sessed the intellect and strength of purpose that is seldom found either in man or woman. He had heard many addresses in his time, but he had never heard one which was more eloquent or contained more words of wisdom. If they acted upon what she had said, they would be all better men and women. (Applause.) Mr. HENRY LEE supported the motion, and expressed a hope that the bazaar would be a great success. He had been very much pleased with the remarks her lady- ship had made. They had the true democratic ring about them, and it was not often they got from a lady sentiments so broad and so sweeping. (Applause.) Mr. E. BARLOW also supported the motion, and said it was a pleasing variety to come to Warrington after the turmoil of the Manchester election, and to see such a different scene. He hoped they would soon have occa- sion to congratulate themselves upon a victory which would be of the utmost importance to their party. (Ap- plause.) The rgolution was then put, and heartily agreed to. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes next handed a bound copy of the official handbook containing a suitatale inscription to her ladyship. The COUNTESS, in reply, said: lam very grateful to you for the very kind manner in which you havereceived the motion. I would also thank the ladies of the War- rington Women's Liberal Association most cordially for this most beautiful bouquet. I am delighted to have heard your Secretary, Miss Dutton. lam sure that the Women's Association will prosper, as it is guided by such ardent and excellent women. Our business to-day and for the next two days is to gather up £l,OOO, to enable us to prosecute our fight. We must get to work and raise that amount. The next business will be to find a candidate, to run him and to make him victorious. If you wilt do these things, add to them a third: extend an invitation to me to come and fake part in a coag,ratu- latory meeting over your successful Liberal candidate, you will not find me refuse the privelege. (Applause) The band then played the National Anthem and a a grand march which had been composed for the occa- sion by Mr. Whitehead.

platform did much to grace the room. It contained plants and ferns wnich had been sent from the gardens and conservatories of Mr. John Crosfield ; Mr. Natal', of Nutgrove Hall, St. Helens ; Mr. Robinson, of The Twiggery, Manchester-road; and of Councillor Shaw- Green. The refreshment stall on the platform was heavily burdened with a very choice selecbion of edibles, and was gracefully attended to by the ladies in charge. The Gypsy Tent and the Tradesmen's Stall, although in the unpretentious background, were by no means un- noticed, and did a very considerable business. Up in the gallery the Firth Mattrass Company,of Friars Green. Warrington, displayed some of their wire mattrasses and bedsteads.

• and their clear consciences to help them in the course which they were persuing. It had been said by one whose name they all named w ith reverence—he spoke now the words of John Bright as nearly as he could remember them—that that legislation failed which did not reach the cottage, for after all, a nation dwelt in the cottages. (Hear, hear.) And so it came that, year by year, they were more determinedly setting themselves to that legis- lation which should go home to the cottages of their sountry and should purify the lives of those homes. He had spoken of the keen wit and readiness of action which characterised their women, but let him enjoin them not to expect too hasty a result from the efforts which they put forward as politicians. They would need to possess themselves in patience. The study of history without which they could do little to amend the evil of the present, history which had been called the teach-s jug of philosophy by examples, marked certain eras in the case of a nation's life, but those events which bulked largest were simply the catastrophes, and they were too apt, he thought, to look for results which should bulk large before their eyes and overlook the persistent steady effort which they must patiently make to achieve the objects which they had in view. An American poet had spoken of the "page of mingled blood and war, pillage and strife, which man called history." Now, they wanted to achieve some of those great things, but let them make sure of the footing upon which they were seeking to achieve those things ; let them plod along, in the background if need be, to make the ground sure and safe and firm for those who should come after them, and do even greater deeds than they were seeking to accom- plish. History was still going on around them, and therefore he appealed to their memories in proof of what he had just said about the need of patience. They found that many ladies who were coming into the arena of politics now for the first time, were very full, as a woman's heart must need he, of a desire to see their pet objects immediately accomplished and they were some- what hasty, and if he were not speaking of women, he might perhaps say petulant, when they found that other things had to precede the subjects they had at heart. Let him remind those who had been observers of politi- cal events during the last 30 years that if they would pass through their minds the questions which to-day seemed to be ripe for accomplishment, they would find that they had been ques- tions which had been agitated now for nearly a generation. Perhaps there was no subject which was more ready forrlegislation than that of Sunday Closing lf public-houses. (Applause.) They would say they all wanted it, and why should that not be one of the first things that a Liberal Government should undertake? (Hear, hear.) Why,it was in the year 1852 that Scotland gct that measure, and in the intervening years Ireland and Wales had attained the desirable goal, and yet they were still looking forward to what they desired. The question of Disestablishment might be treated in the same way. (Hear, hear.) It was another question which was ripe, and it showed them the difference between maturity in politics and maturity in Nature. The ripe fruit in politics remained upon the tree, whereas in Nature it dropped and was forgotten. All those questions were still remaining upon the tree for them to pluck 'the fruit at some future time. They must not expect all their pet schemes to be accomplished at once. (Hear, hear.) They were twitted by their opponents that they per- sistently stuck to the Irish question,but the next speaker after the one who had accused them thus, was almost sure to say that the Irish question was one of which they were ashamed, and which they put into the background. They might well let those accusers reconcile the differ- ences in their own tune, and go on pegging away at the great question which must be removed and which would be removed, so that they might get to other and more domestic questions to them as Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) Mr. CBOSFIELD then declared the bazaar open. Alderman Hounts moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfitld for opening the bazaar and for his well-thought out speech. Mr. T. MORRIS seconded.

Mr. C. Jackson Holmes next presented Mr. Crosfield with a handsomely bound copy of the bazaar programme upon which was a suitable inscription. The vote of thanks was cordially passed, and Mr. CHOSFIELD made a brief acknowledgment.

A glance at the stalls, heavily laden as they all were with an immense varity of articles, was sufficient to de- monstrate how energetic had been the work of the ladies of the Sewing Co:nmittee and with what generosity their efforts had been backed up. And, indeed, the stalls were not at first found adequate to held all the commodi- ties that were to be displayed. The national stalls were arranged around and under the galleries, and each of them -vas fronted with a scene emblematic of the coun- try represented. Looking from the platform to the other end of the room was to be seen the " Ice Palace" of Montreal, to the right were Norway and Canada, and to the left Switzerland and Siberia, and filling up vacant places between these groups of stalls were the Gipsy Tent and the Tradesmen's Stall. On the platform itself was the refreslimant stall, and immediately in front the flower stall. Away in a corner was the entrance to the "Fairy Grotto or Mystic Cavern." In addition to the pic- torial embloms,some of the assistants at each stall wore costumes suggestive of the garb of the nations they: for the occasion, represented. Each of the stalls contained one of Jones's sewing machines to be sold on commission, but the price of the first machine sold was to go to the bazaar fund. Copies of the Grand March, composed by Mr. E. Whitehead, dedicated to the Coun- tess of Carlisle, were also to be had at each stall. The Switzerland stall contained a large quantity of rich material and beautiful needlework ; and there were also gipsy tables, dolls, and much variety of wearing apparel tastefully displayed. The appearance of the Siberian stall which adjoined was varied by some neatly framed pictures, although it, too, contained a very full assort- ment of plain and fancy work. On the Russian stall were some fine paintings by Miss Mary Burgess, and other notable objects on this stall were a handsome silver- mounted, claret jug, and an art blanket. At the other side of the hall, the English stall was graced with a marble bust of the Prince of Wales, a hand-painted screen, and a very attractive looking album. Besides these of course it was stocked with an endless variety of other commodities. The exhibits at Norway stall were exceedingly varied, but the one which *drew most his skill. div.head: AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: THE AMUSEMENTS.

A feature of the bazaar was the variety and the excellence of its amusements. The visitor who could not find something in this line to suit his taste must have been of a singularly unaccommodating temperament. The gallery was partitioned with curtains into a number of apartments and in these the various performers enter- tained their patrons. The Warrington Amateur Minstrel Troupe, who claimed to be the "great rivals of the Moore and Burgess and Sam Hague Troupes" and who had never condescended to "play in London," were in evidence every night of the bazaar, and gave the latest comic and sentimental songs, duets, choruses, kc. In fact they were in advance of the times and announced that they would perpetrate "next year's jokes." In addition to these there was a light seance and magnet entertainment, there were "marvellous, mysterious, magical and musical Marionettes," and there were the " wonders of science, or the new cure of the 21st cen- tury," a great " decapitation scene" being introduced. Under the staircase leading to the balcony there was a shooting saloon, at which the charge was one penny "per shot, bullet or dart." One of the most admired of the amusements was the "Fairy grotto or mystic cavern" at the foot of the stage. It had been inuented, designed, and arranged by Mr. F. J. Dell, of Sankey-st., Warrington, to whom it was in every way creditable to him. As a glowing description of the grotto we canno'; do better than quote the following from the handbook of the bazaar :—" The visitor, having passed the portals of tke fairies' mystic abode, finds himself in a vestibule, from which winding paths run in all direc- tions, forming a kind of maze. Taking one of the paths at random, the visitor, after walking some distance, comes across a beautiful cavern, brilliantly illuminated, ia which the weary traveller may rest and partake of refreshment. Whilst sitting here, the sound of rippling water reaches the ear, and taki.lg the path whence the sound arises, a scene of great beauty is presented. Look- ing through a dense foliage of ferns and wild flowers of all descriptions, a waterfall of refreshing loveliness meets the eye, the water falling into a large basin, in which gold fish may be seen disporting themselves. Far in the background is a clear and limpid lake of surpassing splendour, the whole making up a scene of unparalleled beauty." There was also a large and efficient orchestra present under the honorary conductorship of Mr. J. B. Caldwell, and during the bazaar it played many excellent selections. The members of the orchestra were :—First violins, Mr. R. H. Pearson (leader), Mr. W. Brown, Mr. P. Caldwell, Mr. W. Knowles, and Mr. J. Roberts ; second violins,Mr. P. Walsh and Mr. R. Forster; violincellos, Mr. H. Bond, Mr. W. Parkinson, and Mr. Brownlow ; flutes, Mr. W. H. Podmore, and Mr. R. Bennett ; violas, Mr. G. Johnson, and Mr. C. Littlewood ; basso, Mr. R. Whitfield; ohoes, Mr. Thomas Ward, and Mr. J. Boardman ; clarionettes, Mr. Hipkis, and Mr. W. Clarke • horn, Mr. P. Brady; cornet, Mr. J. Hazeldine, trombone, Mr. Joseph Barton ; euphonium, Mr. T. G. Grounds.

div.head: HANDBOOK.
div.p: THE HANDBOOK.

The Bazaar Handbook, which had been printed at the " Examiner " office, contained no fewer than 90 pages. It gave the fullest information relating to everything connected with the bazaar, and many of the pages con- tained apt quotations. In addition to this there was an interesting history of the Warrington Liberal Associa- tion written by Councillor Henry Roberts, and for a frontispiece there was an excellent portrait of the late Mr. J. U. McMinnies, member for Warrington from 1820 to 1885. A handsomely bound copy of the handbook was presented to the Countess of Carlisle, Mr. W. Cros- geld, and Mr. John Rylands, who opened the bazaar on the respective days.

div.head: COUNTESS OF CARLISLE.
div.p: THE COUNTESS OF CARLISLE.

The Countess of Carlisle arrived at Bank Quay Station on Monday afternoon, and was met by Mr. and Mrs. J. Crosfield, and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes. She was driven to Walton Lea, Mr. Crosfield's residence, where she was entertained, a few friends being invited to meet her ladyship at dinner in the evening. On Tuesday afternoon at 4-15, she left Warrington from Arpley Station, her des- tination being Bowdon, where she was.having a ladies' meeting in the evening. • DONATIONS, &c.

Amongst the contributions received towards the bazaar funds were cheques for ten guineas from Mr. John Crostield, £lO from Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., £lO from Miss Harvey, Latchford, and £lO from Alderman Platt, J.P. It may be mentioned that the very handsome bouquet, which was handed to Lady Carlisle by Miss Dutton was the gift of Mrs. Massey, of the Market Place.
WEDNESDAY. SPEECH BY MR. W. CROSFIELD. J.P.

The bazaar was opened on Wednesday afternoon by Mr. W. Crosfield, J.P., of Liverpool. Mr. Z. Armitage presided, and amongst others present were Mr. John Rylands, Alderman Holmes, Councillors W. Pierpoint, H. Roberts, G. Plumpton. A. Browne ; Messrs. G. Mounfield, G. Mounfield, junr., W. Derbyshire, J. Walker, T. Bir- chall, W. Roberts, C. Jackson Hol:nes, &c. The CHAIRMAN, in brieity introducing Mr. W. Crosfield; said there were not very many in that part of Lancashire outside the borough of Warrington who were better known to them than Mr. W. Grosfield and to whose words they more readily listen. (Hear,bear.) He con- gratulated the ladies on the great success which they had achieved on the previous day, when a sum of £475 was raised. (Applause.) Mr. W. CROSFIELD, who was cordially received, said the task to which he had been called was an easy one arisiag largely from the success and the kindly manner in which the ceremony was performed on the previous day by the Countess ef Carlisle so that it seemed that he should but have to name the magic words "Open Sesame " as the signal for the wheels of commerce to go merrily round that afternoon as they did the day before. The words whieh Lady Carlisle addressed to them were in the spirit which marked all her utterances, and were the note of her action in all those kindly efforts which she made for the benefit of her fellow citizens. (Hear, hear.) But her words were also pitched in that tone of Liberalism which was indeed the master key which opened all the doors of opposition which opposed themselves between them and the progress of their nation. (Hear, hear.) That was not by many the first opportunity which had presented itself to him and of which he had availed himself of thanking the ladies of Warrington for their assistance in political matters. It was certainly fit that they should now have the assistance of the women of England. The times were when it was eminently unsuitable fpr women to mix themselves in political strife, but, thanks to Liberal legislation, they had got rid of a great deal of what was distasteful to a pure-minded politician, and certainly must have been distasteful to any woman who mixed herself in nubile life. But now that the paths were purified they could, with a good conscience, ask the women of England to help them in the task in whichthey were engaged as politicians. (Hear, hear.) Some one had said that the hand that rocked the cradle ruled the world, and if that was true it was right that they should ask their women not only to acquaint themselves with their practices and their aims, but that they should so study those matters as to be able by their ready wit

div.head: THURSDAY. SPEECH BY NA. ;CON RYI.4ANDS, .J,P,
div.p: THURSDAY. SPEECH BY NA. ;CON RYI.4ANDS, .J,P,

On Thursday afternoon, the bazaar was re-opened by Mr. John Rylands, J.P., in the presence of a fair attend- ance. Mr. W. Pierpoint presided, and amongst others present were Councillors Fleming, H. Roberts, and Black- burst ; Messrs. Z. Armitage, Claude Morris, T. Morris, C. J. Holmes, G. Mounfield, and W. Roberts.

The CHAIRMAN said that his first duty would be to tell them that, in consequence of the very lavish contribu- tions of goods by the ladies, the Committee found it absolutely necessary to keep the bazaar open for another day, and, with reference to Saturday the Committee had an idea that they would utilise the hall by having a concert of some kind, the objects of course being to help the funds of the Liberal party, which, duringthe last two days, had, he was glad to say, augmentedto a very considerable extent. (Applause.) That showed at all events the Liberal party of Warrington were quite ready to stand by those who -took an active part in its manage- ment. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the services rendered to Liberalism by the family of Rylands, he then asked Mr. Rylands to open the bazaar. Mr. Join./ RYLANDS, who was cordially received, said he thought that on that occasion business was more important than his speech. He was, however, rather pleased to speak at a meeting of that kind, as it was clearly a political meeting. As the Chairman had said, , peoople with his name had generally been Liberals. (Hear, hear.) They would no doubt have had it in their minds that they were likely to have a geueral election before long, and at a general election the incidental ex- , penses were sometimes rather heavy. He did not know the state of theirregister at the present time, but he did know that they would have a sery uphill battle to fight. I It was a curious thing that in every borough where they had a large number of public houses the Liberals always had an uphill fight. The question was, how was it that publicans as a rule were Tories? There must be some reason for it. Mr. Gladstone once said that the drink- ing habits of this country were a greater evil than pesti- lence and war combined, and he believed it was literally true. He had had a sort of political experience for over 50 years and he had thought a good deal about politics, and there was one thine' that struck him. It was this, that during the whole of that time Liberals had been fighting against evils and the Tories had been support- ing them. (Hear, hear.) He remembered as a boy taking a great interest in the question of slavery, and the Liberals were then anti-slavery men. He remembered his father taking the chair at a meeting in those days when young Tories got ander the stairs and let off squibs. (Laughter.) After that he remem- bered big placards with "No Popery,"—they knew what that meant. The Liberals were, then, as usual, on one side, and the Tories on the other. Then there was the question of "Justice to Ireland," and there was again the same division. Mr. Crosfield alluded the pre. vious day to history, and especially Irish history, and his (Mr. Rylands's) impression was that if anybody care- fully studied Irish history of the last 200 or 300 years and did not come out Home Rulers, he should be sorry for them. (Hear, hear.) Again, they saw that the drinking custom was an evil the Liberals were, as a rule, anxious to lessen, but what evidence did they see amongst the Tories that they wished to do anything of the kind? The publicans expected that, if they got any advantage out of any party, it would be the Tories. He perfectly well remembered at one election in Warrington he was at a poiling booth with a marked list in his hand, and it was his business to see if the voters voted as they were marked: During the first hour there was not one who was marked Liberal who did not vote Tory, and there was scarcely one that was sober. They all under- stood that. (Hear,hear.) After the first hour and a half the voters polled exactly as they were marked. He wa s

DEATH OF MR. W. H. SMITH.

Mr. W. 11. Smith, First Lord of the Treasury, and leader of the House of Commons, died on Tuesday afternoon at Walmer Castle, at ten minutes past three, after suffering acute pain towards the close of his life. At the time of his death only his wife and daughter (Mrs Codrington) were present at the Castle, the rest of his relatives having left owing to the improvement which until last Friday was manifest in his condition. A serious change set in on Friday night. On Friday lie went out as usual in his yacht and cruised about the Goodwins, but there was a strong easterly breeze at the time and it was very cold. There is no doubt that he caught a chill, for, upon his return to the Castle, symp- toms of gout manifested themselves, and he rapidly grew worse. Thepatient's condition caused great anxiety to his friends during Monday night. In the course of Tuesday morning his condition grew alarming, the gout pain becoming very acute. A telegram was accordingly despatched to Dr. Powell,who, taking the first train from Charing-cross,travelled to Dover, and drove over to Wal- mer, which he reached about one o'clock. At that time Mr. Smith was in a very critical condition, and it was soon seen that he was sinking fast. He passed away at ten nunutesafter three o'clock, the gout having, it is stated, reached his heart. Mr. Smith's illness first assumed a serious aspect so far back as the 12th July. For some weeks previous to that his health had been unsatisfactory, but wit:i characteris- tic conscientiousness he struggled with the arduous work which devolved upon him as Leader of the House until actually prostrated. His indisposition is understood to have originated in a severe attack of Russian influenza, but his most serious malady was gout, the attacks of which were rendered the more dangerous by the pro- found antemic state of the patient. The first telegram announcing the fatal termination of the illness was des- patched by the private wire which connects Walmer Castle with Lc,ndon, to the Queen at Balmoral, and the news was also promptly telegraphed to Lord Salisbury in the South of France, and to other members of the Cabinet. Mr. Gladstone on receiving the news sent the following message : " Mrs. Gladstone and I received with grief the news of Mr. Smith's death, and shall long retain the recollection of his kindly nature, his fine qualities, and his distinguished devotion to the public service."

Mr. Smith was born in London in 1525. His educa- tion began at the Tavistock Grammar School, was continued not at any University, but in the training school of business and political life. He began early to assist his father in the newsagent's business which has now reached such gigantic proportions, and he assisted with a will. It is said that there was no detail of the business, however humble, in which Mr. Smith was not ready to take apart himself; so that the workers in every department had in him a getwine leader, and must have had the feeling that they were assisting him, not I doing drudgery to which it was beneath their employer's dignity to put his own hand. A. sympathy was in this way established between Mr. Smith and the employes of Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son that never subsided. He had throughout his life the reputation of a kindly and considerate employer. He was extremely reluctant to t. 34 9ffice who it 7as IVO offered t 9 him, hie difficulty being his attachment to his own business pursuits. The man, however, who had the good fortune to defeat Mr. John Stuart Mill, as Mr. Smith did in his second contest with him in 1868, could not but be prominent. Mr. Disraeli bore him in mind, as he also bore in mind the hero of the South-West Lancashire contest ; and the Conservative party was more or less astonished to find included in the Ministry of 1874 the Lancashire lawyer Mr. (now Viscount) Cross and the London newspaper agent Mr. W. H. Smith, the former as Home Secretary and the latter as Financial Secretary to the Treasury. Both appointments were popular, at least outside the immediate ranks of disappointed aspirants after office, and upon the death of Mr. Ward Hunt Mr. Smith was promoted to the position of First Lord of the Admiralty. Mr. Smith married in 1858 Emily, the eldest daughter of the late Mr. Frederick Dawes Danvers. She survives him.

It has been arranged that the funeral of Mr. W. H. Smith shall take place to-day (Saturday) at Hambleden, where he worshipped when in residence at Henley. The ceremony will be as private as possible. At the same time a service will, it is believed, be held in London. Messages of condolence have been received from the Queen, the Prime Minister, and people of every shade of political opinion. The memorial service in memory of the late Mr. W. H. Smith will be held in Westminister Abbey on Satur- day afternoon. Canon Duckworth will officiate, and it is understood that representatives of the Queen and Royal Family will attend. A memorial service will also be held the same day at the Parish Church, VValmer' the Mayors of Dover, Sandwich, and Deal, and the Locil Boards attending.

div.head: CHURCH CONGRESS.
div.p: THE CHURCH CONGRESS.

The Church Congress at Rhyl dealt, on Thursday,with education. The Rev. H. Maude described theological study as occupying a more conspicuous place at Oxford now than it had done for centuries, vet he considered that the principal part of a student's training for the ministry should be got in a theological college.—Principal Rendall took the contrary view, believing they would be better trained in association with other men at univer- sity colleges or universities.

div.head: MA.NCHESTER ELECTION
div.p: THE MA.NCHESTER ELECTION

The decisive conflict between Sir James Fergusson and I,lr. C. P. Scott was fought out with tremendous energy in the ballot-boxes on Thursday. No petty election for many years past has been conducted with more keenness on both sides, and none has excited greater enthusiasm or more widespread interest throughout the city. The polling opened at eight o'clock under condition which, from a meteorological point of view at all events, were favourable. With all the prestige of having as their candidate a member of the Government. with a powerful organisation and a majority on the register,the Unionists were in high feather. That the Conservatives were provided with a superabundance of conveyances was shown by the fact that a perfect cavalcade of carriages and cars were to be seen drawn up in front of their committee rooms. In this matter the Liberals were a little deficient; but with the materials which they had at hand they worked with unflagging zeal up to the last moment, inspired by the presence of Mr. Scott and their doughty leaders, Mr. A. Forrest, Mr. Schwann, M.P., and Mr. Symonds. The poll closed at eight o'clock, and the ballot boxes were without delay taken to the Town Hall, the entrance to which was guarded by a force of police and barricades. Sir James Fergusson and Mr. Scott arrived while the counting was in progress, and were well received by the vast assemblage of people. At half-past nine his Worship declared the poll as follows : Sir J. Fergusson (C) 4,058 Mr. C. P. Scott

Majority l5O The result was received with great cheering, mingled with hooting by many hundreds of people. Sir James Fergusson moved, and Mr. Scott seconded, a formal vote of thanks to the Mayor for officiating. The newly elected member and his supporters at once adjourned to the Carlton Club, where speaking from an upper window, the Postmaster-General said he had had a hard fight, but the conduct of the election had been honourable to both sides, and he thanked his opponent for his kind and generous treatment. He was proud to be again one of the members for Manchester. A vast crowd had assembled in front of the club pre- mises, and they cheered vociferously, but some discord- ant sounds now and again interrupted the right hon. baronet's speech. The Liberal candidate and his friends went to the Reform Club, where Mr. Scott thanked the electors for substantially reducing the Conservative majority, and expressed the belief that at the general election it would be wiped out altogether.

FOOTBALL.

" Philistine " of the " Athletic News," gives a very readable account of the Warrington v. Widnes match on Saturday. iThe 'd following are his "crispy criti- ques" of the game --" A pleasantly contested game on the whole,though possibly disappointing to many. me unknown quantity—or rather quality—of Widnes has been demonstrated to their disadvantage. In the first half they had not a vestige of system or combination. They appeared too eager to think, too zealous to play, and too indiscriminate to score. They were fairly smothered at half back, and their troubles generally be- gan at that point. Whon the imaginative iusuris tjf possible victory had passed from them, and the bitter pangs of defeat were staring at them, then they began to strive with more skill to mitigate the evil that had fallen on them. But they were outclassed behind thei pack, and their efforts were without avail.

Warrington certainly possesses a team strong enough to defeat any combination in Lancashire. In the two Bates —they have got a couple of men who play together like machines and the young gentleman who delights in the pretty pet name of" Smack "is a player whose claims for county honours cannot be overlooked long. He is not a Senior Wrangler, but he can play football. Evans EIIOWS a disposition to be selfish and erratic in his passing. Of the wing men Lawless was very much off, while Webs— ter showed good form in the first half until he was in- jured,when his speed and usefulness were much curtailed. Boscow makes a full-back whose merits resemble the price of lard—fair and middling.

Of the forwards, Warrington are proud and justly so. They are a fine lot, smart, speedy, and good tacklers, and will compare with any other club with favourable re- sults. The Widnes team might be well called " Great Explctations," for this is what the imaginations of the dwellers in the town of chemic think about them. The forwards are distinctly good, and fairlS held their own in the contest. The team was let down badly behind, as before mentioned, but when they can get the halves into the way of getting the leather without the trouble of get- ting offside to do it, better things may be expected. The three-quarters and full-backs are smart enough,but they must have more idea what to do in an emergency than they exhibited on Saturday. Experience will do that for them, and they can't have it too soon.

Six league matches were disposed of on Saturday, and in every instance there was a big attendance. At Sun- derland about 10,000 persons witnened the defeat of Everton, who, as was the case last season, were beaten by a goal. Both clubs had opposed Scotch teams during the week, Everton defeating the Rangers at Glasgow, whilst the Wearsiders were vanquished at home by Queen's Park. The success of Sunderland on Saturday was therefore of the nature of a surprise. By their con- quest of Aston Villa Derby County go to the top of the League table, as they have the better goal average. This was the first reverse for the Villa this season, andstamps Derby County as a tip-top team. Moreover, they were without a player for nearly half the game. The Bolton Wanderers have lost four points in three days—two at Nottingham on Thursday, and two at home on Saturday. In this instance they went down before Accrington, thanks to the indifferent goalkeeping of Sutcliffe.

It is a question whether any Association club is just now as strong as Notts Forest. They are having a magnificent time of it, their only check being that at Everton by two goals to none. They ran away from the Canadians last week, and on Saturday disposed of their old rivals, Notts County, by three to one. At this match there were over 10,000 persons. The Canadians were strengthened by two new arrivals for their fixture with Scotland at Glasgow, but they were once more easily de- feated for all that. They must he Urine''s of these con- tinual losses. They are not proving the draw that was. expected, their matches being sparsely attended as a. rule. Notts Forest only took £6 at the gates, and yet had to pay the Canadians a guarantee of £4O.

Information was received at Hartlepool on Monday, of the foundering of the steamer Wolveston and the loss of half of her crew, while on a voyage from Bristol to New York. The crew of the abandoned Carnarvon steamer Annie were on Monday landed at Falmouth. Mr. Goschen, replying to a correspondent through one of his secretaries, states that income tax is payable on January Ist in each year, and the collector, having made one personal application for payment without effect, may distrain immediatoly without further notice for the amount.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. OCTOBER 10. 1891.

Lady Carlisle The four days' Liberal bazaar at which has been held in Warrington Warrington. during the week has been an excellent thing in many respects. It has been the means of removing the debt which was hampering the efforts of local leaders; it has brought both sexes together in arduous work for the common cause; it has resulted in the formation of a Women's Liberal Association, and an address from the Countess of Carlisle at the opening of the bazaar which is worthy of being read and re-read by every politician in the kingdom. It is the fashion in some quarters to decry the appearance of women in the political arena; it is assumed without any measure of prof that they are ,unfit for such duties; but if Lady CARLISLE and Miss DUTTON —who spoke on behalf of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association—may be taken as samples of what is to follow, we shall begin to think that the objection which men make to women taking part in polities is btsed not on a sense 'of their superiority but on a consciousness of their inferiority. For our part, we heartily I welcome the new departure, and look upon it as the beginning of a day of better things; but, at the same time, we recognise that Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD hit the nail on the head when he remarked that Lady CARLISLE is "a very uncommon woman, and she possesses intellect and strength of pur- pose which is very seldom found either in man or woman." This being the case, tkere is every reason for giving the fullest consideration to the utterances of her ladyship. It should be remarked, in the first place, that she is a strong advocate of temperance, and it is th profound conviction she has of the need of grappling with the evils of the drink traffic that has guided her purpose, stimu- lated her energies, and brought her actively into the field of politics. She thoroughly understands temperance workers, as one of them; and was en- tirely to the point in urging that "where there is a real, strong temperance party there is never any lack of enthusiasts, for the work that the tempe- rance party has to do is so uphill that it has turned temperance workers into enthusiasts." Further, she speaks of that which she knows and testifies of that which she has seen when she adds :—" Where much endeavour is made, joy is felt in the work, and endeavour brings its own satisfaction, even when no immediate result is achieved."

As the bazaar had its origin in "the eternal lack of pence," it was natural that Lady CARLISLE should make some reference to ways and means. She seems, however, to have got a wrong impression as to the state of affairs in Warrington in conclud- ing that a number of rich Liberals are "giving in their allegiance to the Tory brewer." It has not been by change of scene but • by passing off the scene altogether—it is by the death of well-to-do Liberals that the party in Warrington has seriously suffered. Still it is quite true that the rich through- out the country have a habit of dropping periodi- cally from the Liberal ranks : the more they have to conserve, the more Conservative they become. And this is what Lady CARLISLE has to say of this tendency : This exodus of the rich has taken place else- where too, and perhaps some of you might think it a great disaster; but I, for one, do not think it is wholly a loss, for when a political division is

managed by a few wealthy and socially influential persons, the constituency ia apt to become enervated and apathetic—the few have a tendency to think and decide and pay for the many, and we do not ges a sound robust democratic basis for our organisation,. and the absence of that basis is not compensated for by all the purses in the world."

These words are golden, and should be "learnt by heart " and acted upon by every Liberal in this district. It is no use blinking the fact that the. Liberals of Warrington,at any rate, have in the past been enervated through being relieved of the bur-

den of finance by such men as Mr. John CROSFIELD (who is still with us), and the late Mr. George CROSFIELD, MT. MCMINNIES, and Mr. Peter RYLANDS. All honour to the dead anti to th& living for what they have done, and they are held in honoured remembrance; but the time has come when the mass of Liberal electors, as they have ob- tained power and assumed responsibility, must be called upon to contribute a fair share of the sinews of war. There are few who cannot give something ; those who cannot give money must give their services ; and in this way the party may become strong not only financially but socially and , morally. We have not lost sight, it is to be hoped, of the lesson of the widow's mite. The workman who contributes his shilling—if it is all he can spare—will feel that he has a full title to exercise a voice in controlling a policy which may involve expenditure; and from the moment he becomes a contributor he will be more watchful alike as ix), policy and expenditure. Party management will thus be insensibly lifted out of the narrow groove in which it has a tendency to run, and Liberalism will be the healthier and the stronger for it. We have seen what can be done by a big bazaar; the good work which has been accom- plished by the women must be followed by the men in the same spirit of determination,persistency, and self -sacrifice,and the result will be that, in due time, we shall have Lady CARLISLE in Warr ington again—to congratulate the Liberal party upon victory achieved at the General Election.
Mr. GLADSTONE closed his labonrs The Freedom in the north with a speech, on of Newcastle Saturday, on accepting the free-

dom of the city of Newcastle' It has been a trying time for "the old man eloquent," but it is a delight to Liberals to kno w that, according to the latest accounts, he is- no worse for his visit to Scotland,and the centre of Liberalism in the north of England. By his speech to the members of the National Liberal Federation

he has set his seal to a great programme—a pro- gramme which shows that, apart from giving Borne Rule to Ireland, the Liberal party is the party of pro- - gress—the party, which has at heart the intereste of the masses, and the capacity to shape the means to the ends they have in view. On Saturday Mr, GLA DSTONE spoke as the newly-enrolled citizen rather than as the politician ; and the specific references which he made to Newcastle as it is now, and it as it was when it visited it twenty- - nine years ago, must have been very pleasing to the Tynesiders. Who but he with his unrivalled experience and unrivalled memory could have. given in brief the history of the agitation as to harbours of refuge, which led the people of Newcastle to provide works and dredge their own river on that gigantic scale which has had such a stimulating effect upon the growth and prosperity of the city? The lesson taught was one of the- benefit of self-help, and of the utility of the wide application of the principles of self-government I _ and free trade. Mr. GLADSTONE was not by any means slow to point the moral and adorn the tale,. at the same time referring regretfully to the fact. that the people of the United States have taken &- retrograde step in the matter of Protection. He believes that they will retire from the unsafe position which they have taken up; but in any ease, as England has stood so long alone by Free- Trade and benefitted so largely it, she cannot do better than continue to set a good example to the rest of the world. Proceeding, Mr. GLADSTONE said :

That is a triumph, gentlemen, upon which I dwell not so much because it has addod, as it has added, enormously to the wealth and number of our capita- lists, but because it has gone down to the middle classes and to the masses of the people,and because although we have still much to, do for them, in amending as I hope the conditions of their life, yet this great amendment has been achieved mainly through the operation of legislation from protec- tion to freedom—this great amendment has achieved that and upon the whole, as we know from the' labours of the best and most impartial statiscians, 50 per cent. have been added to the earnings of our workmen in general—sometimes more, sometimes less—but under such conditions upon the whole that. there is no over-statement of the case. The custody, gentlemen, of such results is a sacred duty. It is a duty that will require all your firmness, becausd after all there are temptations, to which we cannot expect all men al ways to be insensible, to seek their own particular interest by what they do not see to be,but what really is, the secrifice of the public good.

Looking ahead, the great statesman perceives that a time is rapidly approaching when there will be a keen struggle for establishing what he terms "the rights of industry " ; and when, as he believes, England will again lead the way, and be as a beacon light to other nations. That his sym- pathies are with the masses has been shown in a thousand ways; and those who may think the prospect gloomy may take hope and courage in the fact that the hero of a hundred fights is still hopeful and courageous. He has faith in the future, and he kindles faith, for he speaks from experience, and his example is inspiring.

div.head: DANGERS OF THATCHED ROOFS.
div.p: THE DANGERS OF THATCHED ROOFS.

On Saturday afternoon, the thatched cottage in which Mr. Richard Bate of Crow-lane, Newton, re- sides, caught fire in the roof,and but for the prompt and energetic measures adopted, the result might have been serious. The cottage is one of three which are built in a block, all of which have thatched roofs. On Saturday afternoon a son of Mr. Bate observed smoke issuing from the roof, and at once informed his mother, who gave an alarm. Several men weie quickly on the scene, and they lent will- ing aid in the endeavour to quench the fire. A steady breeze was blowing, which greatly assisted the fire, but with a plentiful supply of water in buckets the workers were able to subdue the out- break, and beyond a large gaping hole in the thatch no serious damage is effected. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 61, I.lridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt.
IRISH MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

The Irishmen of St. Helens held an important meeting in the Assembly Room of the St. Helena branch of the Irish National League, Salisbury-st., on Sunday afternoon. There was a crowded attend- ance, Mr. M. Hackett, president of the branch, occu- pying the chair.—Mr. P. Hoare moved, "That we, the Irishmen ot St. Helens, pledge ourselves to help, by every means in our power, in sustaining the Irish evicted tenants in their struggles for justice." (Applause.) Mr. Geoghagan seconded, and Mr. M. Condon (Lancaster) supported the resolution. Councillors J. Burchall and J. A. Chadwick assured the Irishmen of their hearty sympathy with the cause of the evicted tenants, and said they should be glad to assist in any way they possibly could. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. John Kelly, St. llelens, also supported the resolution, which was carried unanimously.— Mr. John Kelly moved—" That we, the Irish elec- tors of St. Helens, pledge ourselves to support the Liberal candidates for the various wards through- out the town." --Mr. M. Briody seconded the resolu- tion, which was passed.—The proceedings termin- ated with votes of thanks to the speakers and to e chairman.
