Under the extraordinary pressure on our space this week, several letters and various items of news are crowded out.

In 1885 Sir J. Fergusson's majority was 1448 ; and in 1886 it was 327. On Thursday last it was reduced to 150; and yet the Tories call this "a great victory !" Another such " victory " at the General Election and Mr. Scott will be in while Sir James will be out.

Sir Benjamin Baker has been called in to in- spect the progress of the works for a permanent pipe line at Fiddlers Ferry in connection with the Liverpool Water scheme. He suggests sundry modifications in the way of working, but no great change, as he is of opinion that, slow as is the rate of progress nothing better can be done than keep "inching along." Meantime the Corporation are to be allowed to extract what comfort they can from the saying that "Rome wasn't built in a day."

At St. Helens the other day a publican who was summoned for selling adulterated whisky was in the happy position of finding the case dismissed because the liquor:sold was only 2A per cent. too weak. But if the law is broken it is broken; and it is the duty of magistrates to administer the law —not to make it. Henceforth the publicans of St. Helens will know that the magistrates will allow a 2a- per cent. infraction of the law. "It is only a little one," as the young woman said who was reproached for bringing a child into the world ma/ apropos.

After hearing Lady Carlisle and Miss Dutton at the Warrington Liberal Bazaar, on Tuesday, the remark was general that the gentlemen must "look to their laurels." But why look? They are gone. There can be no question that "the, lords of creation "were eclipsed by these "bright particular stars." We can't keep Lady Carlisle amongst us ; but the Women's Liberal Association have found a most able and graceful spokeswoman in Miss Dutton, and they must make use of her. She will be an acquisition to the platform of the Liberal party.

-- Raffling at bazaars held for religious objects is almost at an end—except in connection with the Established Church, where the conscience is free and easy as to this matter; but at political bazaars it goes merrily on as if it was quite the right thing to do. It was the rule at most of the stalls at the Warrington Liberal Bazaar,though " Switzerland " stall was an honourable exception. It will go on, we suppose, until some magistrate or Town Coun- cillor is dealt with, according to the language of the law, as "a rogue and vagabond." There are cases when it is a virtue to break the law, but they never occur in connection with raffles or lotteries.

Can any good thing come out of Warrington Writing in referonce to the Handbook of the Liberal bazaar,a master printer says: "I am mighty pleased with it ;" and, as he is an authority on the art of printing, we are "mighty pleased "with the compliment, though no mention of it would have been made, if it had not reached us from several sources—in one instance from a Liberal Councillor —that there are people who are offering to bet that the Handbook has not been printed in War- rington. Betting is not in our line, but we are will- ing to give £lO to the Infirmary if we do not prove, to the satisfaction of any two Councillors the sceptics may name, that every letter, line, and illustration has been set up and printed off at the " Examiner " Works, Bewsey-st., Warrington.

The death of Mr. W. H. Smith is a serious loss to the Conservatives. He was not a brilliant man, but he was a safe man—straightforward, even- tempered, and kindly. He ought to have been allowed to take his ease in the House Of Lords, seeing that his strength and health had failed for some time, but Lord Salisbury feared to face the difficulty which would be raised by having to find a new Conservative leader in the House of Com- mons. Who was it to be—Mr. Goschen or Mr. Balfour? It was hard to say, and so Mr. Smith, sacrificing himself, was induced to hold on as the leader who least divided the Tory party.

But the death of Mr. Parnell is the sensation of the week, a sudden victim to rheumatic fever. It is a relief now to look beyond the black year of his fall, and think of him as the bold, resolute, and clear-headed leader, who fought for the Irish cause against fearful odds, and led it to the verge of victory. From this point, his transgression was great, and the way was made hard to him. The incessant struggle and incessant worry of the last nine months have been too much for him. We cannot but leel sorry to think of his death; and yet, as in the case of the death of the Prince Imperial, it is obvious that his removal from the scene•will be for the good of a distracted nation.

The Weaver watermen, to the number of 300, are on the eve of a strike against the Salt Union. "The fiatrnen claim that they are DOW forced to work seventy hours at a stretch, and that the syndicate have stopped thirty steamers and barges, and wrongfully dismissed seventy employes, causing the other watermen to work almost night and day without cessation." Can it be that these English Trust-mongers are imitating their American brethren in grinding the faces of the poor? We shall see when the full facts become known.

Mr. J. T. Hibbert, Chairman of the Lancashire County Council, was appointed chairman of the Joint Committee which has been formed for the purpose of dealing with the pollution of the Mer- sey and its tributaries. He is .just the man for the post—with an energetic Committee behind him—for his experience has been large and varied, and, whilst clear-sighted, he is moderate-minded— qualities of the first importance in dealing with local authorities and private firms who make mischief in these waters. The task is a great one, but it must be accomplished, or the Ship Canal will become a nuisance instead of a blessing to the community.

Councillor Greening was on the right track, at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday, in urging that the information which the General Purposes Committee have obtained as to the appointment and emoluments of stipendiary magistrates should not "lie on the table," but should be given to the members and to the public. It happens far too often that Committees of the Council act as if they were the masters rather than the servants of the ratepayers. No resolution was adopted ; but it is understood that the inform- ation is to be lifted from the table and given to the public.

So far as there was any discussion on the subject, it was amusing to see how the magistrates repre- sented themselves as very superior persons who were in no need of the direction of a Stipendiary. But the most diverting thing of all was to see the Siamese Twins—Alderman Burgess and Councillor H. )1oberts—p11ll1no• hard for once in wholly different 41irections. The Alderman didn't at all enjoy being trotted out by his better half—so to speak—but everybody else did; it was done so nicely.

The object of the Church Congress at Rhyl is obviously to back up Churchmen in Wales in view of the disestablishment campaign. It was a matter of coarse to expect to hear that there were signs of Church progress in the Principality; but it was not expected that the President (the Bishop of St. Asa,pli) would venture to say that the Noncon- formists who were seeking to get the Welsh Church disestablished and disendowed were but a minority of their own cl”s. Where has his grace been living to get such nonsense in his head? Has he just dropped from the clouds?

Tt must be very nice, bye-the-bye to be Bishop of such a sleepy hollow as St. Asaph, with nothing to do and £4,200 a year for doing it. Who would wish to be disestablished from such a post? The writer remembers being one of a congregation of half-a-dozen at a service at St. Asaph. There was neither a bishop nor dean in evidence, and yet the officials were as two to one of the congregation. The lines of these ecclesiastics have indeed fallen in pleasant places. After the bishop, comes the dean

with £7OO a year; four Residentiary Canons with £350 each; and then there are two Archdeacons, with a Chancellor, Registrar, Deputy Registrar, and Secretary, all salaried of course. It is a pity to disturb such a happy family; but—oh the times and the manners !—they will be disturbed.

It has been held that magistrates who are share- holders in Railway Companies which possess licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquor render themselves liable to a penalty of £lOO, if they vote as Licensing Magistrates. It is obvious that their interest is ridiculously remote. Two magis- trates, who are holders of railway stock, recently voted not for, but in opposition to, the license for the Manchester Palace of Varieties. One of them has challanged an action in order that the point at issue may be clearly determined; and writs have now been issued against both of them. It is satisfactory to observe that the action is,in a sense, to be a friendly one. The decision, whichever way it goes, will affect the position of a large number of justices who have hitherto scarcely known what to do as holders of railway shares.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

CHRIST CHURCH WESTON POINT. The Jubilee celebration was continued on Sunday, when the Rev. 0. Cookson preached two sermons to large congregations. ST. AMBROSE CHURCH BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES. The winter session was opened on Tuesday evening by a tea party and magic lantern entertainment. There was a good attendance. Mr. Reay of Bold, manipulated the lantern and the Rev. G. A. Le Bert, presided. POOR BATE FOR RUNCORN. On the application of Mr. W. Sutton, assistant over- seer, Runcorn, the magistrates on Monday signed a poor rate of Is. in the L for that township for the ensuing half year. This rate is estimated to realise £2,857 13s. There are no arrears on the old rate. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH:WIDNES. The pulpit at this place of worship was occupied on Sunday by the Rev. James Marwood, of Seacombe, who preached on the subject of " The Christian Race," and "The Mind of Jesus." There was a large congregation at each service.

WIDNES TRADESMEN'S CRICKET CLUB. At a meeting ot the club on Wednesday, Mr. James Carroll was presented with a bat, given by Mr. T. Smith, president of the club, for the best batting aver- age, and Mr. J. A. Briggs was also presented with a bat in commemoration of his first 50. ST. MARY'S CHURCH, WIDNES. The harvest thanksgiving services were continued on Sunday, when the Rev. G. Garrett, M.A., rector of Kil- meague, County Kildare, Ireland, preached two power- ful sermons. fhe choir rendered special music. At the evening service the church was crowded to excess. TEACHING FRENCH AT RI7NCORN. Monsieur Mounier, of Liverpool, teacher of French to Runcorn School Board, delivered a free lecture in Green- way-road Board School on Wednesday evening. The title of the lecture was" How to learn French" and , proved highly interesting to the large number present. LICENSING MATTERS AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the licenses were transferred of the Camden Hotel, Surrey-st. from the late William Collett Mason to Frederick Hancock; Rutter's Vaults, Brunswick-St., from Mrs. Priss to Peter Brown; the Halton Castle Hotel, from A. H. Brookes to Ellen Powell. HUTCHINSON-ST. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. On Sunday the annual services of thanksgiving for the harvest were held and the preacher was Mr. James Peters, of Buckley. In the afternoon a musical service entitled " Gleanings from the harvest" was rendered. Mr. Newburn occupied the chair, and Mr. S. Drought was the reader.

RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. The first concert of the season will be given in the Public Hall on Monday evening, and those who neglect to be present will miss one of the greatest musical treats of the season. The following celebrated artistes have been engaged: Vocalists Miss Dews and Signor Foil ; solo violin, Senor Arbos ; solo pianist Senor Albeniz. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES. The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday, v‘hen the Rev. J. E. Rattenbury, of Didsbury, preached to large congregations. He also delivered an address to scholars and friends. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown. Brief and appropriate addresses were delivered by several members of the congregation. GOSPEL UNION MisstoN, RubroonN. The hardest thanksgiving services were held in Hope Hall, on Sunday. In the morning the local evanglist preached, the Rev. J. Martin (Methodist Free Church), in the afternoon,and Mr. Yeomans, evangelist of Widnes in the evening. On Monday evening the service of song "Seed time and harvest " was rendered by the Widnes Gospel Union choir, under the leadership of Mr. W. Mar- shall. Mr. Woodland read the narrative. HALTON TRINITY WESLEYAN CHAPEL. The harvest festival in connection with this chapel was held on Sunday, when special sermons were preached, in the morning by the Rev. W. Arrowsmitla, and in the evening by the Rev. J. W. Lightly. A ser- mon waf also preached on Monday evening, by the Rev. J. Hanby. The chapel had been prettily decorated for the occasion by lady members and friends of the congre- gation. The services were well attended, and collections were made in aid of the trust fund. CONCERT AT WIDNES. In aid of the proposed Parochial Buildings in connec- tion with St. Paul's Church, a concert was given in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening, and a large company as- sembled. Mr: .Tosef Cantor's concert company was en- gaged. and included Madame Laura Smart, soprano : Miss Kate Meredith, contralto; Mr. J. T. Jones, tenor; Mr. Edward Grime. bass ; Mr. V. L. Needham, solo flute; and Mr. Cantor, buffo and humourist. A programme of varied and admirably selected items was gone through in capital style, and the audience demonstrated their appre- ciation. Seleetions of music were also given by the Jubilee Brass Band under the leadership of Mr. J. Ains- worth.

RUNCORN CADETS OP TEMPERANCE. On Tuesday evening, the Committee, officers,and mem- bers of the Runcorn Guide of Youth section of Cadets met at Regent-st. Schoolroom for the purpose of pre- senting to Master John D. Bisbrown, two prizes won by him in the National Cadets' prize competition, the first prize being a handsome volume, "The Realm of the Ice King," a narrative of Arctic exploration, awarded for the best writing from a copy of a piece of composition ; and the second prize,a beautiful volume," Leaders in Modern Philanthropy," by W. G. Blaikie, D.D., awarded for the second best drawing of the front elevation of a house.— Mr. Thomas Cooke, Grand Scribe of Cheshire, presided. Mr. Thomas Heesom, Grand Patron of Cadets, in mak- ing the presentation, said he felt equally as proud in making the presentation as Master John D. Bisbrown, the winner of the prizes, would be in receiving them. The competition had been no mean one, nor yet -.cnfined to a small circle within their own locality, but had been open to all cadets in England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, which made the honour so much the greater. He then handed over the two volumes to Master Bisbrown,amidst much applause.—Mr. John Taylor, a member of the Corn- mittee,then made a few appropriate remarks.—Mr. Ed. Key, secretary of the Runcorn section, said he thought if anyone needed to feel proud and pleased at the success of their cadet member, he (the secretary), had. Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A WIDNES MAN AT RHYL. The Rhyl police,on Thursday morning, arrested a man named Elias Jones, late of Widnes, now em- ployed as a sweeper at the Church Congress build- ings, on a charge of stealing from the cloak-room at the Congress Hall,a silver-mounted umbrella,belong- ing to Mr. Bullock Webster, of Ely. The proceeds will be in aid of the Seamen's Institute, and it is hoped that the gate money will give the fund a good lift. FREE MA,,ONRY AT RUNCORN. 011 AN AT WIDNES. named Mary Murray, of was brought before Mr. folice Court, on Monday, charged w. y wounding Michael Murray. The pro -d a distant relation of the prisoner's and on S day night he went into her husband's house. A quarrel arose and it was alleged that the prisoner struck the prosecutor on the head with a poker. Dr. O'Keeffe said he attended the man on Sunday morn- ing. He was suffering from a contused lacerated wound on the back of the head, an inch-andi-a-half long, penetrating to the bone. There was also a wound on the top of the head and another on the side of the head.--As the prosecutor was not fit to appear, the prisoner was remanded for a week. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-øt., Warringtoa.—Advt.

SHOCKING ATTACK WITII A POKER AT. WIDNES. Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. T. S. Timtnis, Bridget Hughes, aged 47, and Michael Hughes, aged 20, her son,were charged with having on the previous afternoon unlawfully wounded Martin Hughes, the husband and father of the prisoners. It appeared that the father and mother had been separated for some time, and on the previous afternoon Hughes went to his wife's house in Barn-st., and stayed there drinking. Eventually a dispute arose, and the prisoners at- tacked him, and one of them, it was alleged, had strick him several times on the head with a poker. He ran into the street bleeding profusely from wounds on the head, and the prisoners were ar- rested. Dr. Hudson said the man was in the hos- pital and unable to attend court. He was seriously injured about the head, and both his eyes were blackened. The prisoners were remanded.

div.head: TtlE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, – OCTOBER 10, 1891.
div.p: TtlE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, - OCTOBER 10, 1891.
, W IDNES COUNTY COURT.-THE JUDGE AND
SCOTCH DRAPERS.

His Honour Judge Shand, yesterday, held q, sit- ting of this court at Widnes, when 239 plaints and 106 judgment summonses were dealt with.—Alfred Cohen, a Scotch draper, sued Thomas Cross, of Davies-st., for 75., in respect to a dress piece sup- plied to his wife.—The defendant said he did not know anything about it until he got the County Court summons. His Honour gave judgment for the defendant addressing the plaintiff, he said. "I have no sympathy with you. I know the way these things are done. If you supply goods to wives without the knowledge of their husbands you do it at your own peril."—Peter Nicholls, of Man- chester, sued Cross for 19s. for a dress piece also supplied to the wife, and the defendant obtained a verdict in this case. As the defendant was a flat- man and had had to travel from Rhyl, he allowed him .E 2 4s. 4d. for costs and loss of time and ordered the two plaintiffs to jointly pay the money. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—L and W. DurroN, Sankey-at.. Warr ington.—Ac'vt.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at the Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, Mr. J. Knowles, the vice- chairman, presiding. There were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. A. Thomas, J.P., and C. Reynolds,J.P., ex-officio; E. Aaron, J. Weir,T. Lewis, P. Hall, J. Hall, J. Brandreth, J. Edwards' John Wh itlow. Jas. Wbitlow,Baxter, Lowe,Parr,J. Stokes, and J. Ashton. clerk. FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME STILL DELAYED. At the fortnightly meeting of the Frodsham Parochial Committee on Friday, the clerk read a copy of a letter he had written to the Local Government Board on the 10th September, in respect to the formation of a special drainage district, consisting of portions of the township of Frodshain and Frodsham Lordship for the purpose of charging upon such district the expenses of providing and maintaining a water supply. The Board replied that they found from their official records that the Rural San- itary Authority had already borrowed money for works of sewerage and water supply for the township of Fred- sham and they pointed out that even if a special drainage district were formed in this case the loans in question would still remain chargeable upon the whole township. The Authority had already the means of effecting the object which they had in view, viz., that of charging the cost of the supply which it was now contemplated to provide upon the persons benefited by means of water rates and rents levied upon consumers under the provi- sions of Section 56 of the Public Health Act, 1875. Un- der all the circumstances the case did not appear to the Local Government Board to be one in which they would be disposed to give their approval of the constitution of a special drainage district,—After discussion Mr. Edwards moved that a deputation be appointed to wait upon the Liverpool Corporation and ascertain upon what terms they would supply Frodsham with water.—This not be- ing seconded, the motion was not put.—Mr. Robinson then moved, and Mr. Davies secGnded, "That this Com- mittee see no reason to alter their vieivs as set out in the resolution 'passed at the meeting of the Committee on the 10th August, 1891, That the scheme prepared by Messrs. Timmins for supplying the township of Frodsham with water except as to the erectioa of stand pipes be and is hereby approved and adopted, and that the neces- sary steps be taken to carry out the scheme, and to ob- tain the sanction of the Local Government Board to the loan required for the parpose and such resolution be and is hereby affirmed.'" There voted- for the motion Messrs. A. Thomas, C. Reynolds, sT. Robinson, T. Davies, And H. Tiley-5 ; Against, Mr. Sits. Edwards-1. Mr. Thomas moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr, Aaron seconded.—Mr. Edwards moved that the minutes be not confirmed; and he should not be acting up to his con- victions if he did not offer strenuous opposition to the scheme, which he said did not commend itself to the ratepayers,who were entirely against it. His proposition to send a deputation toLiverpool Corporation was a very simple one, as up to the present they have only an offi- cial statement that their charge for supplying Frodshain would be 9d. per thousand gallons for the 'first ten or fifteen thousand and 6d. per thousand gallons for the excess.—Mr. Stokes : Who puts in the plant ?—The Clerk: Frodsham township—the Sanitary Authority.— Mr. Stokes: That is important to consider.—Mr. Edwards said Tarporley was supplied at 6d. with a minimum of 3,000 gallons.and if Frodsham got water on anything like those terms it would be for a cheaper scheme than that of , Mr. Timmins. He had made a calculation and found that the latter scheme would be an annual charge on the ratepayers of £385. Under the Public Health Act, they had to provide 20 gallori.s per head of popula- tion. The population of Frodsham was 2,000, so that they would require 40,000 gallons per day. Now if they took the water from Liverpool Corporation at a mean price of 70., they would have an annual charge of £340 25. 6d.— Mr. Reynolds: Without a reservoir ? Mr. Edwards: Yes. There is not the slightest need of a reservoir. He mentioned several towns that had no reservoir. For such a simple purpose as ascertaining the charge of the Liverpool Corporation to be rejected showed the complete infatuation of the members of the Parochial Committee to Mr. Timmins's Scheme. Out of the 5 who voted for it two were gentlemen who com- manded the respect of the Board, but they were inhabit- ants of the Lordship and did not contribute one penny to the township. 'this scheme had been thrust upon the township by the Lordship. Mr. Reynolds: Question.— Mr. Lewis denied the allegation.—Mr, Edwards : What about the Vicar's letter P—Mr. Lewis : Re belongs to the Township as well as the Lordship. He is the Vicar of the parish.—Mr. stokes : what would be the cost of laying 6 miles of mains from Kingsley to Frodsham P—Mr.Thornas said it was estimated at £1,200 and there would be a meter house, which was a very costly thing indeed.— Mr. Stokes: What is the cost of the present scheme for pipe line and machinery P—Mr. Thomas: About £l9OO, but this included laying the pipes through the whole town. —Mr. Edward said the distance from Kingsley was only about three miles, and they had nothing official as to the £l,2oo.—Mr. Thomas : What will it cost for a water meter ?—Mr. Edwards : Say £loo.—Mr. Thomas : Nearer £5OO before you have finished with it. They are things which get very much out of repair.—Mr.Edwards: So does a gas engine.—Mr. Thomas: I beg your pardon. —Mr. Reynolds said the whole thing would have to be thrashed out before an official sent down by the Local Government Board, who would not sanction the expen- diture of a single penny until they had satisfied them- selves of the desirability of the scheme. He had asked Mr. Edwards whether he was afraid of a public inquiry by a Government official, because if not he (Mr. Rey- holds) did not 'see why he should not make an excellent case before him. As to Mr. Edwards's position it seemed to him that he was rather like the juryman who being one man out of twelve, could not understand how it was that eleven were so stupid that they could not agree with him.—Mr. Edwards said it was better to have an al- ternate scheme to bring before the Government Inspec- tor.—Mr. Thomas said the alternative scheme had been thrashed out before the Committee several times. He did not think the Liverpool Corporation would accept any less than Mr. Parry, the engineer, had quoted to their clerk, and they could not do without a reservoir.as they would then be entirely: dependent upon Liverpool for water. The mains might be turned off at any time; and if they had not a supply of water they would be left in the lurch.—Mr. Edwards : Oh dear, no! It is ridi- culous !—Mr. Thomas: How much water are they getting through the pipes now ? They are getting far from the full quantity as the pipes are blocked up with sand at a certain place.—Liverpool Corporation could cut them off at any time by giving notice after they had spent all the money inlaying mainsotc. They would have to pay much more to Liverpool Corporation than they could pump it for, and as the population increased there would be more profit for those who supplied the water. ,If the Government Inspector did not consider Mr. Tim- mins scheme a good one he would not pass it, but it was the cheapest pumping scheme ever proposed. The compensation te be paid would swamp any gra- vitation scheme; and the late Mr. E. Thiarnins an experienced and clever man, said the only scheme for Frodsham was a pumping scheme.—Mr. Stokes pointed out that several farmers who would not receive any benefit from a water scheme would have to contribute towards it and he entered his protest against such a state of the law.—Mr. Thomas: The Local Government Board won't grant a district.—The discus- sion had continued for an hour, and Mr. Brandreth pro- posed that it be adjourned.—Mr. .T. Whitlow seconded. —Mr. Reynolds asked if they would be any nearer after 12 months. They had been discussing the question for the last 15 months.—Mr. Edwards: Yes, we shalL—Mr. Reynolds pointed out that the scheme was carried by a large majority.—Mr. Rrandrath suggested that the ques- tion should be referred to a small special Committee.— Mr. Reynolds: You must absolve your Parochial Com- mittee before you do that.—Mr. Edwards: It is not a representative Committee.—Mr. Thomas: I beg your pardon.—Mr. Edwards: I don't beg yours.—Mr. Rey- nolds said the fact was Mr. Edwards was afraid to face a Government inquiry.—Mr. Edwards: No I am not.— The adjournment VMS carried by nine votes to six. BAD SANITATION AND FEVERS. The Medical Officer reported that an outbreak of typhoid fever had occurred at Stockton Heath. Pigs were kept about 15 feet from the door of the cottage and also at three adjoining cottages,while the pig manure was deposited in the privy receptacle of tyro of the cottages; the drainage was defective and one sewer inlet was not trapped. There were only two privies for four houses. He suggested the discantinuance of the pig keeping, re- construction of drainage, the provision of two additional privies with roofed ashpits. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Helsby. It was probable that the disease had been contracted elsewhere than on the premises, where there was nothing to account for the disease. The water supply on the premises was bad, but was not used for drinking purposes. Two cases had occurred at Manley awl one Jeath had occurred. Three cases of scarlet I fever were leported from Halton.—The usual instruc- tions were given. tra. H. G. LINAKER AND THE CLERK. A letter was read from Mr. H. G. Linaker, dated sth Oct., stating that with the exception of the books and papers required for audit he handed to Mr. Ashton on •

div.head: AL..RGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.
div.p: AL..RGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. Gossage at Widnes police court, on Monday, James Ryan, of no fixed abode, was charged wish burglariously breaking and entering the dwelling house, 20, Water-street, between Saturday night and Sunday morning, and stealing therefrom a quantity of provisions and clothing the property of Danial Crawley. About 4 o'clock on Sunday morning P.S. Strickland met the prisoner in Water-street. He was carrying a bundle, and in reply to the inquiries of the officer, he said he had received it from two women whom he did not know. lie was locked up on suspicion of stealing the goods and afterwards the sergeant discovered that they had been taken from Crawley's kitchen.— In asking that the prisoner should he remanded for a week, Superintendent Nohlett said there had been a large number of burglaries in the town lately,and he believed he should be able to connect the prisoner with some of them.—The prisoner was remanded. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et., ' Warrington.—Advt. THE OBSTRUCTION OF AN EXPRESS AT ST. HELENS.

At St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, Charles Woods, lodging in Raven-st., was charged on remand with unlawfully obstructing an express pas- senger train at St. Helens Railway Station. Mr. A. Preston prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-western Railway Company, and stated that on Thursday, 10th May, 1888, the prisoner, who was formerly a loafer at the station, was seen crossing the lines at St. Helens with one of the company's trucks. He was shouted to and warned not to cross, but he persisted in doing so. When he found! that an express train was upon him he left the truck, which was smashed.—Mr. D. Moss, station- master, gave evidence in support of the charge.— John Abberly, porter, and John Griffiths, signalman, gave corroborative evidence. Police-constable Jackson said he apprehended the prisoner under a warrant, and prisoner pleaded not guilty.--Prisoner informed the bench that it was true he dropped the truck, but he did it to save his own life.—He was then committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. CONFIRMA.TION OF A. DARRSBITRY LICENSE.

At the meeting of the Licensing Commiisiee- for the County of Chester held at the Session House, Knutsford, on Monday last, Colonel France Hay- hurst being in the chair, Mr. Arthur Browne, of Wart ington, applied for the confirmation of a seven days' license granted at the last Daresbury sessions to Mr. William Whitlow, of the Hotel, Preston Brook,in lieu of a six day's license previously held. Mr. Browne pointed out that this was no new ap- plication, inasmuch as about eight years ago Mr. Whitlow had a seven days' license, but gave it up for family reasons, and that he now wished to have the seven days' license for the purpose of supplying bone fide travellers and people connected with the Cana! Traffic. Mr. Whitlow had sometimes 60 horses in his stables and provided them with their require- ments,but could not supply the men with the ordin- ary necessaries of life. Mr. Whitlow gave evidence, as also did Mr. Jonathan Horselleld and Dr. Carru- thers, of Halton, near Runcorn, the latter saying that when stimulants had been required forpatients of his none could be got, as no one about had any license, and he had to beg it from Mr. Whitlow. The Committee unanimously granted the confirma- tion. PREMIER SAFETIES. Caah or Hire.—GARLAND. Warrington, —Advt.

div.head: AN HOTEL THIEF AT NEVirTON.
div.p: AN HOTEL THIEF AT NEVirTON.

At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednes- day, Henry Bolton was charged with stealing, on the morning of the Ist inst., two bottles of stout, the property of Henry Hibbert, of the Blue Bell Hotel, High-st., Newton, Mary Addison. barmaid at the hotel, said the prisoner came there and had something to drink at the bar. She had occasion to go into the kitchen,and on coming back missed the bottles. She found the prisoner in the stack yard, and saw that his pockets looked bulky. She asked him if he had got the stout, and he took the bottles out of his pockets and handed them to her. P.C. Cameron deposed to apprehending the prisoner, and his replying to the charge, "I can't say anything at all." The prisoner was then charged with stealing, on the 30th ult., a box containing 32 cigars, value 145., the property of Jane Mai sh, land- lady of the Hand and Banner Hotel, High-street, Newton. The landlady proved the case. The theft had been perpetrated during her absence from the bar. P.C. Cameron said that on searchiag the pri- soner on the Ist inst., he found 17 cigars in his coat pocket. He said he had got them from a labouring man the previous day, and afterwards that he did not take them from the Hand and Banner. The prisoner now stated that he had given some coppers to a man who begged from him, and he gave him the cigars in return. It appeared that the prisoner had been convicted in 1890 of stealing brandy ,in Otley, Yorkshire. He was now sent to jail for 14 days with hard labour.

He noticed in the newspaper reports that Mr. Ashton was reported to have said in reply to a question asked by Mr. Thomas , Lewis as to whether he had asked for the plans at his , office "No, I have not asked for them, they are sup- , posed to have handed everything over to this Authority. If I were to ask for anything I should like the authority of the Board." The letter continued "I would point out that your reply has given rise to remarks being made that I had purposely kept back certain plans and papers in order to cause trouble and annoyance to the Authority and yourself. I would inform the Authority that this is not so. Moreover I have always been willing to give you every assistance in my power with respect to the work of the Union generally, and your son, Mr. George Ashton, will doubtless bear out what I say, as he has frequently come up to my office for information, which I have always freely given. I trust that you did not mean to convey any reflection such as is spoken of. So far as my memory serves me the plans of the Weston sewerage will be found either in the Deed Chest or in the Sanitary Cupboard attached to ' the contract for the sewer. The plans of the Appleton and Frodsham sewerage were handed to Mr. Wells or Mr. Farrington for use in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, in respect of the sewers and out- falls of sewers within the district of the Authority. In conclusion I may say that I shall always be pleased to give the Authority or yourself any assistance that lies in my power."—ln reply Mr. Ashton stated "The news- paper report is not correct. My reply to Mr. Lewis could not and I certainly did not intend that it should bear the construction you say has been put upon it. I meant it in this way, that I did not think it necessary to ask you as you would already have handed over everything you had belonging to the Authority, and when I was directed to write and inquire I merely asked to have my instruc- tions in the filiape of a resolution as a better means of recording on the minutes what had taken place. This was the invariable practice of your late father, and I have not sat so many years at the Board without profit- ing by noticing his mode of doing the business. You are quite right, as you had to return some of the books until after the audit. I have frequently had to communicate with you and you have always freely given whatever information I have required. I shall of course read your letter to the Authority and as this letter explains what was meant and will I trust remove any wrong impression there may be."—The Clerk said he would refer to the contracts.
..._,..4//p.--. VOLUNTEER SHOOTING MATCH.

On Saturday, a friendly match took place on the Weaverham range, between a . team of ten men ' from the Runcorn Rifle Club, and a similar number ' of the members of 1-1 Company, belonging to the same regiment, viz., the 2nd (8.C.) V. B. Cheshire' Regiment. The day was fine, but as the visitors were late in arriving, it was decided to commence firing at 500 yards. Seven rounds per man were fired at this distance, and also at 600 yards, when it was found too dark to fire at 200 yards, and the match was declared finished, the result being a victory for the visitors by five points. Considerable interest was aroused when it was found previous to the firing by the last two men on either side that the number of points made by the teams were exactly equal. div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF UUCRDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF UUCRDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Mr. Jarnqs Birchall (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. T. Stapleton- Bretherton, J.P., Johnson, Hellas, Wareing, W. 8., Long- ton, Ranson. Middlehurst, Lowe, Buckley, Peover, Sy- der, and A. F. Mann (clerk). RELIEF.—The Clerk reported that there were 448 per- sons in the workhouse this week, 531 last week, and 491. in the corresponding week last year: Outdoorrelief had been granted to 2,711 persons at a cost of £2lB 95., against 2,966 at a cost of £248 6s. id. last year. ACCOMMODATION FOR LIINATICS.—A letter had been re- ceived from the County Lunatic Asylums Committee asking the opinion of the Guardians in regard to the proposed increased asylum accommodation. The Clerk was instructed to reply that the Guardians preferred to remit their pauper patients to the ltainhill Asylum as it was within the Prescot Union and the conveyance was less compared with what it was to other establishments and the friends of the patients were able to visit them frequently. Eaving regard to the statistics for the union, i namely, 1 lunatic n 639 in 1881, and 1 in 600 in 1891, the Guardians did not regard the increase as abnormal. They anticipated the increase to continue at the same , rate.—The Chairman asked if the Guardians had any ' other remarks to add to the reply.—Mr. lididdlehurst suggested that the Guardians should recommend that medical officers be paid annual salaries for their examina- tions in lunacy cases instead of fees. He thought that in many doubtful cases the fees might determine the case.—The Clerk pointed out that this would require qn amendment of the Act of Parliament and the subject dropped. THE WIDNES VACCINATION DISTRICT.—A letter was read from the Local Gevernment Board intimating that they could not assent to the division of the Widnes Vac- cination District into two districts.—Mr. Peover gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the ap- pointment of Dr. -McLennan as vaccination officer for the whole of the district. RESIGNATION.—A. letter was read from Miss Elizabeth Clarke resigning her post as assistant matron. This was the principal business.

div.head: RIVAL BUTCHERS AT RITNCORN.
div.p: THE RIVAL BUTCHERS AT RITNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Tom Clough: butcher, Regent-street, was summoned for assaulting George Tams, butcher. A summons had also been issued charging Tams with using threats to ClGugh, who alleged he was in fear of bodily harm. Mr. E. W. Humphrey's appeared for Tams and Mr. F. A. Lake for Clough.—Mr. Humphreys said for five or six years Clough had been in the employ of Tams, who kept two shops, one in Church street and one in Regent-st. It the beginning of . year Clough left his employ and set up an op- position shop in Regent-street, directly opposite Tams, , and until this occurrence on Saturday flight the 26th September, Tams had nevor spoken to Clough. There had been some friction between the assistants of these rival butchers, and on Saturday night about a quarter. past eleven, dough's assistant, Charley Watson,caine in- to Tams's shop and had some words with the assistant, Slater. 'rams quietly ordered him away,and then, with- out warning or any preparatory quarrel, Clough came across and struck Tanis a violent blow on the mouth, causing it to bleed profusely. Tams had no vindictive feeling, and he had written to Clough saying he would accept a written apology and allow proceedings to drop, but he had received no reply. As to the charge of utter- ing threats the only thing that could be construed into a threat was the fact that Tams after he had been struck said had he had his steel he would have run it through him.—Mr. Tams corroborated this statement, and John Bostock, an employO, gave similar evidence. He said on the day previous to the assault, Watson dough's assistant shouted to Slater "You had to cry to come back," Slater replied " what else have you on besides fleas ?" Watson on Saturday night came to ask what Slater meant by this, and Mr. Tams ordered him away.—Harry Webster and L;zzie Squire also proved the assault.—Mr. Lake said there had been considerable feeling between the assistants of the two tradesmen, and on Friday Slater suggested that Clough's shop contained nothing but fleas and disinfect- ing powder, which was a disgusting suggestion to make, and would tend to injure a man in the meat trade bum- ' ness. On Saturday night when Mr. 'rams visited his shop, Clough sent Watson to inquire what was meant by such a statement. Slater said he meant nothing by it, and then Tams ran him out of the shop and told him to go away. Ciough,thinking Tams was about to assault his assistant,went across, and Tams,gesticulating wildly, ordered him from the pavement, Ile called Clough a scamp, a scoundrel, and trash, and Clough thinking Tams was about to strike him, did what he was perfectly entitled to do, struck the first blow. Tams rushed into the shop shouting "Where is my steel? If I had only got my steel I would run it into him." Clough was called upon and gave his version of the affair, and stated that 'rams was a violent man and he was in bodily fear.—P.C. Dutton, C. Wat- son, Mr. Boyle, and Mr. Bancroft, all gave evidence as to the threat.—Mr. Humphreys pointed out that it was , not until he had received the summons for the assault that Clough thought it necessary to ask for pretection. —Mr. Reynolds said the Bench considered the assault proved, and though Cough had had some provocation, it was not from Mr. Tams but from his assistants. He would be fined ss. and costs. The summons with regard to threats was dismissed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS

Mr. J. Knowles presided • over the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday. Present Rev. .1. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P., and Mr. A. Thomas. J.P., (ex-officio), E. Aaron, J. Weir, T. Lewis. P. Hall, J. Hall, J. Brandreth, J. Edwards, John Whitlow. James Whitlow, Baxter, Lowe, Parr, J. Stokes, T. Lea. and J. Ashton (clerk.)

div.head: SCHOOL INQUIRY OFFICERS.
div.p: SCHOOL INQUIRY OFFICERS.

Mr. Baandreth moved that the services of the School inquiry officers for Runcorn, (Mr. Bowyer and Mr. Howard) be dispensed with, subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board. Mr. Brandreth re- marked that now only about 2s. 81. a week was re- quircd for school fees, whilst previously it had been about £lOO a year, and these officers were not required. Mr. Weir seconded tho molon which was carried. MR. H. G. LINAICER'S CLAIM.

The next business was the consideration of the claim of Mr. H. G. Linaker for services rendered to the Board from the death of the late clerk until his successor com- menced the duties of the office. The claim was for £46 16s. 4d.—The Clerk said he preferred to be out of the room whilst this discussion proceeded, and he thereupon left the room.—Mr.Brandreth said this question had been before the Committee two or three times, but they had not come to a decision upon it. They had had several letters from Mr. Linaker, in one of which he had threatened that if the Board did not settle the matter he would make them. The Board had paid Mr. 11. G. Lin- aker's salary, £2 10s., as assistant clerk up to the 30th June, and they had voted him besides £lO for extra ser- vices. The late clerk died on the 16th March and Mr. Ashton was appointed on the 21st April, therefore Mr. Linaker was acting as clerk for about 37 days. The Board had paid the executors ef the late clerk up to tho 25th March. During the period Mr. Linaker was acting as clerk he received for the election of Guardians £67 ss. ld., £lO from the 'Rural Sanitary Authority, £4 4s. for removal cases, and £2 10s. as assistant Clerk, making a total ot £B3 19s. id. There was also voted to him £lO from the Board of Guardians, but this he refused, and sent in the account they were now con- sidering, which was for proportion of clerk's salary, re- muneration for posting up ledgers, preparing balance ?heets, &c.—After a brief discussion Mr. Stokes proposed that Mr. Linaker be paid £25 to cover all claims in order to avoid any unpleasantness.—Mr. Aaron seconded.— Mr.Jno.Whitlow proposed an amendment that he be paid £lo.—Mr. James Whitlow seconded.—The amendment was carried by ten votes to seven.—Mr. Brandreth : Well, we must exuect some law now. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The fortnightly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present. Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. Mc- Dougall, Mr. A. Salkeld, Mr. G. Moss (clerk.)
A YEAR'S SCHOOL ITTENDANCB.-INCREASE THROUOH FREE EDUCATION.

The Clerk presented a report of the School Attendance Committee for the year ending 29th Septemlser, 1891. This contained the following :—Although the Committee have dealt with. an increased number of cases, there is not a corresponding improvement in the attendance, but this is fully accounted for by the terrible winter whieh caused so much distress amongst the poor, and later by the sickness amongst children during the inclement months of spring, down to the end of May. The percen- tage for the year is, within a fraction, the same as for the previous three years, between 80 and 81. It is interest- ing to note that boys put in a percentage of 84.7, girls 77.6 and infants 77•4. The general average for England and Wales is 79.2. The number of children on the rolls has increased by 85. It does not appear that the Ship Canal Works have caused any great influx of children into the schools, as the annual rate of increase for five years before the works were commenced was 60, and since then it has averaged not more than 70 per annum. All the schools on the south ride of the Canal are made wholly free, via :—Newtown infants' Greenwav-road boys and girls, Mill Brew infants, and Roman Catholic mixed and infants. On the north side of the Canal, the, National Schools charge a Id. throughout. At the Wes- leyan Schools infants are free; boys, standards 1., 11., and 111., id.; standards IV., and V., 2d. ; and VI., and VII., 3d. Girls, standards 1., 11., and 111., id.; higher stan- dards 2d. Trinity Schools, infants and standard 1., free; boys and girls in standard 11., id.; 111., Id. ; IV., and higher standards Li. The number of free places, reckoned on the certified accommodation of the schools is, as fol- lows :—Boys and girls : Greenway-road, 481 ; Trinity, 86 ; Catholic, 124; total, 691. Infants: Mid Brow Board, 124 ; Trinity, 222; Wesleyans, 180; Catholic, 100; Newton, 130; total 756, making a grand total for boys, girls, and infants of 1,447. The total accommodation in the town is 3.289.—The visi- tors' reports for September showed a gratifying increase in the school attendance, consequent on the reduction or abolition of school fees, and freedom from sickness amongst children. There were 3,559 scholars on the rolls, 102 more than in September last year. The average attendance showed 213 more and the percentage 84•3 against 80.6. Dr. Gastaldi in moving the adoption of the reports said it seemed to him that many parents instead of taking advantage of the great boon of the new Education Act were acting in a contrary manner and that was the reason so many had been sent b,sfore the magis- trates the previous week.—Dr. hicamcall seconded the motion.—The Chairman observed that it would be the duty of the Board to exert more pressure than hitherto. --AP 'notion was carried. TEMPERANCE LECTURES FOR SCHOLARS.

Mr. H. T. Wynne Humphreys, organising secretary of the Runcorn Women's Temperance Society, on behalf of that society, asked for permission to enable Mr. C. Wil- son, the Day School Temperance lecturer, to visit the Runcorn Board schools for the purpose of giving a scientific temperance lesson te the scholars of Standard H. and upwards. It was understood that the lectures I hould be given'subject to arrangements with the head seachers.
RUNCORN DISTRICT NURSF. FUND.

The annual meeting of subscribers was held at the Town Hall, on Monday afternoon. Rev. Canon Wood M.A., presided, and there were present, Mrs. Maitland Wood (secretary), Mrs. Preston, Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Marwood, Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Abel, Miss Andrews, Messrs. S. Taylor, E. Tuckey, N. J. Grice, J. W. Lightburn, F, A. Lake (treasurer).

THE REPORT. The Committee in their second annual report recorded with satisfaction their conviction both of the utility and practicability of the enterprise, and add that it is likely to be of permanent value to the increasing population of the town. They based thcir opinion upon the fact that through the exertions of some ladies of the Committee they had a subscription list of more than £6O a year and that the public opinion of the town regarded the work of the District Nurse as really useful to those afflicted with sickness or accident. The number of visits paid by the nurse during the year was 4,048, as compared with 3,122 in the previous year, an Increase of 1,296. In the opinion of the Commit- tee it was. desirable to vest in the names of Trustees the capital sum of £275 and the subscribers were invited to elect five gentlemen as trustees for that purpose.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the re- port. He remarked that the actual amount of work done during the year was very satisfactory, and the total number of visits paid by the Nurse showed a very large increase,hut she had never been obliged to say that she was not able to cope with the work. He moved the adoption of the report, which was seconded.—Mr. Grice supported the motion. The motion was carried. THE FINANCES. The statements of accounts showed that the receipts amounted to £389, including a balancq brought forward of 26745. 3d. There was a balance in hh.nd of £299 3s. 6d. —Mr. Taylor moved the adoption' of the treasurer's report and referred to the admirable manner in which Mr. Lake had managed the finances.—Mr. Lightburn seconded.—Mr. Lake said a most satisfactory item was the increase in the annual subscriptions. Last year they amounted to £49 3s. 6d. and this sum included £lO from Mr. Walker and a large subscription from Canon Wood. Now, in spite of them not having the subscrip- tion from Mr. Walker, the total subscriptions amounted to £63 55., which was a. substantial increase on last year. What was still more satisfactory the number of subscribers was largely increased which showed a largely extended interest in the institution.—The report was adopted.
TIE?. COMMITTEE.

On the proposition of Mr. Lightburn seconded by Mr. Taylor, Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Barker and Miss Andrews were re-eiected members of the Committee.—Mr. Lake declined to again accept the position of treasurer, on the ground that it was good for the institution that there should be a change, and on the proposal of Mr. Lightburn seconded by Mr. Lake, Mr. Taylor was unanimously appointed treasurer.—On the motion of Mrs. Preston seconded by Mrs. Barker, the following gentlemen were appointed trustees of the capital sum of £275 :—Canon Wood, Messrs. F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn, S. Taylor, and Dr. Robinson.
Votes of thanks were accorded to the Chairman of the Commissioners for the use of the room and to the secre- tary of the Committee (Mrs. Wood) and the chairman (Canon Wood).

It is stated that Lady Blanche Hozier has entered an appearanee to defend the divorce action brought by her husband Captain Hozior. The steam trawlers Malta,and Lamberton collided in the Firth of Forth on Thursday. Toe Malta sank, and two of the crew were drowned. The conflagration which broke out at Santander on Tuesday morning was not subdued till Wednesday, and not before twenty-two houses had been burned. At the Railway Servants' Congress in Birmingham on i Wednesday, resolutions were adopted n favour of the. payment of members of Parliament, and expressing dissatisfaction with the report of the Commission on the Hours of Labour on Railways.
THE LIBEtAL BAZAAR.
(Continued frozn Page 3.) TESEERDA.Y'S RE-OPENING. h. LADIES' DAY.

Yesterday the Liberal bazaar was re-opened by Miss Bessie Dutton. Mrs. Z. Armitage presided, and she was supported on the platform by several ladies, all the gentlemen being relegated to the body of the Hall. Mrs. Z. ARMITAGE, in opening the proceedings, remarked that she was glad that their labours were now coming to a close. They had all worked very hard, and now they should be able to attend to other things that had been put aside, and had, per- haps, been neglected for bazaar work. They had to thank the public very much for the help they had given them. (Hear, hear.) She then asked Miss Dutton to open the bazaar. Miss DUTTON, who was warmly received, said she could assure them that she rose with a great many contending feelings, but she thought that, perhaps, the uppermost was one of commiseration for the Committee and the devoted workers of the bazaar, because they would remem- ber that they opened the proceedings with a real countess, who had an infinite talent, and all kinds of knowledge of the questions she spoke upon, and now see what they had :come to. (Loud laughter and applause.) And then there was another thing they might begin to think of, and that was what happened at Manchester the previous day. But they would not condole with each other. (Hear, hear.) They knew they had lost and they deplored it, but the Tories need not make any premature boasting because one swallow did not make a summer. Besides if the Liberals had victory all along the line they should become enervated in the struggle they had to make for their great enterprise. (Hear, hear.)' After having further alluded to political mattets, Miss Dutton said that in connec- tion with the bazaar, they had had very much to make them bright and glad. What expressions of good-will and what receipts they had had! (Hear, hear.) They had a splendid secretary. (Hear, hear and applause.) Bow indefatigable he had been, and courtcous, and obliging and pleasant to them all. They had all indeed been very happy in their relations with each other. (Applause.) Mrs. W. PIERPOINT, who was received with ap- plause, proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Dutton for opening the bazaar, and for the beautiful speech she made last Tuesday. It imptessed her (Mrs. Pierpoint) very much, and she was sure is did all those who were in the room. It made her feel that the Countess of Carlisle had left Warrington with no mean idea of Warrington women. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mrs. A. IL LEE seconded the vote of thanks, and said that Miss Dutton's remarks would make them all more hopeful and strong for the future. The vote of thanks was then put to the meeting and heartily accorded. Miss DUTTON responded, and moved a vote of thanks. to Mrs. Armitage. Mrs. H. ROBERTS seconded, and it was passed by acclamation. Mrs. Armitage, in returning thanks, said She was always glad to do what she could. She should like to take that opportunity of thanking all those who had so kindly helped in the bazaar. It was very reluctantly that she accepted the post of president, but she had been helped in every possible way, and the position had been made as easy for her as it could possibly have been. (Hear, hear and applause.) RECtEIPTS. The following are each day's receipts : .£ s. d. Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas.

FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTIO;Z:IiIbert Powell and George James, young navvies. were charged with having on Sunday, the 27th September, obstructed the footpath in Church-st. P.C. Crowder said the youths were jostling females and knocking them across the road. Superin- tendent Large said there were numerous complaints about this nuisance. Each defendant was fined 55., in- cluding Costs. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Samuel Leathwood, John Brown,and Ann Welsh; and John Fenny was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

DRUNK AND ROBBRRY.—Reuben Mitchell, a stranger to the town, pleaded guilty to stealing a shilling from the till of the Old Bridgewater Arms, Waterloo-road, the pro- perty of Thomas Heath Barton. He said he had had a great deal of drink, aud was very sorry. He was or- dered to pay 30s. or go to gaol for 14 days. AN Or SOLDIER.—John Clark, 70 years of age, an old soldier, was charged with begging. He was discharged. and advised to leave the town.
WIDNES PETTY, SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock and Lieut.-Colonel Gaskell.
DRUNICENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Mary Neild, Thos. Fallon, Catherine Power, and Margaret Wall.—Michael Allen and Sarah Jervis were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs.

SLEEPING OUT.—Henry Oldham, a tramp,was charged with sleeping in Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works, and he was discharged on promising to leave the town. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—TWO parents were fined ss. for not sending their children regularly to sckool. ALLEGED THEFT.—Catherine Matthews, of Marsh-st., was remanded on a charge of stealing a sheet from a clothes line, the property of Michael Weir, Nelson-st., The prisoner said Mrs. Weir gave her the sheet to pawn. A CLIO BOY.—George Harper James, a youth, was charged with having absconded from the training ship Clio, now lying in the Menai Straits. The prisoner said he was discharged from the ship on July 6th.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday and Superintend- ent Noblett was instructed to set him at liberty in the meantime if his statement were found to be correct. A DiumntEN MAN'S FOLLY.—John McCombe, aged 19, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly and wilfully damaged a glass door at the West Bank Hotel, doing damage to the amount of £1 15s. The prisoner, who is a fiatman from Llandudno, at present lodging in Wright-st., Went to the hotel, after eleven o'clock, and, bee,ause he was refused admission, struck the glass panel with his fist and smashed it. He cut his hand seriously. He pleaded guilty, and was fined ss. and costs,in each case, which,together with the damage. amounted to £3 2s. In default of payment, three weeks' imprisonment.
