Gibson and Son for the construc- tion of a chimney at the Hardy-street depot, the Alderman explained that a short chimney had previously been constructed to carry off the foul air at the depot, but that had been blown down, and the Committee now i proposed to carry out their original intention of having I a larger chimney. Alderman &mom seconded. Councillor DIXON moved an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of recom- mending the payment of £lO to Mr. R. Norman for extra services at Longford depot be not adopted. He considered to make a present to a paid servant of the Corporation was a bad precedent. Mr. Dixon also ex- pressed the opinion that the proposed chimneylwould not avail to get rid of the foul air. Councillor HILL seconded the amendment. He thought that although Mr. Norman was an excellent servant and a man he had every respect for, it was not the right thing he should be paid that £lO, as he had a good salary, and while he was performing the extra services somebody else would have to do his ordinary work. Alderman HARRISON supported the original motion. He thought the Committee would know best whether Mr. Norman deserved the gratuity. The Alderman , further said he had been informed by a high scientific authority in Warrington that the experiment had already been made of carrying a pipe into the chimney at the rubber works which was expected to accomplish the very object the Committee had now in view, and that it had proved a failure, and that the proposed chimney would be equally a failure. Alderman BURGESS defended the payment to Mr. Nor- man. He had, he said rendered important service of a special character for which he had received no considera- tion on the occasion of the outbreak of pleura-pneumonia last year, when a large number of animals were con- demned and slaughtered, and these services had saved the town hundreds of pounds. The Alierman presumed that the high scientific authority who was Alderman Harrison's informant was Mr. Diggle. (Laughter.) It was quite true the Committee had conveyed a pipe from their works to the rubber works chimney for the purpose mentioned, but it was not a failure; it was not allowed to be tried, but as soon as it was in, was ordered by the Company to be taken out. The MAYOR: That is so; it stopped the draught. Alderman BURGESS had no doubt it would have worked effectually. The minutes were adopted as they stood, by a large majority, Councillors Dixon and Hill only supporting the amendment.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTAL

The minutes of this Committee contained the follow- ing :—That the sewer in Thynne-st. be continued to take the drains of new houses in Arpley-st. and Thynne-st., and that the sewer in street off Margaret-st. be continued to take drains of 16 new cottages in street off Birchall- st.; that the contract between the Corporation and the County Council of Lancashire for keeping in repair the Latchford and Wilderspool Causeways now submitted by the Town Clerk be approved, and the common seal of the borough affixed thereto; that the tenders of Mr. Simeon Hough for the labour required in forming and paving the following streets be accepted :—Cartwright-St. £43 13s. 10d. ; Percy-st. £34 3s. 9d.; Back Crossley-St. £l4 us. 2d. ; Manley-st. £7 125.; Approach road to Back Crossley-at. £4 Os. id. ; Laira-st. £35 4s. sd. ; Bostock-st. £B2 15s. id.; that the tender of the Warrington Slate Company Limited, for the supply of 30,000 chequered tiles, delivered at Howley Yard, at 655. Bd. per thousand, be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. John Pendlebury and Co. for the supply of 20,000 chequered tiles, at 635. per thousand, be accepted; that the tender of Darbi- shires, Limited, to supply 400 tons of 2-inch macadam at 9s. per ton, be accepted; that the tender of the War- rington Slate Company, Limited, for the supply of 500 lineal yards of 12-inch by 8-inch curbs, at 3s. 2d. per yard, and the tender of Messrs. Walton Brothers, for the supply of 500 yards at 3s. 2d. per yard, be accepted. Alderman WRIGHT moved the adoption. He pointed out as to the contract with the Lancashire County Coun- cil that this was simply a continuance of the contract that had existed between the Corporation and the Che- shire County Council. The matter has been transferred to the Lancashire Council, and they had accepted the liability. The Corporation would receive £273 per an- turn during the remainder of the term, £67 being paid by the Cheshire County Council for a small portion be- yond the borough boundary. Councillor HEATON seconded. Councillor Dixow asked whether the proposed sewer in Thynne-st. was going to be continued right across Arp- ley, remarking that some of them had had painful ex- perience of the sewer in that neighbourhood. Councillor BLACYHURST asked for an explanation as to the difference in price in the contracts for tiles with the Warrington Slate Co. and Messrs. Pendlebury and Co.

Alderman HARRISON said that was the very question he was going to ask himself. It only proved that great minds thought alike. (A laugh.) It did seem strange to him that a firm should -supply 20,000 tiles for 2s. 6d. a thousand less than another firm charged for a much larger quantity. Had it been the reverse way he could have understood it.
• The MAYOR: There is a difference in quality. Alderman HARRISON said if that had been stated be- fore it would have obviated discussion.

Councillor JENKINS, referring to the recommendation of the acceptance of a tender for macadam, expressed the hope that the macadamising of the roads would re- ceive the earliest attention. He noticed that this work was sometimes done in July, which was not a very pro- per time. If there was any work that required special attention, it was this.

Alderman Mucurr referring to the tenders for tiles said he was not present when the subject came up, but his experience was that the Committee always dealt with such matters on their merits ; and they were quite capable of judging as to such matters. There had been times when the Committee paid 80s. to 85s. per 11000 for tiles, and very often, he believed, these had proved the cheapest in the end. The tiles at 655. 6d. per 1000 were to be delivered at Howley Yard, those at 635. at the station. This largely accounted for the difference. The Committee always made a point of doing their macadamising at this time of the year, and the Committee were determined on having the roads put in as good order as pessible. As to the sewer in Thynne-st., it was for people building new houses who demanded that the Corporation should do this, and as these people were liable to sewer rates they could not be refused. The sewer was a continuation of the old sewer in Thynne-st.. to the east side of Arpley-st. What was Mr. Dixon's objection? Councillor DixoN Every day I have painful expe- rience of it. The minutes were adopted.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COM3diTtEE.
THE WARRINGTON SCHOOLS AND FREE EDUCA- TION.

This Committee recommended that a petition, which was printed in the minutes, be sent to the County Coun- cil in favour of the provision of truant school accom- modation. The Clerk had also been instructed to send a letter to the correspondents of the public elementary schools urging them to accept the fee grant under the new Act; also a letter to them pointing out the desir- ability of all children entitled to sit at the forthcoming examinations should be placed on the list of those to be examined for labour certificates. Councillor FLEMING moved the adoption of the Com- mittee's report. The managers of the Warrington schools had, he said, been asked to provide free schools or free places, and they did not seem anxious to do so, although they had done so in some instances. He should like to know where the School Attendance Committee were in this matter. Some schools had settled it to suit their own convenience. He should like an expression of opinion from the Council as to what they should do in the future about these schools. Councillor SHAW GREEN seconded the motion. He was sure that if the Corporation knew of the number of boys that came before the Committee to be dealt with as truants, they would not be surprised at their petition to the County Council. Every week or fortnight they had from six to a dozen such cases, the boys being entirely beyond the control of their parents. The Committeeput much moral force into their remarks on these cases, and if that was not successful sent them to the magis- trates, whose only way to deal with them was to send the boys to an industrial school or the ship Clio, which were both exceedingly expensive. If there were a number of truant schools in different parts of the country, boys could be sent there for 3 or 4 weeks, or perhaps 3 months, until they were cured of their truancy. They could then come home under licenses from the authorities and possibly become better citizens, and useful men. He would also like to make some remarks as to the circular sent to the different schools. The managers of those schools held a meeting in that room about a month ago, and it was thought that conjointly they would possibly come to some arrangement for establishing free schools in the borough, or if not, providing free places, in the bulk of the schools, if not all of them. He excluded the People's College from the category, because that was above the ordinary run of the national schools. In other schools, he beard these free places were not to be provided; and he and his colleagues on the Committee were puzzled what to do. Hitherto they had been able to send poor parents to the Board of Guardians to have school fees remitted, but under present circumstances the Committee did not know what to do. The effect he took it of the present condition of things would be that by-and-bye the town would have a School Board imposed upon it. (Cries of "No.") According to the Act of Parliament unless there were free places provided within a certain period the authorities in London would compel a School Board to be formed. (Cries of "Hear, hear.") He felt the ex- treme importance of the matter, and considering that an increase in the rate of from 4d. to 10d. in the £ might be involved, the Corporation must look the matter fairly in the face. But he thought there was a different way of dealing with the matter if the managers of schools would only take into consideration the position in which they were placed. The Roman Catholic schools of the town had been declared absolutely free, but they provided only for one class of religionists; and the Corporation had the large majority to provide for. Unless the managers seriously took matters into account what was before them there would be a School Board whether we liked it or not. There was another fact which showed that matters were tending very strongly in that direction. There were at that moment in the schools varying rates of fees. The Roman Catholic schools were free the Heath Side schools had a low fee, the National schools in Church-street a little higher fee, Wycliffe schools had about the same, and altogether there was about as great a mixtu're in the value of the education given as could possibly be im- agined. It did seem an extraordinary thing that the managers could not agree upon one sum to be charged for each standard all round. The present state of things would, if continued, help to support the claim which would shortly be made for a School Board. The school- master of one of the chief schools told him his managers did not care how soon a School Board came. Personally, he (Mr. Green) did not care, because he believed it was the proper thing that .those who provided the money should have something to do with the government of the schools. (Cries of " Hear, hear.") At the same time he thought they ought not to have a School Board if it could be avoided, because of the excessive amount of rates, which everyone must be anxious to bring down rather than increase. _ --

In reply to Alderman GREENALL, Mr. GREEN said the Corporation contributed to Father Nugent's School as well as the Clio. Alderman GREENALL agreed with Mr. Green that unless something was done there would be a School Board, though he objected strongly to such a Board—unless the schools of the different sects would work together to pre- vent it. Councillor Mum thought Mr. Councillor Green had tried to steal a march upon the Corporation, in making a speech about inaugurating a School Board. (Cries of "No.") He thought the question not being on the agenda was out of order. The MAYOR : It is on the agenda paper, on page 8. Councillor Mum begged pardon; he had not seen it. Several schoolmasters of the town had told him that the schools were within the limit of the law in what they were doing. He did not think it was the province of the Council to interfere with their management. Councillor JENKINS said the petition of the Committee gave him very great concern and also great cause for self-congratulation. He; felt somewhat assured that his position as a bachelor was not altogether without its blessing. (Laughter.) When he saw the difficulties the Committee had as to truant children, he was happy to think that bachelors, who were sometimes treated lightly did not live altogether on the wrong aide of the fence.

The MAYOR: No, you don't do your share. Councillor HEATON assured the Committee that so long as there were parents who could not pay school fees' the Guardians would continue to pay them,therefore the Committee stood as to poor children exactly as before. Councillor H. ROBERTS said Councillor Heaton entirely misunderstood the position. The Education Act required that a certain number of free places should be provided; and if they were "provided there would be no necessity for parents to come before the Board of Guardians or any Committee. If the managers of the schools, who un- fortunately did not seem to be acting in concert, would only put their heads together and formulate a scheme for all the schools of the borough, this would meet the requirements, and no fear of a School Board could enter anyone's mind. There was plenty of school accommo- dation, he understood, and all that was wanted was a disposition to provide the free places. If they were not provided it would not be a question of whether the town would like a School Board or not, the Education Depart- mens would take such steps as they thought necessary. Perhaps they would withdraw the grant from the schools which would inevitably lead to the establishment of a School Board.

- - Alderman Strrrox thought the petition and the sugges- tions made in reference to a School Board were al- together premature. There was ample school accommo- dation in the town, and as provision had been heretofore made for all the poor children,so he believed it would be made. The new Act was quite a new thing, and the managers had not yet had the opportunity of seeing how it worked, but he was quite satisfied that if the School Attendance Committee had any difficulties whatever in regard to poor children being accommodated in the schools it could not have them long. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH thought the Committee were rather too hard on the schools, because the managers had to deal with an entirely new state of matters, and did not exactly know where they were, therefore had to feet their way. If any parent wanted to send a child to the nearest school, he did not think any school would re- fuse to receive the child. Councillor DIXON reverted to the time of the forma- tion of the School Attendance Committee, and said Coun- cillor Green's speech was just a copy of Mr. Milner at that time as to the necessity of a School Board. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDIY, OCTOBER 10, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDIY, OCTOBER 10, 1891.
MUSEUM, LIBRARY, ARTS, AND TECHNICAL IN.
STRUCTION COMMITTEE. THE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES,

The minutes of the Committee contained the following items in addition to those published last week. The return br the month of August was :—Visitors to the Museums, 3,065, increase 4 per cent.; books issued in reading-room„ 1,398, increase slight; books issued in lending depart- ment 3,270, increase 54 per cent. compared with August, 1890. Report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :,-- Proceedings of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society; two parts in continuation, from the Society; proceedings of the Liverpool Engineering Society, vol. 12, in continuation, from the Society; reports of the British Association, 19 vols., from the Association; reports of the Free Libraries at Hanley. Leeds and Northwich, from the Committees.

Councillor H. Hominy moved the adoption of the minutes. He said the anticipations formed by the Com- mittee as to the number of entries ef students in the technical instruction classes had been largely borne out by the results. There were now upon the books some- thing like 400 students, Most of these having enteredin two classes ; there being in all 560 class entries. They were distributed thus :—ln commercial classes there were about 317, in science classes 155, in domestic work classes 71, and in those for manual training 17. The Committee expected these numbers would increase ; and they believed this was only the beginning of a much larger and more important work. Some little feeling seemed to have arisen in the town upon the question of fees ; and he thought there was much misconception on this subject. In those places which had an endowment, or some assistance from the rates in addition to the amount received from the County Council, possibly the tees were somewhat lower than in Warrington. But it was hardly fair to compare Warrington, which had as- sistance from the County Council only, with those. places. Compared with the fees in places similarly situated, they were in Warrington rather lower than the average and the average of Warrington compired with a neighbouring district—Leigh—was only 73.6 d. as com- pared with 7g. 3d. The Committee did not pretend for a moment that their scheme was perfect, but they did believe from the results attained that it had in it the elements of popular success, and more than that, the' bulk of their students were of a character that would do credit to them in the examinations.

Councillor TIMMINS expressed the hope that classes in agriculture would be formed. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH thought instrumental music should be included in the syllabus. There were numbers of people whose taste for this might be so de- veloped that they might take the places of German pro- fessors who came to this country to teach it. Councillor Pumpourr drew attention to the satisfac- tory return for August as to the library and museum. As to the technical school, it was only in an experimental stage. The Committee did not want to put their hands out further than they could very well manage to reach. If the Committee had the funds at their disposal they would only be too ready to extend their operations. Alderman HARRISON suggested that type-writing should be included among the subjects of instruction. He asked if the Committee had received any definite in- formation as to the amount the County Council would place at the dispesal of the Committee. The Instruction Committee of the County Council had recommended that the SUM of £l3lO be allowed, but so far as he knew it was not definitely arranged. Councillor F. W. Moults invited the members of the Council to show their interest in the work by being pre- sent to witness how the classes were conducted. Councillor Rouser& endorsed this invitation. He in- formed Councillor Jenkins that agriculture was one of the subjects, but, owing perhaps, to inadequade advertising, there were not many applicants to learn it, but the Com- mittee would try to remedy this omission. The subject of instrumental music had been under consideration, but it was a moot point whether the Technical Instruction Act would allow its inclusion,hence it was not included. But the matter would not in future be overlooked, if the subject could be introduced. The Committee had con- sidered the question of teaching type-writing, which he himself had introduced, and there had been applications from young men engaged in commercial pursuits to learn it. The use of the type-writer formed a subject of instruction in the Manchester technical classes. The secretary, Mr. Madeloy, was making enquiries on the matter, and would repert to the Committee. Councillor Roberts assured Alderman Harrison that there was not the slightest doubt, from official and unofficial informa- tion the Committee had had that the County Council would endorse their Committee's recommendation, as to the allowance for technical instruction in Warrington; indeed he thought rather more would be received than had been expected. MiIiBTRRY.
THB

The report of the registrar to the Cemetery Committee showed that during the past four weeks the interments were as follows :—Adults, 34; minors, 52 ; stillborn and premature, 12; corresponding period last year, adults, 35; minors, 48; stillborn &c., 4. The receipts for the four weeks were zeo, 17s. ; corresponding period last year, £6O 17s. 3d. The minutes of the Committee were confirmed -on the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor JRNICINS.
TRH BATHS.

The minutes of the Baths Committee contained a recom- mendation that the tender of Messrs. J. Gibson and Son, for the erection of a•swimming bath, &c., at £3,686 45., be accepted. Alderman CHANDLEIY, in moving the confirmation of the minutes,said they would see the Committee had acted promptly upon the instruction of the Council with regard to the new baths. Ho expected that the extensions now decided upon would serve for some time to come. Councillor FLEMING : How long? Alderman CAANDLEY : Until we see the bathing pro- clivities of the borough. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS asked if the Committee were aware that persons who used the sixpenny baths were only supplied with one towel to dry themselves with. The MAYOR: They ought to have two. Councillor Dixon would like to know what the debt of the borough was before the £5,000 to be borrowed for the extension of the baths was added to it. Alderman CHANDLEY said the Committee had not re- ceived any complaints about the baths, and if anyone felt aggrieved and they wrote to him, as chairman of the Committee, the complaint would be seen to. The minutes were confirmed. THE MARKETS.

The minutes of the Markets Committee contained the following :—The total income from all sources was £330 Bs. id., corresponding period last year, £304 4s. 3d. ; increase, £26 13s. lod. It was resolved that the Market Hall be closed every Monday and Thursday evening at seven o'clock instead of eight o'clock as heretofore; and also that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to confer with the gas engineer and report to this Committee on the best means of providing additional lighting to the Markets.
The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Alder- man GREBNALL, seconded by Councillor BLACKHURST.
THE WATHRWORES.
The minutes of the Water Committee the most import- ant parts of which were published last week were sub- mitted.
The MAYOR, in moving their adoption said the report of Mr. Jas. Bolton completely corroborated everything they had received from the Waterworks Company.

Councillor GMENING wished to know Aix; reason of Alderman Harriscn'S resignation from the Committee, but to this no reply was given. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said the Corporation might expect to have good results from their purchase of the Waterworks. The 'grass purchase money of the under- taking was £274,412, and it would be found shortly, when the results were a little better known, that it was cheap:it the price. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed. THE STIPENDIARY QIIESTION.—A. LIVELY. DS-

145.) This resolution be rescinded, and the works be open for the public. Councillor PronsProN seconded. Alderman BURGESS asked if the Council wished Wen to say anything on the subject. (ft No.") The motion was then put and as only the mover rind seconder voted for it, it was negatiVed. Councillor DIXON next moved the. following :—As the' answers given by Chairman of Sanitary Committee were so very unsatisfactory in reference to, the account to which the question referred, namely :—Messrs. Manlove, Alliott andem's contract for machinery,•A2,lBo ; Bryan, Donkin, and Co., for patent furnazes, £132 9s. ; Marshall, Sone and Company, for vertical engine and boiler, £176.4d. All ad,riee notes and invoices which have any reference, be produced, and if they are signed or endorsed by anyone, the' same be requested to point out the portion of machinery which such advice note or invoice has reference to, so that the members of the Council may be- certain all the machinery has been received. He addbti that if Ire. did not get a satisfactory answer the question would come on again. H 6 was not going to be put down, and there were others behind him. The MAYOR said 4 he could get the whole' of the information by appling to the borough treasurer. Conncillor DixoN strid he had applied for the informa- tion once or twice and the repty was unsatisfactory ,and painful. He could get information from,: other Corporations better than he cculd from his own.. There were other peoplh helping him, and other steps, might be taken.

Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the motion to. put 'himself in order in questiAling Mr. Dixon. He wantedt Winton,- if Mr. Dixon meant that machinery which Itad been contracted for by that Corporation had not lifen receivea,. but had been pairifor. Councillor Dixon said he did not wish to answer SWAT questions.. Councillor PIRRPOINT said he shouldnow like to ask Alderman Burgess if it was not a fact that such machix- nery had been. supplied and was now ar Longford. Councillor GRERN would hicc-to know•by whom those; papers•wereto be produced, and when and where. Councillor BOLTON did not think machinery would be paid for unless it was received. Alderman BOIMESB explained that machinery had been Sent inbyMessrs. Manlove, Anion and Co., but their contract was not yet completed, but nothing had been paid for that had not been recei7ed. He again replied that they had got nopatent furnacesfromgryan, Donkin and Co. what they had got were-bars forth° furnace; and with • rt3gardi to Marshall,Son -4, and Co:,•the apparatus they-had 'got was to drive fans and • nothing else. He wanted to know what answer woula satisfy Mr. Dixon and his co-conspirators who, he said; he had at his back. M. Dixon.was a gentleman he had the highest esteem for-,-(laughter):--but Mr. Dixon was• Mr. Divan. Nature had not beenhountiftail with him; she-had been niggardly, —( laughter)—and in consequence of that it would be cowardly to say anything against,hinpand he (Alderman Burgess) never would- His infirmities-were sacred with him, he should'therefore say nothing against him, and Mr. Dixon knew that well enough. (Laughter.' Alderman ,SroTTON. said it was unreasonable- to re-open questions which-had received the sanction of.the Council twelve months ago or upvrards. Councillor '11": ROBEIRMS said there was a very serious implication in the resolution. (Hear, hear.)) He knew perfectly well that all money expended was passed in Committee, with the endorsement of the borough trea- surer as to arithmetical accuracy, and the endorsement of. the particular official, in whose department the ex- penditure had been incurred. That being the case,what did he mean by-that resolution? The imptii3ation in it was that therhad paid InCiley for goods they- had not received. (Hear,. hear.) Councillor Dixon 4 had been asktd tasay if that was-the, meaning of his resolution, and be declined to 'say whether he meant that,. and he (Councillor Roberts) thought very wisely. (Eder, hear.) But it was time to put ant end to that sort of thing. Were they to be continually badgered upon subjects of that kind which-were purely-matters of detail, ,and upon which Councillor Dixon. had, not even taken the trouble to satisfy hirnselens to any-accuracy or inaccuracy. It was a monstrous-waste of public time and an-insult to the Committee.. If Counciller Dixon had got any power- fulbackers behind him—and:he very much doubted it— he would advise him to' get one of the teachers of the elementary schools to teach them grammar andvonsposi- tion, so that they might put before them a resolution they could understand. (Rear hear, and laughter.) lhe resolution was then put to the meeting, only Mr. Dixon voting.lor it. Council* Dtxda: next rnevedi as follows :—"The full particulars of the said travelling expenses, Ste., of Thos. Longdin„ Esq.!, the Borough Surveyor, as entered in the Borough Treasurer's accounts for the year commencing March 26th, 1680,-o March2sth,lllol, a detailed account ' and a copy of the same he furnished to each member of the Council as soon as possible:" There were objections to this-resolution on thecy•round that it was out of order, but the-Mayor declared it to be in order.

Councillor DIXON' said it.was not his resolution} but he had been requested to .Traore it.. The MAYOR said he could get all3the information if he went about it in the right way. councillor Ducom said he .had been after a good many things, but unfortunatellr,7trerturnstrit- renCfrom what the Mayo? midi, The last' time he asked for information,-a certain 'gentleman held up hie hand and said, "I dare not give you it" The resolution found no supporters. The meeting then ended.

div.head: TEE GAS COMMITTER.--THE COMMITTEE AND THE WAGES
div.p: TEE GAS COMMITTER.--THE COMMITTEE AND THE WAGES
OF ITS EMPLOYES.

Tne minutes of this Committee contained the follow- ing :—The average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 18.62 candles at both works. The following resolutions had been passed That the tender of Mr. George, Wallington to construct ceiling and plaster walls, &c., of engine house at Long- ford at £2O be accepted; that the wages of Mr. Harold Barker be increased from 10s. to 20s. per week ; that the tender of Messrs. John Woodward for the supply of nine valves at £B3 be accepted. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH moved the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman WRIGHT ser.;onded.

Councillor FLEMING thought the rise in the wages of Mr. Harold Barker from 10s. to 20s. a week was a large one to give. Councillor DIXON said the Gas Committeo took some extraordinary steps at times. He knew people who got salaries at the Gas Works who did not work 30 per cent. of their time. He was proceeding to reflect upon the conduct of Alderman Holmes, the chairman of the Com- mittee, when there were loud cries of "Order." The MAYOR thought Councillor Dixon should not call into question the actions of one of the most honourable men in that Council.

Councillor DixoN : I know what is going on. (Loud cries of "Oh " and "Order.") I have been in a row be- fore to-night. The MA.YOR : Mr. Dixon we must- Councillor DIXON (loudly) : I have had some ex- perience and perhaps more painful than any one else in this matter. Councillor H. ROBBRTS supported the proposed in- I crease in the salary of Mr. Harold Barker, who, he said. ' had qualified himself for a good position, and was cheap at the price. Councillor Mum deprecated interference with Com- mittees as regarded salaries. Gentlemen who were will- ing to voteawa,y thousands of pounds hesitated to give a working man under the Corporation a shilling a week extra. Alderman Surrox said that some of the most strenu- ous advocates of the resolution that recently passed the Council with regard to contracts were the very first to object to any Committee of the Council setting an ex- ample of giving fair rates of wages to workmen in its employ. Councillor SRAW GREEN, as a member of the Gas Committee, could assure the Council that Mr. Barker was well worth the money they were giving him., Councillor BOLTON supported the proposal of th 3 Com- mittee. It was, he said, generally found that the Gas Committee was the first to attempt to drop the wages of the working people. He hoped that when they had any of their men before them and found they were en- titled to an increase of wages they would give it and not wait till they were forced. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BIIROESS said he should like to know how many of their friends were going to their constituencies. (Near, hear and laughter.) The amount of generosity he saw displayed in that Council he had never seen equalled • if it had been the month of February instead of October they would not have heard what they lia'd heard that night. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SON.
div.p: SON.

The General Purposes Committee reported that the Town Clerk had submitted a statement obtained by him respecting the appointntent and emoluments of stipendiary magistrates, and that, after discussion, it had been resolved that the information obtained lie on the table.
The MAYOR moved the adoptiorziof the minutes.

Councillor GREENING submitted that it was for tho General Purposes Committee to say whether Warrington was to have a stipendiary or not ;and it was a question for the Council. There was a strong feeling in the town that they should have one and he' saw week by week that the court could not be carried on through the non- attendance of magistrates. lie moved that the informa- tion be supplied to each member of the Council.

Councillor H. ROBERTS seconded the amendment be- cause the very object he had in moving the resolution relating to the stipendiary was that information should be supplied to every member of the Council. When it was supplied it would then be a question as to whether they should go into the subject or not. In the absence of that information they were as much in the dark as be- fore. His object, further, was not that the information should reach merely the members of the Council but also the people at large. He knew that:thero was a feeling in Vrarring,ton of the appointment of a stipendiary magis- trate.

Councillor JEuxins supported the amendment; and he mentioned what had taken place at the police court that morning toshow the necessity of some one presiding in a court of Justice who had had such a training that he could look dispassionately on every matter which came before him. He (Councillor Jenkins), had applied for a summons-against a burgess of the town for an offence which hewould not mention. One of the magistrates obvirved that he had very great sympathy with, his ap- plication, although it was unnecessary for the gentleman to express any thing of th kind. The other gentlemen on the-bench. observed that if persons were to be • sum- moned for an offence of that character and possibly con- victed', he did not see reason why licensed victuallers should'be allowed to sell beer and other things on a Sun- day. He (Kr. jenkins) could not then he so rude as to point'nut to the last-mentioned gentleman that his remarks were-totally illogical, or he should have recom- mended him,to read Archbishop Whateley on "Logic," and then he would* have seen that his remarks were•per- feet]," ridicnlbus, because a man who chose to go and drink on a Stinclay exercised a free will, but the other person who -made his men work on Sundays did not allow them -to.exercise their free will. That showed them that they vrantad' a gentleman presiding over the bench of magistrates.who had read Whateley on "Logic," and who was conversant with rules of law, and whose mind was RO matured' and instructed as to prevent him from making such ridiculous remarks as were made to him (Councillor Jenkins) in the court that day. COuncillor Mbar said he did not think that was the place to discuss such questions. A stipendiary would mean an expenditure of ELMO or £1,500 a year, and a great addition to the rates. (Oh, oh," and No, no."> CouncillOr BOvron did not see any.reason why the in- formation asked for Should pot be given. He did not sees- however, that there was any guarantee that a stipen- diary would have any more commonsense than some of the magistrates already on the Bench. Councillor BkowNs supported the amendment. The MAYOR said the amendment was out of order but there was net the slighest reason why they 'should net have the information they wanted. Councillor W Rrossirrs asked upon what grounds the Town Clerkruled it out of order. The TOWN CLIIRK said it was really a substantive motion and not an amendment. Councillor StIAPPGREEN said the matter bad simply been referred to the Town Council,and nothing had been; said about a report. Alderman IhrIIGESS- said that with an indebtedness ef • over half a million of money, which attached to the bnrongh at the present time, the Council could not afford to indulge in " fads" or excite the minds of the people outside on the merits or demerits of such a ques.- tion. He was far from thinking that stipendiaries were Isuch very grand' folks. He thought it would be found that, in proportion to their number, they did more mis- chief than the unpaid magistrates. (" Oh, oh !") With such a Bench or magistrates, with ttleStiryor at th i e, head, there was no necessity for a stipendiary n War- rington. The Mayor's decisions were marked by wis- dom, and fraught with a great deal of that mercifulness. which was seldOm found' in those of a stipendiary. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Henry Rcesurrrs said he was sure the Coun- cil would appreciate the modesty of the magistrate whe had just addressed them on that impartant subject. (Laughter.) Alderman BURGINS : I hope so. Councillcir H. Roamers added that it was well known that there was in- Warrington a body of gentlemen sitt- ing on the Bench whose decisions were past criticism, and they were not afraid of telling the Council so. Ili fact, sortie of them-seemed to take a delight in posing their Solomon-like wisdom upon the public. Unfortun- ately, however, there were people who did not take them at their own estimate of their own value. Whether the magistrates liked it or not, there existed in Warrington ; a doubt as to the wi'sdom of continuing the present con- dition of things. The statemeht that stipendiary magis- trates did more barn than good was a very curious one ' in face of the fact-that the boroughs of this country were increasingly appointing stinedianes. That proved that they, at anyrate, had confidence in such gentlemen— (hear, hear —in spite of the circumstance that a magis- trate claimed for-his order something approaching per- fection. Alderman BIIRMISS. deniei that he had said that the magistrates were perfection, or that they did not do wrong. He simply said that they did not want to have an imperfect stipendiary forced upon the town. Councillor HENRY. Roazirrs said there were two or three ways of saying the same thing. If Alderman Bur- gess did not say in so many words that the magistrates of Warrington were without fault, he certainly under- stood him to do so,
Alderman BtrnoEss : Then I did not say so ; it was not creditable to invent stories like that. _ _ _

Councillor HENRY Roma.Ts accepted Alderman Bur- gess' S disclaimer.. He also agreed that some of the mag- istrates„were certainly not perfect. (Laughter:) The supporters of theproposal were not faddists, and when the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee posed as an economist, he posed in a feature which was . certainly newt° him. Councillor DTXON Hear, hear. (Laughter:), Alderman BURGESS said if the Mayor allowed' this, he should certainly ask to be allowed to reply. Councillor Rowena's thought there was a disposition to wilfully misunderstand what he had said. 'lts he had said many times he thought the expenditure of the Sani- taryrommittee was fully justified but for- Alderman Burgess to pose as an economist was a new, feature of things. Alderman SUTTON said that as another mod'est magis- trate--(laughter)—he would like to remark that one of the reasons urged in favour of the appointment of a stipendiary was that the magistrates were frequently front the Bench, and the business was. delayed.—He thought that a great deal more fuss was,made of that matter than there was any necessity for. It did happen someti mes•th at magistrates were prevented/ from attend- - Mgr, on their- proper days, but the Court was only kept waiting haltan hour,or three quarters of an hour, whicb, did not put anybody to any 'great inconvenience. Councillor BROWNE said he was rather surprised to hear Alderman Sutton say that no inconvenience was caused by a delay of half or three quarters of an hour. On several Friday mornings lately there has been long delays. •

Alderman HARRISON: No. Councillor BROWNE , I am prepared' to say, and I ask the reporters to corroborate me, that we have had to wait. Alderman SurroN : They will sa,y anything. (Laegh- ter.) Councillor BROWNE Slid it was:absurd to say that the delay caused no inconvenience. Ha was not prepared to say whether or not he was.-ibfavour of a stipeacliary but the Council ought to be supplied with the particulars which had been obtained onthe sobject. Alderman CNANDLEY said Councillor H. Roberts had several times suggested thetthe opinion of the town was that the present state of things ought not to exist at the Police Court. By what authority did the Councillor speak the feelings of the town? Councillor BOLTON : Fle is the town. (Laughter.) Alderman CEANDLEY said he was a public man, but ha. had never heard any complaints. Councillor H. RonEncrs• said he did not profess to re- present the town- Alderman CHANDLEY : You said the town. Councillor H. RonEnrs : / never said anything of the. sort. I said there was an opinion in thetown. Alderman CEANDLEY : It is the something. Councillor 11. Ronaars It is a very different thing. I don't arrogate to myself the right to represent the feelings of the whole of the borough upon any question whatever.
The minutes were then passed. MR. DIXON'S RESOLUTIONS.

Councillor DIXON then in accordance with motion, moved Council meeting held June 3rd, 184, it was resolved :—" That no person other than a member of the Town Council be allowed to visit the' depot at Longford without the permission of the Chairman of the Committee." R. DIGGLE AND THE INTERCEPTING
DEPOTS.
ill WANTS TO LECTURE ON THE QUESTION.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court; on Monday, Mr. William Diggle was in attendance and Waited some time in order to interview the magis- trates on the, subject of the intercepting depots. On his coming forward to make his statement, the Mayor only was left on the Bench, his colleagues, Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, and Wright, having retired. Mr. Diggle said he had to apologise to hiS Worship for appearing before him to again bring, before him the subject of this abominable nuisance, of which he bad still to complain. The Mayor promised some months ago that if he would only be quiet a little while it should be removed. He ap- peared that morning as a ratepayer, because he found the Corporation were going to lay out a lot more money to abate this nuisance which the Sanitary Committee declared was not a nuisance, and he wished to say that this outlay would be a useless expenditure. He did so because he had submit Led plans to the Sanitary Committee show- ing that this arrangement for the manipulation of it would be avoided by the adoption of a proper method of dealing with it. He desired that morn- ing to ask if the Lecture Hall at the Museum could not be granted to him so that he might explain his plans to the public, and show them that the Cor- poration were wasting money, and would never ac- complish their object by taking the course they were doing.—The Mayor: Mr. Diggle, lam not sure I have got the power. I will consult the Town Clerk, because if the Sanitary Committee are all wrong, and you have got the secret and are willing to impart it to an audience I think it is a pity the town should not have the benefit of it. —Mr. Diggle: That is my view of it.—The Mayor: Butes you say, they are trying to abate the nuisance; does not that show their willingness? But you say that they are wrong utterly.—Mr. Diggle: They have had eight trials and laid out a thousand pounds. Now they have tried a chimney. Was that a failure ?—The Mayor : You are wanting us to tell secrets. I will see the Town Clerk, and if possible he will find you a room to give a lecture in.—Mr. Isherwood: You might refer him to the Technical Instruction Com- mittee, who might engage him to deliver a lecture. —The Mayor: I quite agree with that suggestion. I will make inquir3 this week if we can do any- thing about this lecture.—Mr. Diggle : I have not a long time to live, and I want to do what good I can while I am here. Good morning; lam much obliged.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday night. Mr. Rat- cliffe presided, and there were also present Messrs. Davies, Aukland, Diggle, Mather, W. Houghton, Clarke, Jolley, Dobson, Turton, Humphries, Smith, Ribbert ; and J. C. Sutton (clerk.)
THE RESPONSIBILITIES OP CANDIDATES FOR OFFICE.

ILII the minutes of the previous meeting it was stated tCat Mr. W. Poffitt, of Oldham, had been appointed assistant, :nester at Padgate Schools, but having after- wards de,clinej to undertake the duties of the office he was called upon to pay $3 13s. 4d.—Mr. Aukland thought the Guardians had no lega! right to demand such a large !fem. All they were entitled to was the amount they had been out of pocket —The CLERK said they had been more than the sum out of pocket as they had had i 0 advertise again and pay the expenses of the man who accepted the position and who came from the South of England, When a man applied for a situation he had ol3lsortunity to fully consider the matter before his acceptance, and there were also other candidates who would have accepted the appointment. As a matter of law they should both give and receive a month's notice or a month's salary.—Mr. AUXIAND : Can We by law get this money P—The CLUX : I think so.—Mr. AIIKLAND : I differ from that—The CLERK said that no doubt if he got one counsel's opinion and Mr. Aukland the opinion of another they would differ. (Laughter.)—The minutes were then passed.

div.head: WORKHOUSE,
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE,

The CLERK read the following entries which the Medi- cal Officer for the Workhouse (Dr. Spinks) had made in his report book :—Diet: The rice puddings are not suffi- ciently cooked. The potatoes are sent unpeeled to the sick. Drainage: Good. Ventilation: The children's sleeping ward in the female hospital is very defective. Sick ward or Infirmary: Measles having become epi- demic, the ward for the children is too small and the ventilation is bad. Recommendations: I particularly wish that the large empty ward over the old women's infirm ward be occupied by convalescent cases of measles. The report was dated 22nd Sept.—The CHAIR- MAN said he should be glad if the doctor would meet the Committee and point out all these things and they would be remedied; but he seldom visited the Committee, and it was difficult for them to get him to meet them.—Mr. Diactix said the did attend the Committee on the last occasion. He (Mr. Diggle) had taken some of the rice home to have it cooked to test the statement of the doctor and he did not find it very suitable. He also to some extent corroborated the doctor's statement as to the want of ventilation and the peeling of the potatoes. —Mr. CrAnsig said the Committee did not recoguise everything the doctor said. With regard to the rice the majority of the Committee considered it satisfactory, although it might not be as good as rice at 3d. a pound. With regard to the removal of the convalescent children the Committee had given order for the room to be got ready as early as possible.—Mr. TIIRTON fully endorsed ' Mr. Clarke's statement.—The CHAIRMAN said so far as his own observation vent the rice would have satisfied him.—ln answer to a question, the WORKHOUSE MASTER said that when there were about thirty rice puddings to cook they could not get them all uniform.—The CLERK asked if the statement of the Medical Officer was a general or an exceptional one.—The WORKHOUSE MAS- TER: It must be quite exceptional.—Mr. TuaroN said it was only fair to mention that one rice pudding was not so good as another they saw.—The WORKHOUSE MASTER said all the cases-of measles were convalescent now. The mistake had heen in not treating them in the infectious ward at the' stirt.—Mr. DOBSON thought the complaints were very paltry.—The CHAIRMAN moved,and Mr.Jou.Bv seconded, that the doctor should be requested to attend befcre the House Committee to make his complaints in person when he had them to make.—Attention was then drawn to the fact that on the date mentioned in his report given above Dr. Spinks had also filled up a form at the end of the report book ta the effect that, with the excep- tion of ventilation, other things were satisfactory at the Workhouse.—Mr. DAVIES said that when that report was read to the doctor, he seemed astonished that he had signed such a statement. —Mr. DIGGLE 'then referred to several small matters which he considered might be im- proved at the Workhouse.—Mr. DAVIES thought that Mr. Diggle wanted to make out that the House Committae had grossly neglected their duty, but he contended that there had never been a committee who had been more earnest and desirous ot attending to the sick people and the general affairs of the Workhouse. He did know whether Mr. Diggle was seeking popularity. (Laughter.) Be had fallen out with the Sanitary Committee,and now he seemed to want to fall out with the Workhouse Com- mittee. Mr. TIIRTON also strongly criticised the methods of Mr. Diggle, and Mr. Diggle told Mr. Turton that some of his statements were not in accordance with the truth.—The CHAIRMAN at length put an end to the lively repartees of these two gentlemen, and the motion he had proposed was then adopted. GIFTS.

Gifts of flowers and fruit for the inmates of the Work- house from Cairo-st. Chapel, St. Paul's Church, Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, and Christ Church, Latchford. Also a box of tobacco from Mr. G. W. Pritchard, Horse- market-st.

VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN. Mr. Curiiis referred to Dr. Watkins' account, and said he wished to know by the next meeting whether the vaccination of Daniel Cooper's child was in the bill, as he had been threatened with a summons respecting the affair.

A report prepared by the Assistant Clerk (Mr. S. Sut- ton) as to the business that was dealt with at the recent North-Western Poor Law Conference was read. A vote of thanks for the report was afterwards passed to the Assistant Clerk, This was all the business.

THE TEACHINGS OF THEOSOPHY.

ir,—l shall feel obliged if you will permit me, in an- swer to "Inquirer," to state that:l believe in many of the teachings of Theosophy, because they are not opposed to the discoveries of science, and because to me:they seem to be in harmony with natural phenomena, and the impressions which zature has produced upon me. When we look around upon the gladness of life and th beauty of the earth and sky a feeling of reverence and love for the Power which produced it is inspired, and when we reflect

On stars that gem the vaulted sky, And ever bright in splendour shine, And the vast universe beyond, Stupendous power we may divine. There can be no doubt about the magnitude of that Power, for it is a certainty, and I think the gradual evolution of life, the geological condition or formation of the earth and the beauty displayed around and above, and the blessings we possess are a sufficient evidence of the goodness and wisdom of that Power. Perhaps "Inquirer "and others may think this is all supposition, and ask how we know these ideas to be true or aproach- ing the truth, to which I reply that civilized mankind do and must act on the inferences they draw from what they see and know, and that what we call the ideal preceeds and is in advance of the real ; such is in every discovery and advancement the case. The wen of faith and insight get the idea that certain things are or that certain things can be done. Thus Stevenson's idea that steam could be utilized for purposed of locomotion pro- duced the steam engine; his ideas brought about that reality. The conditions were always in nature, but his ideas made those conditions manifest, which before had been discredited by those who prided themselves on practical wisdom. And so It is in the moral world ; those who have a liNlng faith in the justice and benefin- once of nature based upon the facts of life may seem to some to be deluded and deemed by others faithless. But the question is—are the teachings of Theosophy generally true ? Shall the chemical elements though changing form remain the same, and conscious life be blotted from the universe ? Have we no interest in it beyond the hour of death ? Will our conduct continue to influence others when we have ceased to be affected by what we have done? Are the best aspirations of mankind but vain and foolish? Has nature failed in her divinest work? Those who have no faith in nature or to whom her purposes are but little manifest may think there is nought but cruelty in the struggle for existence, and that there is no life beyond the tomb, but Theosophy teaches that there is, and that life is an inestimably blessing, a blessing so great that nature has guarded it, and veiled in dark shadows the angel of death.—Yours Warrington, October, 1891.
S. KENYON.

WARRINGTON PUBLICANS AND THEIR IM- MUNITY FROM CONVICTION. Sir,—The decision in the recent case in which a War- rington publican was charged with supplying beer to a customer after hours was one which was in accordance with theeyidenee ; and the magistrates had no alternative but to come to that conclusion. But the Chief Constable has recently informed the Bench that a wholesale system prevails on the part of local publicans of supplying bottled liquor during illegal hours at night. In this con- nection the question naturally suggests itself—how is it that with this extensive and flagrant defiance of the licens- ing law going on, and considering the large:number of per- sons who must be concerned as principal offenders ad as abetters,there is not some proof furnished by the authori- ties of a determination to put a stop to it. Surely the Warrington police cannot be so far behind those of other towns in point of acuteness and enterprise that they are unable like them to bring some of the delinquents to account if they are only resolved to do so. Why not set the keen Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, who is such an adept at bringing other culprits to account, to try his hand among some of these law-defying publicans? Very few thieves in Warrington escape; why should the publicans enjoy such immunity from punishment for their misdoing,s ? I will not pretend to lay down here all the causes that have conduced to such a condition of things, but it is a notorious fact, that the conviction of publicans in Warrington is a thing almost unknown—a matter almost of antiquated legend. Indeed, I might, without exaggeration, describe Warrington as a publicans' paradise. It is a good moral sign that the authority which plays the part of the St. Peter of this paradise seems determined that no future candidates shall be admitted except on absolute necessity 'for the good of the community. But a publicans -paradise Warrington has become truly, and hence by a, converse necessity, it has to a corresponding extent be- come a hell for its decent inhabitants. I have had many • years' residential experience of the principal city of this • country, and I unhesitatingly say that in three months one may in Warrington see more drunkenness and more of the hardened and flaring iniquity which is its immediate consequence than one will see in a whole year in the metropolis. A local publication recently described Warrington as "a dirty little town without an idea." Had drunken been put after dirty • the description would have been more comprehensive. - It is deplorable to think that such an observation should have to be made by a citizen about his own town ; but ;it is desirable that the unpleasant truth should be told plainly in all its hideousness by temperance reformers— and Ido not mean by these, merely abstainers—both on the platform and in Press. Warrington undoubtedly is drink-cursed and drink-soddon to a degree paralleled in but few towns, and it behoves us to be up and doing to redeem it from this state ofinfamv and degradation, and make its record something that does not shame us daily .but that we can point to without fear of the present in-
THE SHIP CANAL.
MAN KILLED AT NORTON.-INQUEST.

An inquest was held by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, at the Latchford Hospital, on Thursday afternoon,concern- ing the death, on Monday last, at Norton, of Thomas Kirk, engine driver on the Ship Canal, an unmarried man ,aged 34,residing at 6,Leinster-st., Runcorn.—Adam Hampson, of Sheffield, identified the body as that of his brother-n-law, and stated that he had been employed for the last three years on the Ship Canal.—William Cooke, fireman, of 2, Mount-pleasant, Runcorn, said about half- past 2 p.m. on Monday, he was engaged in his duties on an engine which was taking eight trucks of ballast down an incline in the cutting. The deceased was driving the engine. When near the pipe track across the canal, the engine gave a leap and left the rails. It was coming down the incline at the rate of about 15 miles an hour, to get force to go up another incline. The force of the wagons behind the engine, which was a small one,caused it to turn round on its side. It came in contact with the pointsman's cabin, and injured him. The road was in good order. The pointsman, Amos Looney, aged 16, was picked up and taken in an unconscious state to the Canal Company's hospital, at Latchford. Witness did not see what had become of the driver.—Richard Archer, rope runner, said he was getting his dinner on the engine when it was going down the incline, and sud- denly it left the rails, and he jumped off it. Then he saw the engine on its side, and he found the deceased lying on his back amongst a heap of ballast, and quite unconscicus. He was bleeding in the face. Witness extricated him, and lie was placed on an engine and con- veyed to the hospital, witness accompaniyng him, but as soon as he arrived at the hospital he expired. He never uttered a word after being placed on the engine. —Win. Goodwin, foreman platelayer, said the road was in good order, and he was of opinion that the weight of the wagons behind the engine had caused it to leave the rails.—The Coroner said there was no blame attaching to anybody, but he thought there was no necessity for the deceased to go down the incline so fast. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.
FLREVirELL DINNER AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday night about 40 gangers ani foremen employed on the Ship Canal Works in the neighbourhood of Runcorn sat down to dinner at Wilson's Hotel, and passed a pleasant social evening together. The dinner was in honour of Mr. James Mankin, the foreman car- penter, who is about to leave this country for Mexico,to take Charge of a dredger and of the carpentering de- partment of Messrs. Pearson and Sons, of London, who are there constructing a large canal. After the repast, Mr. Wm. Naylor took the chair, and proposed the usual loyal toasts. He then proposed" The guest of the evening —Mr. Mankin," remarking that Mr.Mankin had always acted like a gentleman, and he hoped he would prosper wherever he went.—Mr. D. Kenworthy said Mr.Mankin was an honourable, upright, and straightforward gentleman, and had they had the same class of men all through the canal, the work would 'have gone on much smoother than it had done.—Mr. J. Shelley said Mr. Mankin and he had been shipmates together, and had sailed many seas, and had -weathered many a storm up to the present time. The toast was enthusiastically honoured.—ln reply Mr. Mankin said he had been most happy with the men on the canal, and he thought he had always done his best 'to please the men. If he could not do them a good turn he would not do them an ill turn, and rather than get anyone into trouble he would sooner get into it himself. He felt much gratified that they should give him such an ent3rtainmeot, and if ever he could help any of them heshould only be too glad. (Applause.) He proposed the health of Mr. Shelley, which was heartily drunk.—The Chairman also proposed" Other Sections," coupled with the names of Mr. Kenworthy and Mr. Shelley. The other toasts were "Success to the Ship Canal" and "The town and trade of Runcorn." During the evening a programme of music was gone through, and several selections by the "Big Field Band" were much enjoyed. Mr. J. Ravenscroft was the accompanist and pianoforte soloist.

The Marquis of Bute was on Wednesday afternoon presented with the freedom of the City of Glasgow, and afterwards opened the Mitchell Library. Considerable disturbance took place on Monday at the Carr9n and Hermitage Wharves, Wapping. London, in connection with the strike of carmen and labourers. A reward of 3,000 florins has been offered for the arrest of the miscreant who laid the shells on the bridge near Reichenberg, which were assumed to have been aimed at the life of the Emperor of Austria. It is stated that Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone have accepted. Mr. Lacaita's invitation to occupy his house at Florence during the autum. A correspondent says that Mr. Glad- stone will not leave for the continent until December.

On Wednesday afternoon a bag containing £950 in gold and silver was stolen from the carriage of Mr. William Harris, of the Central Market, London, while that gentleman was talking to his manager in the Silver Grill Restaurant, Strand.

LAWS OF NATURE AND THEISM.

Sir,—lt is not my intention to enter into a discussion with Mr. Peers and his opponents regarding the efficacy or inefficacy of the prayers offered in behalf of the Prince of Wales. Whether the failure is owing to unbelief on the one side, or to the existence of a persistent old Adam on the other, Ido not determine. Such questions I leave to the decision of those who pride themselves on their superior education as being "on a higher standard than that of the Conventicle." In his remarks, Mr. Peers seems to me to deal with far more important and serious questions which affect the very foundations of religion. Mr. Peers tells his oppo nent, he has "forgotten that the reign of Jupiter has given place to the reign of Law," Now, if Mr. Peers means by the "reign of law" the laws of nature taken absolutely by themselves, having no communication with mid, it means absolute fatalism or absolute necessity. But if so, it is absurd to say that the reign of Jupiter has given place to the reign of law, as an absolute neces- sity or fatalism must have existed always. As it is now, so it ever was,and ever shall be. Accordingly,if a reign of Jupiter existed in the past, its very existence must have been due to the reign of law. In reality, however, the reign of Jupiter existed only in the imagination ; and with the advance of knowledge the laws of nature,which existed from the beginnit°eT were better understood. It is curious to find that Mr. Peers should confuse the two cases, that, along with accuracy in our knowledge of nature, there should arise, at the same time, a similar necessity in nature. Such a slip of anthropomorphism on his part can only be regarded as due to ignorance of his own principles. It is in the same spirit as the above that Mr. Peers regards an answer to prayer as rudely breaking the "linked concatenation of nature's laws.r But the laws of nature are of great complexity. The law of gravita- tion is absolutely universal. Not so with the laws of chemistry, which are more selective in their operation and capable of modifying gravitation. In doing so they do not rudely break law, but they introduce a higher stage of law. It is the same with vital laws and also with the laws of mind. They do not rudely break the lower laws, but modify their working to higher ends and purposes. It must not be forgotten that physical and mechanical laws are quite consistent with chaos as has been the case in the primeval fire from which originally s sprung the universe. The origin of an orderly universe from chaos cannot be accounted for by laws of nature taken absolutely, as these are compatible with the con- dition of chaos. This phenomenon, however, must be accounted for so long as man is in possession of a rational faculty; and such the Theist finds in the existence of a Divine Being. Mr. Peers coolly asks his opponent whether he has reflected on the serious consequences which would ensue if the linked concatenation of nature's laws were broken in answer to prayer. Has Mr. Peers, on his part, re- flected on the serious consequences which would ensue if the laws of nature were taken absolutely by themselves havinc, no connection with mind? It would mean that laws of nature having given rise to the reign of Jupiter in the past, would do so in the future. Mr. Peers seems ts forget that laws of nature existed in the past; and whatever they originated in the past they may do so in the future. To this it may oe replied that man has the power of modifying nature. But whatever force this objection possesses arises from the fact that man pos- sesses a free will which is not subject to laws of nature, but is capable of modifying and regulating them. Moreover, if man is completely left to the tender mer- cies of the laws of nature taken absolutely, it shuts out all hope of the future. Injustice, crime' and misery, have reigned in the past, and if these are due to laws of nature, there is no reason why they should no: exist in the future, nor is there any reason on such ground why man should try to ameliorate his condition, and also those of his fellowmen, as the laws of nature cannot be broken, and have existed absolutely in the past, so must they•do in the future. All efforts made for the ameli- oration of humanity can be justified only on reasons which imply free will in man and God in nature. Mr. Peers also says" No logic with which I am ac- quainted countenances any connection between prayer and meteorology." But whether there is or is not a con- nection between the two can be decided scientifically, only by appealing to the methods of science ; that is the methods of inductive or deductive logic. Accordingly, his acquaintance with logic is more conspicuous for its ignorance than anything else. Mr. Peers speaks rather disparagingly of those who , have prayed for the welfare of the Prince of Wales ; and among the choice epithets- which he flings at them' ' occur those of "wind bags" and " silly supplicants,' &c. But surely to one like Mr. Peers whose training and education has been" on a higher standard than that ' of Conventicle" it might have occurred that among them ' there could be„included such men as Canon Liddon, Mr. Spurgeon, Mr./Gladstone, and many others. It is almost needless to say that long before Mr. Peers proves his conclusion he will find that his pluck is far ahead of his science.—Yours, &c.,
GNOSTIC.
