div.head: DEATH OF MR. PARNELL.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. PARNELL.

Mr. Parnell died just before midnight on Tuesday lat his residence near Brighton. Although it was recognised that the stress and strain of recent inci- dents had tended to weaken his aonstitution, and 1 to unfit him for the shock of a severe illness, it was not generally known that he had been confined to his house. This was not a matterof surprise, inas- much as Mr. Parnell's residence is, for practical purposes, as far removed from the centre of Brigh- ton as if it were twenty or thirty miles away. It is in the vicinity of the house in which Mrs. Parnell stayed for some time before being divorced from Captain O'Shea, but it lies further westward. Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea, as she then was, after- wards lived next door to each othex in Walsingham Terrace, one at number nine and the other at num- ber ten. It was from Walsingham-terrace that they set forthto go to Steyning to be married. Since that event Mr. Parnell and his wife had retained inssession of both houses which were used together. It was in the bedroom on the first floor, that Mr. Parnell died during a night of storm and rain. Throughout Wednesday a constant stream of news- paper representatives visited the, house; but the servants either knew little of the circumstances attending their master's death, or had received instructions to say nothing. Mrs. Parnell had given directions that she was not to be called upon to see visitors under any conditions whatever, and it was stated that she was so utterly prostrated by the shock that, even had she wished to communicate anything, it was doubtful whether she was in a fit state to be spoken to. The only other person in the house besides the female servants was one of Mrs. Parnell's daughters. That lady also declined te be seen.

Mr. Parnell returned to Brighton from Ireland on the Thursday of last week, coming from the station alone, and being received at his house by Mrs. Parnell and the daughter who was staying with her. Even then he was not at all well, and com- plained of suffering from a chill. Next day he ap- peared to be worse, and it was deemed advisable , that he should remain in bed. He became gradually worse, and on Sunday Dr. Jowers was sent for and attended him. Mr. Parnell was then suffering from acute rheumatism and congestion of the lungs, his illness being attended with intense pain. He was indeed completelyprostrated. His condition showed no improvement on Monday, and hr. Jowers, as well as his son, was in constant attendance, but without being able to afford the patient much re- lief. On Tuesday he again passed a day of severe pain,and towards the evening reached a state of snch collapse as, it is believed, to lose conscious- ness. The medical men were summoned about seven o'clock, and on reaching the house something like an hour later found Mr. Parnell to be in a con- dition ot extreme exhaustion. Every effort was made to give him relief from pain, the doctors being assisted by Mrs. Parnell, who throughout the illness had nursed him with unremitting attention. Death ensued about half an hour before midnight. The progress of Mr. Parnell's illness had been so rapid that no relatives had been notified of his condition, nor, indeed, was it suspected that the end was so near, consequently Mrs. Parnell was, with the ex- ception of Dr. Jowers, alone with her husband when he breathed his last. Mrs. Parnell and her daughter were alone in the house on Wednesday. Telegraphing later, a correspondent adds: On making further inquiries at Mr. Parnell's house at a late hour on Wednesday night, I was informed that Mrs. Parnell was still too much overcome to see any visitors, and Miss O'Shea also declined to see any one or give information, and that neither of them had received any visits during the day ex- cept from the medical man. I asked whether there was any foundation for the rumours that had been in circulation to the effect that Mr. Parnell's death had been accelerated by an act of his owa. The housekeeper said the rumours had reached the house, but they were absolutely false. She had Miss O'Shea's authority to give them an unqualified contradiction, besides which she was in the room at the time Mr. Parnell died, and could contradict the statements from her own knowledge. Mr. Parnell was born at Avondale, county Wick- low, in 1846. He has descended from an old Eng- lish family that passed over from Congleton, Cheshire, to Ireland, and many of his ancestors have played prominent parts in history. Thomas Parnell, the poet, was one of the family. Mr. Par- nell's mother is the daughter of Admiral Charles Stewart, a celebrated American naval officer. Mr. Parnell was educated at various private schools in England, and at Magdalen College, Cambridge. Ile was first returned to Parliament for the county of Meath, after having fought an unsuccessful contest in the county of Dublin.

div.head: REMAINS TO BE BURIED IN IRELAND.
div.p: THE REMAINS TO BE BURIED IN IRELAND.

A deputation of Parnellite members, including Messrs. John Redmond, Pierce Mahony, John Nolan, and John O'Connor, attended at Mr. Parnell's house on Thursday, and received from Dr. Jewers, jun., the official statement of the cause of Mr. Parnell's death. This was declared to have arisen from an attack of rheumatic fever.accom- panied by excessively high temperature, which induced failure of the heart's action. The death was perfectly natural. Mr. Parnell had a brief interval of conscious- ness just before death, and almost his last words ware, "Let my love be conveyed to my colleagues and to the Irish people." When this affecting message was con- veyed to his colleagues it moved them to tears. The deputation then passed a resolution ex- pressing deep sorrow at the demise of their chief, and heartfelt sympathy with Mrs. Parnell. Mrs. Parnell was unable to see them, but her daughter was present, and acted as the medium of communication. An earnest representation was made to the bereaved widow to assent to a public funeral in Ireland, and after some pressure the wish was acceded to. The funeral will take place either at Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin, or at Mr. Parnell's family burying place in county Wicklow, and communications are in progress with Dublin making arrangements. Mrs. Parnell was on Thursday joined by Mrs. Dickin- son, Mr. Parnell's sister, and by Mrs. Pierce Mahony, who travelled from Avondale on Wednesday night. Mr. Parnell's colleagues are terribly shocked by the loss of their loader, and decline, at present, to consider what the effects will be en their party, or on the Home Rule question. The" Dublin Evening Telegraph "states that Mr. Par- nell's funeral will take place on Sunday in Glasnevin Cemetery, Dublin, and will be public. The body was on Thursday evening enclosed in a shell. One of Mr. Parnell's most devoted followers ex- pressed his satisfaction at the fact that many of those who recently had been so sharply divided from the hon. member for Cork had sunk all differencbs and had joined sincerely in the universal expressions of sorrow at an un- timely and unlooked-for death, and had shown a ready appreciation of the great services which Mr. Parnell had rendered to their country under .circumstances of un- precedented difficulty.
DUBLIN CITY COUNCIL AND THE LATE LEADER.
- At a special,meeting of the Municipal, Corporation, of Dublin the fcllowing resolutions were adopted unani-

mously :—" That the Municipal Council express theii- ' heartfelt sorrow at the death of Charles Stewart Paznell, for se many years the leader of the Irish people, to whom he rendered untold services, and we tender to his family our sincere sympathy in their affliction." " That as a mark of respect for the memory of Charles Stewart Parnell, in the event ef the funeral being a public one,. the Corporatien of Dublin) do take part in it in state, AO d that the Lord Mayor or his locum tenens be empowered to make the necessary arrangements."

div.head: DEATEI OF SIR. JOHN POPE-HENNESSY,
div.p: DEATEI OF SIR. JOHN POPE-HENNESSY,
M.P.

The death occurred on Wednesday morning, at Rostel- lan Castle, Cloyle, of Sir John Pope-Hennessy, K.C.M.G., Knight of MaIta,F.R.A.S.,F.G.S,M.P.for North Kilkenny. He was born at Cork in M 34. Mr. Hennessy was edu- cated at Queen's College, Cork, and in 1861 was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple. He was already a member of the House of Commons, having been elected in 18. Ea as the representative of King's County,which he repre- sented until 1865. His course in Parliament was one of some independence, and, was not always easy to square by the party lines then existing. A lengthy colonial career began by his appointment in 1867 as Governor of Labuan ; he was successively appointed Governor of the West African Settlemente.in 1872,0 f the Bahamas in 1873, of the Windward Isles in 187511, of Hong Kong in 1877, and cE Mauritius in December 18E2. The last gres,t event in his varied career was in December, 1890, wheto he contested North Kilkenny under remarkable circumstances. The seat was vacant by the death of Mr. E. P. M. Marum' who in 1886 was returned unopposed,.aad in 1885 had 4,084 votes to his Tory opponent's 174. Sir John was in the first instance the nominee of Mr. Parnell, but after the exposure in the Divorce Court he declared against the deposed chief, and stood as the candidate of the Irish Parliamentary party. Mr. Vincent Scully was then brought forward by the Parnellites. The contest was everywhere re- garded as a test of the strength of the two parties. Mr. Parnell and Mr. Davitt both took part in the struggle, and in the excitement of the election both were injured. The result of the poll was decisive. Mr. Scully received 1,356 votes and Sir John Pope-Hennessy 2,527,'. He has not lived to enjoy, except for a very brief period, his return to the House of Commons, from wWcia he had been absent for about a quarter of a century.

div.head: PROSECUTION OF ANOTAER PUBLICAN. I
div.p: PROSECUTION OF ANOTAER PUBLICAN. I

At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Sutton, Major Pickmere, Councillor James Fairclough and Captain Ridgway, John liiddle, licensee of the King's Arms, public-house, was charged with allowing his house, on the 19th ult.,and divers other dates to be the habitual resort of reputed immoral women and also with allowing them to remain longer than n3cassary for rea- sonable refreshment. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle ap- peared for the prosecution and Mr. Mulhol- land, barrister, of Liverpool, instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw, for the de- fence. Mr. Whittle in his opening statement said he believed there had been no previous complaint against Liddle since 1885. On several occasions women well-known to be of bad character had frequented th 9 house, and they remained longer than necessary.—P.C. Bell said on the 119th ult., about 20 minutes past seven, he saw Elizabeth Allen Fleming and Annie Daley, two women of bad character with several convicted thieves there. The women left the house at 10 minutes past 8, and remained tilll a quarter to 11. Ile and Inspectors Spinks and Bowen then went into the house and saw Fleming and two Annie Daleys.—The Chief Constable said though there had been no case against the defendant since 1885 there had been plenty of complaints.—Mr. Mulholland : Well now, we don't want you. Go into the box if you want to give evidence.—P.C. Bell, cross-examined, by Mr. Mulholland,said he never heard of the defendant be- ing complimented by the bench 12 months ago for prose- cuting immoral women. A woman of immoral character was turned out on the night in question because it I was 11. o'clock. That night he saw Liddle's son strike a man who had been annoyed at being turned out for immoral conduct with a woman on the premises. The man admitted to witness that he had been put out for such conduct.—lnspectors Bowen, Cox and Spinks gave corroborative evidence, the last-named also deposing to there being,six immoral women and three convicted thieves in the house on the night of the 17th.—Mr. Mulholland described the case as a most monstrous one, and charac- terised the statement that his client had been previously complained of as a lie. The defendant had hadan oxcel- lent character and turned bad characters out of his house on the night of the 19th. Hehad been complimented by the Bench for keeping his house clear of these bad charac- ters. He reviewed the evidence, and urged that there was no proof of the charge.—The defeadant was sworn and said he had kept the Borough Arms, Grappenhall, three years before coming to his present house, and pre- vious to that held an outdoor license for four years. There had never been any complaint or charge against him. He denied that any women of bad character known to ' him had been allowed to remain unnecessarily long in the house. He denied knowing any of the women, till the police on the night of the 19th, pointed them out. He was out the chief part of the evening. He never allowed them to be in more than ten minutes. He put out the man and woman who had been mentioned for suspicous conduct.—Mr.Mulholland said the Recorder of Liverpool had ruled that half-an-hour was not an un- reasonable time.—The defendant's daughter and son gave evidence.:She stated that defendant had instructed her not to serve such women, or if she did, not to allow Clem to stay, and the son said he had been instructed not to serve women of bad character with more than one glass. The son detailed, the puttino, out of a maa for immoral conduct.—Messrs. Morse, 'G. Buckley, and Rogers gave the house an excellent character. The Bench considered the case privately for a short time, arid on their return the Chairman intimated that though the case was one of grave suspiction, yet from Liddle's character and conduct to women of loose character coming to his house, and the evidence being not conclusive they would dismiss the case. The Chairman, however, cautioned the defendant, and declared the police justified in their action.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.—The classes in 2nd grade drawing, mathematics, machine construction and draw- ing and mechanical engineering formed by the Prescot Local Board committee have commenced this week. The classes for mathematics, freehandldrawing,and machine construction and drawing were made,the requisite num- ber of students (12) having joined. There were present at the opening Messrs. W. Goldworth, D. F. Roberts, W. L. Hindley, T. P. Hewitt, C. J. Hewitt, and H. Cross, the secretary. HARVEST FESTIVAL—The harvest festival services in connection with the Prescot Parish Church, commenced on Thursday evening, the Ist inst., there being a very large congregation. The collections amounted to £5 3s. 9d. The church was tastefully decorated by the 'ladies of the congregation. The preacher for the even- ing, the Rev. Canon Honeyborne, of St. PhiLimon's, Liverpool, preached an excellent sermon. The services were continued the following Sunday, the preacher, morning and evening being the Rev. P. H. Neale, chaplain to the Croydon Infirmary. In the afternoon a ohildren's service was conducted by Assistant Fell, chaplain to the Seamen's Home.l
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Captain LeCouteur of Runcorn, has been ap- pointed secretary and manager to the Weston Point Steam Towing Company in succession to Cap- tain Whitfield, who has accepted a post under the Ship Canal Company.

The dispute between the Frodsham gas inspectors and the Gas Company has been settled by a com- promise, and the street lamps have been lit during the present week. The company have undertaken to pay three-fourths of the cost of laying the new pipes and the township will bear the burden of the remaining fourth.

In this month's Parish Magazine Canon Wood says the Runcorn Extension Lectures have caught the " Runcorn disease" severely, and adds that it is possible they may survive the crisis. I suppose the vicar means that after two years' lectures the public interest in the University Extension move- ment is on the wane, and the nerTssary funds are not forthcoming. It is Runcorn's failing to take up a project with enthusiasm, and after a very brief experience to drop it, just as coldly, but I am glad to record that the ' disease" has not resulted in the total extinction of the lectures, The Rev.. Hudson Shaw, M.A., has been engaged to deliver a course of lectures early in the new year, and the immense popularity he gained two years ago should ensure the success of the course.

In connection with Halton Park Church schools; a science and art class for the study of the scitnce of agriculture has been formed. This is a most suitable subject for the district, and the farmers'. sons in the district should be eager to take advan- tage of the opportunity of widening their know- ledge on their most important calling.

Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, sen., has offered to provideH the township of Woolton with baths if the Localli Board will find a site and maintain the baths when erected. His generous offer has not yet elicited a. reply. It may not be generally known that some years ago Mr. Gaskell offered the Widnes Baths to the Widnes Local Board on condition that they bought the silo and maintained the baths. The Local Board of that day refused to accept on these canditione,and 1 befieve that Mr. Gaskell is now reaping a profit from the concern. I wonder what be would the answer of the present Board if Mr. Gaskell repeated his offer..

The Runcorn District Nurse Fund is in a flourish- ing condition. l'he number of subscribers has in- creased in, proportion, and the Committee were able to finish the years'S work with a balance in hand of over £299... Of this sum it has been decided to in- vest £275, which it is doubtless hoped will form a nucleus for the permanent endowment of the insti- tution. Nurse Evans- has had a very bnsy twelve months, having paid no itewer than 4,048 visits, being an increase of 1,2960ver the previous year.

For years Fbadsham has been greatly in need of an- efficient supply of water, and no less than four- teen schemes have been propounded for attaining the desired end but without success_ The last pro- posal is made by Messrs,. Timmins of Runcorn, who have bad great experience ia providing works of water supply and the Frodshatn Parochial Com- mittee have decided that as there is an abundant supply of water and the scheme is practicable, and cheap, to carry it out subject to the-approval of the Local Government Board. Mr.J. Edwards has differ- ent views on the subject,. and contends that it is an expensive and inconaprehensiblescheme,and that the ratepayers of the township are- opposed to it. By strenuous opposition at the meetings of the Guardians and the Union,. Mr. Edwards has delayed the carrying out of the project, and he caused a further delay by. his action, at the Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday last.

Mr:Edwards is never tired of reiterating that the ratepayers are "dead against '' the scheme, but he as yet has produced nothing in support of his opinion. I would remind him that at a meeting of ratepayers a month ago, called through his instru= mentality, a motion was made and seconded and

duly put to the meeting, rescinding this scheme and that not one hand was held up in its favour. The wish of the ratepayerstai there expressed, was that the carrying out of the scheme should be deferred until a water district is formed, the reason being that the incid of the rating will fall very un- equally and very unjustly on severa/ persons in / township. From a letter read on Tuesday, it is quite certain the Local Government Board will not sanction the formation of such a district, and the sooner the Authority set abcout carrying out the scheme approved by the representatives of Frod- sham the better. The present condition of the water supply in the township is a standing dis- grace. Mr. Edwards can lay before the Government Inspector his alternative scheme of obtaining water from the Vyrnwy mains, which does not possess the advantages of Messrs. Timmins', and according to his own showing is little less expensive than Messrs. Timmins' scheme.

Mr. John Aldren Wright 8.A., son of Mr. T. Wright, of Halton, has been successful in obtaining a University scholarship of 50 guineas, at the recent competition at St. Mary's Hospital, London.
A. LATCHFORD BAKER PROSECUTED FOR SUNDAY BAKING.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tnesday, before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), and E. J. Guest, Mr. Jenkins said he was instructed by the Amalgamated Society of Operative Bakers and Confectioners of Great Britain and Ireland to apply for a summons against Jas. Strange, baker, St. James's-st., Latchford, on the charge that he on Sunday October 4th, contravened a statute of William IV, which provided that no baker should after one o'clock on Sunday make or bake bread or cakes of any sort or sell or expose for sale or deliver any bread or cakes or in any mariner exercise his callirw, except setting the dough for baking. Mr. Strange had been exercising his calling as a baker on the Sunday in question, by preparing his dough beyond the point Pre- scribed by the Act. The members of the Society were determined to try to put down such a practice. because it was a very gross breach of the law and prevented other bakers from having fair p'av, as instead of being able to go to church or chapel if they liked they were compelled to work instead.—The Chairman: Why don't you take a summons out in the ordinary course P—Mr. , Jenkins: It is a place convenient where the magistrates ; are sitting. It saves the tronble of going about search- ' ing for magistrates. It is not an unusual thing to apply here in a prosecution of this kind. It is constantly done in the London Courts and others.—The Chairman: Personalty I have no sympathy whatever with Sunday labour of any sort, but it does seem to me an anomal- ous state of the law that while public houses are open a good part of Sunday we should make an exception of that which is a sort of necessary in life. At the same time as the law is as it is one can do nothing else but grant a summons.—Mr. Jenkins: Of course we have not to make the laws.—Mr. Guest: I have sympathy with a prosecution of this sort.—The application was acceded to.

The case came on yesterday before Mr. John White (chairman), Aldermen Harrison and Greenall, and Dr. White. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the prosecuticn and Mr. Browne for the defence. Several members of the Bakers' and Confectioners' Society, including Jas. Lee, 9, Dudley-st., David Hewitt, 62, Winwick-st., John Greely, who had laid the information, H. Granger, and James Houghton gave evidence. Most of these witnesses had from a shed near the defendant's bakehouse, in St. James's-st., seen the men making bread, on Sunday evening, Octo- ber 4th, the defendant himself not being there. They stated that the object of proceeding was to prevent other employers working their men on Sunday. Greeley said the defendant's object would be to get his bread sup- plied before the other bakers on Monday. It was denied that the proceedings were taken out of spite.—Mr. Browne said the statute under which proceedings were taken was passed in 1836, and for a number of years had never been acted !upon, because the common-sense Englishmen had come round to the recognition that if a thing was necessary on Sunday it must be done. The statute was a penal one, and therefore Mr. Strange could not be summoned for the doings of his men any more than a master could be summoned for an assault by a servant. He argued that the statute made the master liable only in case of his being himself engaged in the act of bak- ing ; and that the men, and not he, ought to have been summoned.—Mr. Jenkins maintained that Mr. Browne's defence was ingenious but untenable, and said the master had been attacked as the fountain head, the men not being to blame.—Alderman Harrison said as the prosecution was admittedly brought for mere trade pur- pz.ses and not to enforce the observance of the Lord's Day, the motives were selfish, and not to be commended. —Mr, Jenkins said that was one element in the matter, and thought if his clients had stated the other reason the Bench would have considered it sentimental.—The Bench without retiring dismissed the case on the grounds urged by Mr. Browne. He then applied for costs assert- ing that his client had been maliciously dealt with and had not consented to his men working on Sunday, The application was not acceded to.
A boy named Goulding was killed at Stoneclough, near Bolton, on Wednesday, by falling into a vat of br,l'ing chemicals.

div.head: TEMPERANCE CRUSADE STi' HELENS.
div.p: THE TEMPERANCE CRUSADE STi' HELENS.
THE MINISTER", AND 'THE PUBLICA-SCENIVIN COURT.

One of the most important licensing !cases ever heard in St. -Helens was decided at the local ponce court on Friday.- Mr. John Marsh, landlord of Sefton Arms flotet„ Ormskirk-st.,was s-Anmoned,for supplying drink to,a drunken man, and as the rze-- ceedings were instituted by the Rev.R..T.Ward, gregational minister, great public interest- was CX./. cited. The couct room was packed. Many-publicans were present, and several clergymen and Ministers - also attended. Me. J. C. Eccles appeared on behalf' of the Rev. R. G. Ward,and Mr. J. 0. Swilt'defended' Mr. Marsh. The magistrates on the bench' were. Colonel W. W. Pilkington,Dr. Gaskell,MrtAATalmo4 ley:Cotham, and Mr. A. Sinclair. _ . _

Mr. Eccles remarked that it was usual for such eases ter be commenced by the police a uthorities,but heknew of no reason why private individuals should not take. the steps Mr. Ward had done: The circumstances in last week' Examiner were that on the previous Tuesday the Rev,: Mr. Ward saw two men in the street, one of whom wao-, drunk, reeling from one side of the footpath tothe other._ They entered the Sefton Arms, and were followed by, Mr. Ward. He found them in a room with drink •13e- fore them, and at hie instance the drink was removed; and they were asked to leave. Mr. Eccles asked the bench to consider Mr. Ward's position in the town for so many yeaß7anu-ne•-• theught they would have no diffi- culty in coming to the conclusion that Mr., Mbireh swas guilty of the charge laid against him. The Rev. Mr. Ward then entered the witrtess-bwr amid some hissing. He-gave evidence in accordance with the statement already published, and -in answerto Mr. Eccles as to the-condition of the man supposed to be drunk when supplied with beer, Mr. Ward said he was very palpably drunk.,--Mr. Swift: We all know you are, an absolute teetotaller ?:Pinsecutor (after a pause) `: -Am. I compelled to answenthat question P—Mr. Swift : Yes you are compelled to answer every question I :put to. you, unless it is grossly! insulting.—Prosecutor • lam a citizen of St. Helens—Mr. Swift: Come to convict a. publician, if pcssible,,we all know; but you are.' also sworn to give evidence; and subject, I anticipate to • the- ordinary law. The question I ask is—are you a teetotal- ler? Prosecutor: I am.—Mr. Swift: Holding very strong views with regard to the evil wrought by pubirio• houses and drink P—Prosecutor Yes.—Mr. Swift: -And during the last few weeks have you been making .a sys- tematic examination of public houses—watching them ?- Prosecutor: Yes ; some of them.—Mr. Swift : - And practically acting to the full as an amateur detective -P Prosecutor: Tam acting now not as a tninisteri•not* as a teetotallar, but as a citizen. In regard to the prosecutor waiting for a few minutes outside the Seftoni Armesbe,fore• following the men into the house, Mr.- Swift asked if it would not have beemmore consistent-with hiSprofdssion, if he had attempted to prevent the commission of any- offence.—Prosecutor think I may be allowed to-jildke- of what my profession allows me.—Mt. Swift : would be a very horrible thing for a drunken man to• take more drink from your point of view ? Prbsectitor :- It would be a crirel.- thing to give it to him.—Mh.Stvift and would it be a cruel thing to allow a man to take it when you can prevent it? Prosecutor did not reply:— In answer to questions he admitted that Miss MarslC who had served the drink, said she did not -notice that the man was drunk.—Mr. Swift: Were you excited Pro- Secutor : No. (Laughter.) NO more than lam -now.— Mr. Swift: I hope there will be no more laughing in court. I feel, honestly, that this is,a very unpleasant task, and certainly I don't want to put to Mt: Ward anything offensive.—Prosecutor : Thank you :• P appre- ciate that.—John Littler, of Billinge, who appeared on a subpcena, said he met a friend whose • name he did not know, and after having • two drinks at the Black e Bull, they visited the • Sefton Arms. Mr. Ward followed them in. He denied, that his companion was drunk+ but he naturally leaned to one side, and could not walk- straight. Mr. Swift then addressed the court on behalf of the de- fendant. He did not attempt to denythat Mr.lirard and the men acting with him in that crusade were actuated by good motives, but, however good-the enda were, cer- tainly they were not wise. Police-officers- were by law given an oversight of licensed houses, and Mr. Ward had no more right to enter a public-house upon such an errand than he had to enter his (Mr. Swift's), office when he knew. he was not wanted. If the gentlemen. with Mr. Ward, instead of trying to catch publicans,,would strive to reclaim sinners they would find their efforts more ap- preciated by the people.. Mr. Marsh,had kept the house without complaint for 16 , years, and had had another house at Billinge for five years. His character was of as much consequence to him as was the character of Mr. Ward to that gentleman.. Mr. Ward' and his friends in- stead of playing the role of public-house-detectives, would be mere consistent with their Christrianprofession if they- tried to prevent a drunken man getting drunk.—Mr.. Swift submitted that there was no, corm Jorat;on of Mr. Ward's evidence of drunkenness.—After a number oil witnesses had been called for the defence, the Benoit after five minutes' absence,, fined. the defendant £2 and costs, and unanimously and highly commended Mr. Wand for his action. The decision was' fellowed by loud hiss- ing which being continued despite the Chairman's objec- tion, the police wererequestedta take the names and-ad- dresses of the hissers. As Mr. Ward and his friends quitted the court there were-cries of" Make wayAor the Christians."

At a temperance meeting,. on Monday night,, in the Brook-street Assembly-room,. the Rev. R. W. Ayres, Baptist minister, proposed the following resoltitiou : "That this meetings, having heard of the nobleelforts put forward by the Rev: Robert John War& sincerely sympathises with him,, and wishes him God speed in the work he has undertaken, and hereby pledgte itself to do all it porsibly can to stand by him in the future." Mr. William Dixon seconded.—The Rev. A. G. Bridge replied to the arguments of the solicitor for the.defence and urged that inendeavouring to convict:offending publicans and reduce the number of public-houses they were endeavouring to reclaim sinners.—The resolution was carried unanimously..—The Rev, R. J. Ward, who was received with loud applause, repudiated the charge that he had any animosity against publicans personally, his only object being to try and save poor drunkards. (Applause.)

Mr. S.. Bbighouse, county coroner;.held+ an inquest at:the Parade Room, Police Station, on. Saturday, touching the death of Annie Slater,- wife of John Slater, bricksetter.—The husband said that for the Jest' fourteen,days his wife had been comastantly :under the infruence of drink. On Friday morn- :ing; he went out to work at half-past eight, and left his-wife in bed. He did n sasee irer alive ;again.—A neighbour, named Mrs.: Birchall, said that she called to see the deceased on business, and ;went upstairs and knocked at the bedroom door. Stip received no answer, and so she opened the door f and saw the deceased suspended from a bed-post by a handkerchief. Witness informed P.S. Row. •betham, who cut the deceased down.. Life was ,emtinct. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide while temporarily insane."

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 19th day of October next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 19th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester, on THURSDAY, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton,Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 29th September, 1891.
